Because of its potential medical significance, the KP has received increasing attention. The first and committing enzymes, tryptophan and indolamine dioxygenase, are active drug targets with inhibitors in clinical trials (5, 7, 8).

Recently, a downstream enzyme of the KP (Scheme 1), 2-amino-3-carboxymuconate-6-semialdehyde decarboxylase (ACMSD), has received attention as a potential drug target (6). Inhibition of ACMSD has been shown to slow down the reaction competing with QA formation and boost cellular NAD(H) levels (9).

To date, the KP pathway genes and their corresponding enzymes have not been identified beyond ACMSD (10, 11), although the metabolic pathway was published 53 years ago and has made its way into numerous biochemistry textbooks. One limiting factor for studying KP enzymes is that the identification of their mammalian genes has proved difficult. Initial characterization of the KP enzymes was performed from animal liver extracts (1). Although these studies verified the activities and transformations of the KP, they were unable to provide much insight into the individual enzyme structures and mechanisms. Study of the KP enzymes stagnated until the discovery of an analogous KP in some bacteria (12–17) and that 2-nitrobenzoate biodegradation shares many of the downstream proteins with the eukaryotic kynurenine pathway (18–20). An additional difficulty for studying the KP enzymes, especially downstream proteins, is that several of the metabolic intermediates of the pathway are unstable and commercially unavailable.

As shown in Scheme 1, the substrates for ACMSD and its downstream neighbor, 2-aminomuconate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (AMSDH), are both unstable and spontaneously cyclize via a pericyclic reaction to their respective pyridine products, QA and picolinic acid (PA) (2).

Despite the difficulties mentioned above, much progress has been made in understanding the mechanisms of KP enzymes. Recently, AMSDH from Pseudomonas fluorescens (pfAMSDH) identified from the 2-nitrobenzoate biodegradation pathway has been studied at the molecular level. Crystal structures of the resting enzyme, NAD+-bound complex, ternary complex, catalytic thioacyl and thiohemiacetal intermediates, and several mutants have been reported (21). A hidden isomerase activity of AMSDH has also been uncovered (22). Furthermore, the study of pfAMSDH revealed that, in addition to active-site residues that are broadly conserved across all aldehyde dehydrogenases, the hydroxymuconate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (HMSDH) family possesses two conserved arginine residues that are involved in substrate recognition and an isomerization activity (22).

In this work, we have identified a human enzyme annotated as a retinal dehydrogenase (ALDH8A1) that carries the hallmarks of an aminomuconate semialdehyde dehydrogenase. An overexpression system was constructed, and recombinant ALDH8A1 was tested for activity with two muconic semialdehyde substrates.

The activity of selected active-site variants was also investigated, and the reaction products were verified with NMR and high-resolution MS. All evidence suggests that ALDH8A1 should be reconsidered as the aldehyde dehydrogenase of the kynurenine pathway of tryptophan catabolism.

Results and discussion
Identification of ALDH8A1 as a potential member of the kynurenine pathway
To continue studying the KP pathway at the molecular level, the next pressing step is to identify a mammalian AMSDH, especially the human version. We performed a BLAST search with pfAMSDH as the search sequence. The results revealed a human protein, ALDH8A1 (initially designated ALDH12), with 44% amino acid sequence identity to pfAMSDH. However, ALDH8A1 is currently annotated in the NCBI gene database as a retinal dehydrogenase. It was assigned as cis-retinal dehydrogenase based on its ability to oxidize 9-cis-retinal faster than all-trans-retinal, even though it was most active with benzaldehyde rather than the retinal substrates (23). It was also noted in the original characterization that ALDH8A1 shares the closest nucleotide and protein sequence similarity with AMSDH, but it was not tested for such activity, presumably due to difficulty obtaining 2-aminomuconate semialdehyde (2-AMS).

Here, we present evidence that ALDH8A1 may be more appropriately considered human AMSDH of the KP. AMSDH belongs to the HMSDH family. Our alignment of ALDH8A1 against AMSDH and several members of the HMSDH family showed not only high overall conservation but also that, in addition to residues required for aldehyde dehydrogenase activity (Asn-155, Glu-253, and Cys-287), residues responsible for substrate recognition only in HMSDH enzymes are conserved in ALDH8A1, namely Arg-109 and Arg-451 (Fig. 1, generated with ESPript (24)).

A homology structure model of ALDH8A1 was built using the iTASSER server (25). An overlay of the homology model and pfAMSDH is shown in Fig. 2A. The model shows full coverage of the human enzyme sequence, which overlays well with the bacterial enzyme with a root mean square deviation of 1.15 Å for 472 C-α carbons. In addition, all of the catalytically essential active-site residues from pfAMSDH (Arg-109, Asn-155, Glu-253, Cys-287, and Arg-451 by ALDH8A1 numbering) are in the same location in the homology model as in the pfAMSDH structure (Fig.

2B).

ALDH8A1 can perform the NAD+-dependent oxidation of 2-aminomuconic semialdehyde
The next question to arise was whether ALDH8A1 is able to catalyze the NAD+-dependent oxidation of 2-AMS to 2-aminomuconate (2-AM). Pursuant to this end, an overexpression system was generated. The synthesized gene for human ALDH8A1 was ligated into pET-28a(+) vector with a cleavable N-terminal His6 tag and transformed into Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. The expressed protein was purified by nickel affinity chromatography (Fig. 3A), and its ability to oxidize 2-AMS in a coupled-enzyme assay with ACMSD was tested. As shown in Fig. 3B, ACMS has a broad absorbance band at 360 nm. Upon ACMSD-catalyzed decarboxylation to 2-AMS, the absorbance maximum red-shifted to 380 nm and then decayed as 2-AMS was nonenzymatically converted to PA. The inclusion of purified ALDH8A1 and 1 mm NAD+ in an otherwise identical assay prevented the red shift, and instead, a broad absorbance band around 350 nm was observed that has been previously assigned as the oxidized product, 2-AM, and NADH (Fig. 3C) according to the reaction scheme shown in Fig. 3D. These results resemble those observed from pfAMSDH and show that ALDH8A1 is able to rapidly oxidize 2-AMS in solution.

The presence of the expected product in the coupled-enzyme assay was also verified by NMR spectroscopy. As shown in Fig. 4, the reaction mixture contained resonances consistent with 2-AM and expected cross-peaks in the 1H-1H COSY spectrum to show connectivity. Proton resonances were assigned based on similarity with 2-hydroxymuconic acid, which has been rigorously characterized (26).

Characterization of the reaction product of the ALDH8A1-catalyzed reaction
In initial studies of AMSDH, the identity of the product was inferred based on knowledge of the substrate structure and the catalytic cycle of the dehydrogenation reaction. The in crystallo characterization of the AMSDH reaction revealed that, in addition to oxidation of the aldehyde to its corresponding carboxylic acid, pfAMSDH also isomerizes the 2,3-double bond inside the active site prior to substrate oxidation (22). In the process of trying to determine the conformation of the product of the reaction catalyzed by ALDH8A1, we noticed that the product, 2-AM (λmax 330 nm), is unstable and is nonenzymatically bleached in a single kinetic phase with a half-life of 67 min (Fig. 5A). High-resolution mass spectra were acquired of the 2-AM decay product after purification by HPLC.

Mass spectra were collected in negative mode, and as shown in Fig. 5B, the parent ion matches tautomerized hydroxymuconate, 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate, with 2.55-ppm mass accuracy. Furthermore, fragment ions from cleaving at either side of the keto group can be observed with nominal masses of 113 and 85 Da.

The downstream enzyme of AMSDH performs deamination on 2-AM to produce 2-hydroxymuconate, which is expected to tautomerize to its α,β-unsaturated ketone form, 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate, as shown in Scheme 2. The deamination reaction is not known to be coupled to any other reaction, so it is expected to be thermodynamically preferred. As such, it may proceed nonenzymatically at a slower rate. To lend credence to the proposed nonenzymatic deamination followed by tautomerization, ACMSD–AMSDH coupled-enzyme assays were performed in H2O and D2O in separate experiments, and the reaction products were monitored by NMR spectroscopy (Fig. 6). When performing the reaction in H2O (Fig. 6A), two doublets around 5.8 ppm and a doublet of doublets at 7.15 ppm can be observed to decay while a new doublet at 6.17 ppm and a doublet of triplets at 6.9 ppm arise. These new resonances are consistent with 2-oxohexenedioate observed in the study of 2-hydroxymuconate tautomerization (26).

Alternatively, upon enzymatic decarboxylation and oxidation performed in D2O by ACMSD and AMSDH, respectively, the 1H NMR spectrum shows two doublets at 7.1 and 5.8 ppm, corresponding to the protons on carbons 4 and 5 (Hb and Hc) of 2-AM, respectively (Fig. 6B). The proton at the 3-position (Ha) is replaced with deuterium by running the ACMSD reaction in D2O (Scheme 3). The two doublets coalesce into a single resonance at 6.9 ppm over time. The decay of the resonance at 5.8 ppm indicates that the proton at the 5-position can eventually exchange with solvent, and the shift of the doublet at 7.1 to a singlet at 6.9 ppm implies that a chemical change takes place in addition to simple exchanging of protons for deuterons. The most likely candidate for such a chemical change is the replacement of the nitrogen at the 2-position with oxygen derived from water, i.e. deamination of 2-AM.

Thus, the NMR spectra of the initial and final products of the ALDH8A1 reaction are consistent with 2-AM being the initially formed product, which then spontaneously deaminates and tautomerizes.

Determination of the kinetic parameters of ALDH8A1 and selected site-directed mutants
Although the coupled-enzyme assays presented above show that 2-AMS can serve as a substrate for ALDH8A1, such experiments are not amenable to extraction of enzymatic kinetic parameters. Instead, a substrate analog, 2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde (2-HMS), in which the amino group of 2-AMS has been replaced with a hydroxyl group to prevent the nonenzymatic cyclization reaction, is used to determine kinetic parameters. The 1H NMR spectrum of 2-HMS can be found in Fig. 7 along with corresponding 1D NOESY spectra, which show not only through-space interactions between protons but also in-phase resonances for the enol tautomer, which was previously implicated as an intermediate in the 2,3-bond isomerization reaction. The observation of resonances consistent with the enol form of 2-HMS in solution lends credence to the previously proposed tautomerization mechanism in pfAMSDH by showing that the enol form is energetically accessible. ALDH8A1 exhibits typical steady-state kinetics when acting on 2-HMS (Fig. 8A).

The data were fitted with the Michaelis–Menten equation to provide a kcat, Km, and kcat/Km of 0.42 s−1, 590 nm, and 7.1 × 105 m−1 s−1, respectively. A submicromolar Km is at the lower end for the KP enzymes; however, such high commitment may be necessary to efficiently compete with the rapid decay of its substrate to PA.

To further investigate the specificity of ALDH8A1 for α-substituted muconate semialdehydes, several active-site mutants were constructed. The two strictly conserved residues among the HMSDH family previously shown to be responsible for substrate recognition and binding, Arg-109, and Arg-451, were mutated to alanine, and their kinetic parameters for 2-HMS were determined. As summarized in Table 1, deletion of Arg-109 by mutation to alanine generated a variant with a similar turnover number but approximately 160-fold increased Km as compared with WT (Fig. 8B). No detectable activity could be measured for the R451A variant. Additionally, the active-site asparagine (Asn-155) responsible for stabilizing tetrahedral, oxyanion intermediates in general and involved in substrate isomerization in AMSDH was mutated to alanine, aspartic acid, and glutamine.

The activity of the mutants was too low to determine kinetic parameters; however, specific activities for N155A, N155D, and N155Q were 7.4 ± 0.1, 20 ± 1, and 0.31 ± 0.03 nmol/mg/min, respectively. Of the same mutants in pfAMSDH, N169D also showed the highest activity (22). In other aldehyde dehydrogenases, mutation of the corresponding asparagine to alanine or aspartic acid reduced the activity by approximately 1,000-fold or below detectable limits (27, 28).

Conclusion
The human enzyme ALDH8A1 (ALDH12) was shown to catalyze the NAD+-dependent oxidation of 2-AMS with catalytic efficiency comparable with pfAMSDH. Mutation of the active-site residues, which were shown to be heavily involved with substrate recognition, binding, and isomerization in the bacterial enzyme, resulted in variants with 100-fold increased Km or no detectable activity. As such, the ALDH8A1 enzyme, which was previously assigned as a cis-retinal dehydrogenase, should be reassigned as human AMSDH. It was also shown that the reaction product, 2-AM, can spontaneously deaminate in solution, ultimately forming 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate. This work thus establishes that the aldehyde dehydrogenase of the kynurenine pathway, first discovered 53 years ago from liver extracts (1), is ALDH8A1 (ALDH12).

The kynurenine pathway of the tryptophan catabolic pathway in humans is therefore extended to AMSDH.

Experimental procedures
Cloning and site-directed mutagenesis
A DNA sequence that codes for human ALDH8A1 (accession number AF303134) was purchased from DNASU (Arizona State University) and ligated into pET28a(+) vector with NheI and HindIII restriction sites, creating an N-terminal His6-tagged construct. The resultant plasmid was transformed into E. coli cell line BL21 (DE3), which was stored at −80 °C as a 20% (v/v) glycerol stock. Overexpression systems for R109A, R451A, N155A, N155Q, and N155D were constructed by PCR overlap extension using the WT as the starting template. The forward primers were 5′-CCATGGACATTCCCGCGTCTGTGCAGAA and 5′-CTGCTGGCTCATCGCGGAGCTGAACCTT for R109A and R451A, respectively, and 5′-GCTGGTCTGATCAGCCCCTGGGCTTTGCCACTCTACTTGCTGACC, 5′-GCTGGTCTGATCAGCCCCTGGCAGTTGCCACTCTACTTGCTGACC, and 5′-GCTGGTCTGATCAGCCCCTGGGACTTGCCACTCTACTTGCTGACC for N155A, N155Q, and N155D, respectively. Nucleotides corresponding to the mutated residues are underlined.

Protein preparation
For all cultures, antibiotic selection under kanamycin was used. Cultures were started by streaking the appropriate glycerol stock onto an LB-agar plate, which was incubated overnight at 37 °C. A single colony was selected for further incubation in 15 ml of LB-Miller broth at 37 °C with 220 rpm shaking until an A600 of approximately 0.6 was achieved.

Then 50 ml of LB-Miller broth was inoculated to an A600 of 0.0002 and incubated at 37 °C with 220 rpm shaking. Finally, once the 50-ml flask reached an A600 of approximately 0.6, it was used to inoculate 6 liters of LB-Miller broth in 12 2-liter baffled flasks to an A600 of 0.0002. The flasks were incubated at 37 °C with 220 rpm shaking. Upon reaching an A600 of 0.5, isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside was added to a final concentration of 800 μm to induce protein expression, the temperature was lowered to 16 °C, and the culture was incubated for an additional 12 h. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 8,000 × g and resuspended in 50 mm KPi, 150 mm NaCl buffered to pH 8.0 with 0.1% (v/v) β-mercaptoethanol. Protein was released by cell disruption (LS-20, Microfluidics), and the cell debris was removed by centrifugation at 27,000 × g.

The protein of interest was purified by nickel affinity chromatography. Clarified, cell-free extract was applied to a nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid column and eluted with an imidazole gradient.

The running and elution buffers were 50 mm KPi, 150 mm NaCl buffered to pH 8.0 with 5 mm 1,4-DTT with the elution buffer also containing 500 mm imidazole. The purified protein was then desalted to 25 mm HEPES buffer, pH 7.5, 5 mm 1,4-DTT, 1 mm NAD+, 5% glycerol (w/v); concentrated to approximately 1 mm by 30-kDa centrifugal filters; flash frozen in liquid nitrogen; and stored at −80 °C until use. ACMSD used for coupled-enzyme assays was prepared as reported previously (11, 29–33).

Kinetic assays
The substrate analog 2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde was prepared as reported previously (21). Briefly, 3-hydroxyanthralinic acid was converted to 2-amino-3-carboxymuconic semialdehyde by purified 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid dioxygenase. 2-Amino-3-carboxymuconic semialdehyde was then nonenzymatically converted to 2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde by lowering the pH below 2. After conversion, the solution was neutralized, and excess enzyme was removed by filtration.

The coupled-enzyme assays were initiated by addition of excess ACMSD (1 μm) to rapidly convert all ACMS to 2-AMS, which is in turn was converted to 2-aminomuconic acid by ALDH8A1. In the absence of ALDH8A1 and 1 mm NAD+, the 2-AMS nonenzymatically decays to picolinic acid. Catalytic parameters were obtained using 2-HMS as the substrate.

The decrease in absorbance as 2-HMS (λmax at 375 nm, ϵ375 of 43,000 m−1 cm−1) and NAD+ are converted to 2-hydroxymuconic acid and NADH (ϵ375 of 1,900 m−1 cm−1) was measured with an Agilent 8453 diode-array spectrometer. The reaction rate was calculated as the change in absorbance divided by the sum of the extinction coefficients of 2-HMS and NADH. Initial rates versus substrate concentration were fitted with the Michaelis–Menten equation.

NMR spectroscopy
All NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker (Billerica, MA) Avance III HD 500-MHz spectrometer equipped with a CryoProdigy Probe at 300 K running TopSpin 3.5pl6. Spectra were recorded in D2O or 90% H2O, 10% D2O and referenced to residual solvent (1H, 4.70 ppm). One-dimensional 1H spectra (pulse sequence, zg30) were recorded with 1-s relaxation delays, 65,536 data points, and multiplied with an exponential function for a line broadening of 0.3 Hz before Fourier transformation. Double quantum–filtered COSY (pulse sequence, cosygpmfppqf) spectra were acquired with spectral widths of 13.0 ppm with 2,048 × 128 data points and a relaxation delay of 2.0 s.

1D gradient-selected NOESY (pulse sequence, selnogp) spectra were recorded with a mixing time of 0.3 s and a 2-s relaxation delay and multiplied with an exponential function for a line broadening of 3 Hz before Fourier transformation. All NMR data were processed using MestReNova NMR version 11.0.3 software.

Mass spectrometry
The AMSDH reaction product, 2-aminomuconate, was isolated for mass spectrometric characterization by reverse-phase HPLC with an InertSustain C18 column (5-μm particle size, 4.6-mm inner diameter × 100 mm; GL Sciences Inc.) on a Dionex Ultimate 3000 HPLC equipped with a diode-array detector (Sunnyvale, CA). The crude reaction mixture was ultrafiltered (10-kDa cutoff) to remove protein, and separation was achieved using isocratic elution with 95% H2O, 5% acetonitrile, and 0.5% formic acid. Mass spectra were collected on a maXis plus quadrupole-TOF mass spectrometer equipped with an electrospray ionization source (Bruker Daltonics). The instrument was operated in the negative ionization mode in the range 50 ≤ m/z ≤ 1,500 and calibrated using ESI-L Low Concentration Tuning Mix (Agilent Technologies). Samples were introduced via syringe pump at a constant flow rate of 3 μl/min.

Relevant source parameters are summarized as follows: capillary voltage, 3500 V with a set end plate offset of −500 V; nebulizer gas pressure, 0.4 bar; dry gas flow rate, 4.0 liter/min; source temperature, 200 °C. Mass spectra were averages of 1 min of scans collected at a rate of 1 scan per second. Collision-induced dissociation was achieved using a set collision energy of −20 eV. OtofControl software version 6.3 was used for data acquisition, and Compass Data Analysis software version 4.3 (Bruker Daltonics) was used to process all mass spectra. mMass software version 5.5.0 was used for all exact mass calculations (34).

Human phosphoribosylformylglycineamide amidotransferase (FGARAT): regional mapping, complete coding sequence, isolation of a functional genomic clone, and DNA sequence analysis

Abstract
Purines play essential roles in many cellular functions, including DNA replication, transcription, intra- and extra-cellular signaling, energy metabolism, and as coenzymes for many biochemical reactions. The de-novo synthesis of purines requires 10 enzymatic steps for the production of inosine monophosphate (IMP). Defects in purine metabolism are associated with human diseases. Further, many anticancer agents function as inhibitors of the de-novo biosynthetic pathway. Genes or cDNAs for most of the enzymes comprising this pathway have been isolated from humans or other mammals. One notable exception is the phosphoribosylformylglycineamide amidotransferase (FGARAT) gene, which encodes the fourth step of this pathway. This gene has been cloned from numerous microorganisms and from Drosophila melanogaster and C. elegans. We report here the identification of a human cDNA containing the coding region of the FGARAT mRNA and the isolation of a P1 clone that contains an intact human FGARAT gene. The P1 clone corrects the purine auxotrophy and protein deficiency of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell mutants (AdeB) deficient in both the activity and the protein for FGARAT. The P1 clone was used to regionally map the FGARAT gene to chromosome region 17p13, a location consistent with our prior assignment of this gene to chromosome 17. A comparison of the DNA sequence of the human FGARAT and FGARAT DNA sequence from 17 other organisms is reported. The isolation of this gene means that DNA clones for all the 10 steps of IMP synthesis have been isolated from humans or other mammals.

Keywords
Comparative sequence analysisEnzyme evolutionEnzyme structurePurine synthesis
Abbreviations
CHO, Chinese hamster ovaryCNS, central nervous systemDAPI, 4,6 diamidino-2-phenylindoleFGARAT, phosphoribosylformylglycineamide amidotransferaseFISH, fluorescence in-situ hybridizationHFGARAT, human cDNA encoding FGARATIMP, inosine monophosphateORF, open reading frameTPX, thioredoxin-dependent peroxide reductase gene
1. Introduction
Purines are fundamental biological molecules, serving as components of DNA and RNA, and as neurotransmitters, second messengers, key components of cellular energy metabolism, and coenzymes. Virtually all free-living organisms can synthesize purine nucleotides, either de novo from precursor molecules or from exogenous purine bases (Becker and Roessler, 1995, Rossiter and Caskey, 1995). Mutations in purine nucleotide synthesis lead to severe disease states in humans and animals. These include Lesch–Nyhan syndrome, immune deficiencies, mental retardation and autism, sensorineural deafness, and gouty arthritis (Becker et al., 1989, Hershfield and Mitchell, 1995, Jaeken and van den Berghe, 1994, Jimenez et al., 1989).
The de-novo biosynthetic pathway consists of 10 enzymatic steps leading to IMP. A critical step to understanding regulation of these genes is the isolation of cDNA and genomic clones encoding the various steps of the pathway. For example, cloning of the genes encoding the first, sixth, and seventh steps of the pathway demonstrated that two genes encode these three enzymatic functions and that these genes are bidirectionally transcribed and share a common promoter region (Brayton et al., 1994, Chen et al., 1997, Gavalas et al., 1993). Cloning of the locus encoding the second, third, and fifth steps of the pathway demonstrated conclusively that a single genetic locus encodes a trifunctional protein carrying out all these steps (Chang et al., 1990, Gnirke et al., 1991, Schild et al., 1990). Presently, cDNAs and genomic clones encoding nine of the 10 committed steps resulting in IMP synthesis have been isolated from human and various other vertebrates (Gnirke et al., 1991, Zalkin and Dixon, 1992, Zalkin, 1993). The only exception is phosphoribosylformylglycineamide amidotransferase (FGARAT) (EC 6.3.5.3). which encodes step 4.
We report here the identification of a cDNA clone containing the complete sequence of human FGARAT and the isolation of a P1 clone containing the entire human genomic DNA sequence of this locus.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Identification of a human cDNA encoding FGARAT
To identify a human cDNA clone encoding FGARAT, a gapped BLASTP search was carried out using the NCBI's sequence similarity tool (Altschul et al., 1997). The Drosophila melanogaster FGARAT amino acid sequence (Tiong and Nash, 1993; Genbank Accession No. U00683) was the query sequence.
2.2. Isolation of a FGARAT containing P1 clone
The Dupont human P1 library (Shepherd et al., 1994) was screened by PCR as previously described (Brodsky et al., 1997) using primers that amplify nucleotides 938–1109 (5′ primer=gaagtccgattcctacggcctg , 3′ primer=tgcactggacatctcgaatccg) from the human cDNA sequence. To verify the presence of the 5′ and 3′ ends of the gene, the P1 clone, P97A12, was further analyzed using primer sets that amplify nucleotides 42–141 (5′ primer=gcaaaggacacatctctccag, 3′ primer=tggccagagggacgaacatag) and 4751–4980 (5′ primer=gaggcagtctcactctgtcac, 3′ primer=ggcaggcgaatcacttgaggt) of the cDNA, respectively. To determine the insert size, the clone was digested with NotI and the products were resolved on a CHEF DRII Pulsed Field Gel Electrophoresis apparatus (Biorad).
2.3. Functional complementation of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell FGARAT mutations
P1 clone P97A12 was transfected into AdeB cells using Lipofectamine reagent (Gibco-BRL) according to a standard protocol (Brodsky et al., 1997). Briefly, 4×105 cells per 100 mm dish were plated in Ham's F12 medium supplemented with 5% fetal calf serum. After 24 h, the medium was removed, the plates were rinsed, and 2 μg of NotI-linearized P1 clone DNA in 35 μg Lipofectamine were added to each dish in a minimal volume of F12 without serum. After 24 h, the plates were rinsed with Saline G, and F12 with serum was added for a 24 h. recovery. Finally, the cells were removed from the dish, rinsed, and plated at 5×105 per 100 mm dish in the purine-free growth medium F12D plus 5% of the macromolecular fraction of fetal calf serum. Colonies could be seen after 5–7 days in selective media and were picked into deficient media for further growth and isolation of protein and RNA. Proteins were isolated from cell cultures, and Western blotting was performed as previously described (Brodsky et al., 1997).
2.4. Chromosomal mapping of FGARAT
The primer sets described above were used to amplify DNA from a panel of somatic cell hybrids as previously described (Berger et al., 1995, Pahl et al., 1995). Confirmation of chromosome assignment was accomplished with all three primer sets described in Section 2.2. Linearized P97A12 DNA was labeled with digoxygenin dUTP (Boehringer-Mannheim) by nick translation and hybridized to metaphase spreads of human chromosomes. The P1 clone probe was detected with fluorscein-conjugated anti-digoxygenin antibodies (Pahl et al, 1995). Chromosomes were counterstained with 4,6 diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) in antifade to produce reverse DAPI banding for chromosome identification.
2.5. Analysis of the human FGARAT mRNA and intron detection
To assess the presence of human FGARAT mRNA in various cell lines, RNA was isolated from human (HeLa), CHO-K1, AdeB, and AdeB transfectant cell lines using an RNA isolation kit from Qiagen according to the manufacturer's directions. The RNA was treated with RNAse-free DNAse. Reverse-transcriptase reactions were performed using random hexamers and murine leukemia virus reverse transcriptase (Perkin-Elmer). Specific PCR primers for FGARAT amplifying the human cDNA between nucleotides 3288 and 3463 (5′ primer=cccgagtcgccatcttgcgagag, 3′ primer=atctgcatagctgaagccgccca), which span an intron, were then used in a standard PCR reaction with the RT products as templates.
To determine the 5′ end of the FGARAT coding region, three sets of primers between bases 81 and 190 were designed and synthesized to be used for 5′ RACE. The primer sequences were ; SP1, cagtttcccttgcagtttcctc; SP2, atggccagagggacgaacatag; SP3, atctctgcaggtgtcctttgc. RNA isolated from two separate human cell lines was used in duplicate reactions with these primer sets using a 5′ RACE kit from Boehringer according to the manufacturer's protocol. DNA from a clone generated from each RNA was isolated and sequenced.
To examine the human FGARAT gene for the presence of an intron in the region of the junction between the purL and purQ domains (Tiong and Nash, 1993), the primer set spanning bases 3288–3463 in the human cDNA described above was used. This region corresponds to the region in which the second intron is found in the Drosophila gene. The primer set was used to amplify DNA from the P1 clone and the product size compared to that of the cDNA to assess the presence of an intron. The PCR product was sequenced using an ABI373 automated sequencing system.
3. Results
3.1. Identification a human cDNA encoding FGARAT
The Drosophila melanogaster FGARAT genomic DNA and corresponding genomic clones were previously reported by Tiong and Nash (1993). A BLASTP search of protein sequence databases with the conceptual protein sequence determined from the Drosophila DNA sequence identified a 5338 bp human cDNA clone with an expectation value of 0.0. (Nagase et al., 1997; Accession No. AB002359). This cDNA clone, which was isolated from a human brain cDNA library, was graciously provided to us by Dr Nagase of the Kazusa DNA Research Institute, Japan. The comparison of the human and Drosophila sequences is shown in Fig. 1. The human protein sequence shows 51% identity and 66% similarity with the Drosophila sequence over 1332 amino acids starting at positions 34 and 69 for Drosophila and human, respectively, indicating that a human cDNA encoding FGARAT (hFGARAT) has been identified (Altschul et al., 1997). A significant sequence homology was also detected with putative FGARAT sequences from 16 additional organisms (Table 1, Table 2).
The hFGARAT cDNA contains an open reading frame (ORF) of 4117 bases or 1371 amino acids. The Drosophila DNA sequence contains an ORF of 4062 bases or 1354 amino acids (Tiong and Nash, 1993). The first methionine of the human ORF is at amino acid 34. Comparison with the Drosophila DNA places this methionine within two positions of the putative initial methionine in the Drosophila DNA (Tiong and Nash, 1993). Assuming that the Drosophila translation start site is as indicated, the positioning of a methionine in the human ORF two positions away indicates that this is the translation start in the human clone. The ORF in the human clone extends 5′ to the start of the insert. The putative translation start of the Drosophila gene was determined by comparison with the E. coli sequence. Interestingly, the Drosophila ORF extends an additional 44 amino acids 5′ of this methionine, but there are no additional methionines. To investigate further whether the entire FGARAT coding sequence is present in the human cDNA clone, we performed 5′ RACE on HeLa cell mRNA. Sequencing of a RACE clone revealed an in-frame potential coding region of 10 additional non-methionine amino acids and then an in-frame UAA stop codon. Therefore, we suspect that this cDNA clone contains the entire FGARAT protein-coding region.
A BLASTN search using the Drosophila DNA sequence detected hFGARAT, but the homology was extremely limited. Drosophila bases 2840–2883 showed 86% identity to bases 1643–1686 of the human sequence.
3.2. Mapping of hFGARAT sequences to human chromosome region 17p13
Mapping of the genes for de-novo purine synthesis has been instrumental in determining the number of loci required to encode the proteins of the pathway. We found previously that a locus allowing production of FGARAT protein resides on human chromosome 17 (Barnes et al., 1994). To confirm this and to map the FGARAT gene more precisely, we used PCR primers from the 5′ end, middle, and 3′ end of the hFGARAT cDNA to analyze a human/Chinese hamster ovary hybrid cell mapping panel (Pahl et al., 1995). The result of this PCR analysis using the primers amplifying bases 938–1109 in the middle region of the human cDNA is shown in Fig. 2. The only hybrid showing a positive PCR signal is that containing human chromosome 17 and no other human chromosome. On the basis of the cDNA sequence, this PCR should give a product of 172 bp. The amplimer detected is 259 bp in human and hybrid cells and in the FGARAT containing P1 clone (see below, data not shown), indicating that this amplimer spans the intronic DNA sequence. The presence of an 87 bp intron in this clone was confirmed by DNA sequencing of the PCR amplimer. The amplification of intron DNA is evidence that the primers are not detecting a processed pseudogene.

3.3. Isolation of a P1 clone that corrects the defect in FGARAT deficient mutants of CHO-K1 cells
We used the same PCR primers to isolate a P1 clone, P97A12, containing a 68.5 kb insert. Fluorescence in-situ hybridization (FISH) mapping using P97A12 DNA confirmed mapping of the FGARAT gene to chromosome 17 and refined the mapping to chromosome region 17p13 (Fig. 3).

We have previously reported the isolation and characterization of AdeB CHO cell
mutants deficient in FGARAT activity (Barnes et al., 1994, Patterson, 1975). AdeB cells display 100% plating efficiency in medium containing purines relative to wild-type CHO-K1 cells (approximately 90% of cells give rise to colonies). In the absence of purines, less than one colony per million AdeB cells plated produce colonies. Transfection of AdeB cells with linearized P97A12 DNA allowed clonal growth of 100–300 per 5×105 AdeB cells in the absence of purines. Several clones were isolated and expanded in purine-free medium for analysis. Fig. 4a shows by Western blot analysis that two independent clonally isolated transfectants produce a protein recognized by anti-FGARAT antibody (Barnes et al., 1994) that is not produced in the parental AdeB cells. This protein is the expected size, 145 kDa, for FGARAT.

We then examined the production of human-specific FGARAT mRNA by the same transfectants. Messenger RNA was isolated from human (HeLa), CHO-K1, AdeB, and the transfectants. A reverse transcriptase reaction was performed using random hexamers. The products of the reverse transcriptase reactions were PCR-amplified using the same primers used in Fig. 2 to map the FGARAT gene. Only reverse transcription products from human cells and the transfectants could be PCR-amplified, and the size of the amplimer is 172 bp, as expected if the amplimer is indeed derived from reverse-transcribed FGARAT mRNA (Fig. 4b). These data provide convincing evidence that P97A12 contains all the information necessary to produce functional human FGARAT.
3.4. Analysis of the human FGARAT gene sequence
In B. subtilis, the activity of FGARAT requires two proteins, the products of the purL and purQ genes. The Drosophila protein resembles a fusion of the B. subtilis purL and purQ proteins (Tiong and Nash, 1993). The Drosophila FGARAT gene is reported to have two introns, one at bp 1091 and one at bp 3444 (Tiong and Nash, 1993). The second intron in the Drosophila gene occurs near the putative site of fusion of the B. subtilis genes. We designed PCR primers flanking the appropriate region in the human sequence, bases 3288–3463 in the human cDNA and analyzed the P1 clone. Instead of the expected 172 bp amplimer, a product of 259 bp is seen. Sequencing of this PCR product detected an 87 bp intron at a position in the human gene 8 codons 5′ of the location of the intron in the Drosophila locus (Fig. 1).
An additional interesting feature of the DNA sequence of hFGARAT is that the 5′ end of the cDNA contains three copies of a 19 bp direct repeat, at bases 34–52, 54–72, and 74–92 according to the numbering system of the human FGARAT cDNA sequence in GenBank Accession No. AB002359. The repeats end eight bases upstream of the start site. Fig. 5 shows the first 120 bases of the human cDNA sequence with the repeats indicated by underlining. This sequence was analyzed using RepeatMasker (Smit, A.F.A., Green, P. RepeatMasker at HYPERLINK http://ftp.genome.washington.edu/RM/RepeatMasker.html). No repetitive sequences were detected using this program. This includes Alu, short interspersed repeats, long interspersed repeats, MIR, LINE2, retroviral sequences, LINE1 sequences and other repeats. The significance of these repeats is not known.

4. Discussion
4.1. Analysis of the structure of the FGARAT protein
We present here conclusive evidence for the identification and isolation of both a cDNA and a functional, full-length genomic clone encoding the human FGARAT locus. This evidence includes sequence homology with the Drosophila gene (and 16 other FGARAT genes) (Tiong and Nash, 1993), mapping to human chromosome 17p13, previously shown by us to be the chromosome containing the FGARAT gene by Western blot analysis of a somatic cell hybrid mapping panel using anti-FGARAT antibody (Barnes et al., 1994), and functional complementation of the FGARAT deficiency in AdeB mutants of CHO cells.
Analysis of the amino acid sequence of human FGARAT and comparison with the sequences of other organisms from which the gene has been isolated provide insight into the evolution of the gene and the nature of the enzyme activity. FGARAT coding sequences have been identified for the eukaryotes Drosophila melanogaster, S. cerevisiae, S. pombe, and C. elegans. Additionally, full or partial sequences have been reported for at least 13 bacterial strains including three archaebacteria and 10 eubacteria (Table 1).
FGARAT catalyzes the ATP-dependent transfer of an amino group from glutamine to phosphoribosylformylglycineamide (FGAR), resulting in the production of phosphoribosylformylglycineamidine (FGAM) and ADP. Therefore, the enzyme would be expected to contain an ATP-binding domain and a glutamine amide transfer domain.
These features of the protein are highly conserved in FGARAT from the eukaryotes and all the bacterial strains. Thus, a glycine-rich putative ATP-binding domain (Andreichuk et al., 1997) at positions 327–338 in the D. melanogaster sequence (numbering according to Fig. 1), indicated by underlining in Fig. 1, is essentially completely conserved in the human and C. elegans protein (11/12 identities, one conserved amino acid). In yeast and all 13 bacterial strains, 8/12 amino acids are identical. Interestingly, it is the same eight amino acids that are conserved in all organisms. Two other positions are highly conserved. Position 336 consists of the related amino acids leucine, valine, or isoleucine in all organisms (Table 2). Position 329 consists of alanine in 14 organisms, threonine in three, and glycine in one. The highly conserved nature of this sequence clearly argues for its functional importance. These relationships are summarized in Table 2.
Ebbole and Zalkin (1987) noted three conserved regions of various glutamine amidotransferases. Within these regions, a cysteine at position 1180, a histidine at position 1310, and a glutamate at 1312 were hypothesized to be essential for glutamine amide transfer (Ebbole and Zalkin, 1987). All three of these amino acids are conserved in all 18 prokaryotic and eukaryotic FGARAT enzymes studied here. In Fig. 1, the overline above the first of these domains, 1132–1141 in the D. melanogaster protein, indicates the hypothesized first glutamine amide transfer domain amino acids according to Ebbole and Zalkin (1987). Interestingly, the first five of these amino acids are not highly conserved in all FGARATs (Table 2). However, the next three amino acids, FSY, are completely conserved in all organisms with only two exceptions, an A at position 1141 in M. jannaschii and an F at position 1141 in A. aeolius. The R at position 1313 in the third amino acid domain is conserved in all organisms except M. tuberculosis and M. leprae, which have an H at this position. Thus, the conservation of these residues certainly supports their functional importance. We propose that the FSY sequence at positions 1139–1141 should be considered part of the first of the three glutamine amide transfer domains due to their high conservation. These relationships are also summarized in Table 2.
Previous comparisons of eight FGARAT enzymes revealed a total of 123 invariant amino acid residues (Andreichuk et al., 1997). Since that analysis, FGARAT sequence from 10 additional organisms has become available. Extension of the analysis of Andreichuk et al. (1997) to include these additional FGARAT sequences reveals that 83 of these amino acids remain conserved when the current set of organisms is examined. At least 84% of the 123 amino acids are conserved in each of the organisms studied here, although the exact subset of conserved amino acids is not identical in all organisms. Interestingly, one of the least conserved, at 84%, is C. elegans.
Several investigators have noted that in B. subtilis, two proteins carry out the complete FGARAT reaction, while in E. coli, a single protein carries out both functions. The B. subtilis proteins are designated purL, which corresponds to the amino end of the E. coli enzyme, and purQ, which corresponds to the carboxy domain. By sequence analysis, the E. coli enzyme resembles a fusion of the domains present in B. subtilis. As shown here, the human enzyme is encoded by a single protein, as are the enzymes from D. melanogaster, C. elegans, S. cerevisiae, S. pombe, E. coli, S. typhimurium, and H. influenzae. In the other 10 bacterial strains, two proteins are required for FGARAT activity. These include all three representatives of the archaebacteria. These observations are consistent with the hypothesis that the most ancient organization of this enzymatic step was as two genes encoding two proteins.
It is interesting to speculate on the observation that FGARAT activity is carried on a single protein in all eukaryotes studied and in certain proteobacteria, whereas all other bacterial organisms require two proteins for this function. As pointed out by Tiong and Nash (1993), it seems unreasonable to assume that the eukaryotes evolved from the proteobacteria. Instead, this may be an example of chimeric evolution of the eukaryotic genome (Bult et al., 1996, Lake et al., 1999, Rivera et al., 1998). In this regard, the grouping of genes into two supergroups, informational and operational, offers a way of thinking about the evolution of the eukaryotic genome. According to this grouping, informational genes include those involved in transcription, translation, and related processes. Operational genes are those involved in housekeeping functions such as intermediary metabolism or nucleotide synthesis (Bult et al., 1996, Lake et al., 1999, Rivera et al., 1998). Eukaryotes appear to have acquired their informational genes from an archaebacterium-like organism (e.g. M. jannaschii), and their operational genome primarily, but not exclusively, from a proteobacteria-like organism (e.g. E. coli). FGARAT is classified as an operational gene in this scheme (Bult et al., 1996). The finding that FGARAT is a single protein in human and all other eukaryotes so far examined and in all the proteobacteria, but consists of two proteins in eubacteria and archaebacteria, is consistent with this hypothesis (Table 1).
This still leaves open the question of whether the FGARAT gene encoding a single FGARAT protein arose from the two FGARAT genes encoding the two proteins required for FGARAT activity in some organisms, and if so, what caused this change in gene organization. Tiong and Nash (1993) identified residue 1085 as the primary purQ start site in their analysis of the D. melanogaster sequence. Analysis of the junction between the purL and purQ domains in the organisms containing two proteins indicates that in four, B. subtilis, L. lactis, M. jannaschii, and M. thermoautotrophicum, the purQ protein domain begins in exactly the same site, residue 1085 of the D. melanogaster sequence of Fig. 1, indicated by the designation >purQ; in three, M. tuberculosis, M. leprae, and S. sp, it is two residues away at position 1087; in one, A. fulgidus, it is six residues away at position 1079; and in one, A. aeolicus, it is nine residues away at position 1094. This remarkable consistency of the start site of the purQ domain includes archaebacteria as well as eubacteria.
Tiong and Nash (1993) also identified a presumptive end of the purL homologous region at position 1046. This leaves an inter-domain connecting sequence of 39 amino acids. As discussed above, the D. melanogaster and human FGARAT amino acid sequences overall are 51% identical and 66% similar. The relatedness of the amino acid sequence in the 39 residue connecting sequence is much lower. Only 26% of the amino acid residues are identical, and only 28% are similar. In addition, none of the residues found to be invariant among all FGARATs is within this region. All the purL domains end well before the inter-domain region.
Analysis of the DNA sequence of the 5′ end of the human FGARAT cDNA indicates that the methionine indicated in Fig. 1 is in fact the start site. There is a G at the −3 position, one of the important features of translation start sites (Kozak, 1996). In addition, 5′ RACE found an in-frame termination codon, UAA, 132 bases upstream of the proposed start site with no methionines between the termination codon and the proposed start site.
FGARAT is one of two amidotransferases in the first 10 steps of IMP synthesis (Zalkin and Dixon, 1992, Zalkin, 1993). The other amidotransferase, amidophosphoribosyltransferase (PRAT), is often considered to be the rate-limiting and regulatory step of the pathway and can be allosterically regulated (Becker et al., 1989, Becker and Roessler, 1995). There is minimal sequence homology between PRAT and FGARAT. Interestingly, we have reported the isolation of mutant CHO cells, AdePAB, which require purines for growth and which are defective in both PRAT and FGARAT glutamine-dependent amidotransferase activities (Oates et al., 1980). Somatic cell hybrid studies demonstrate that the AdePAB defects cannot be complemented by AdeA mutants, lacking PRAT, or AdeB mutants, lacking FGARAT (Oates et al., 1980). CHO cell mutants lacking any of the other enzyme activities required for de-novo purine synthesis, when hybridized with AdePAB cells, do eliminate their requirement for purines for growth (Oates et al., 1980). Revertants of AdePAB cells that have regained the activities can be isolated; therefore, these mutants cannot be deletions. We and others have regionally mapped the PRAT locus to chromosome 4q12 and FGARAT to chromosome 17p13 in humans (Barton et al., 1991, Stanley and Chu, 1978). PRAT and FGARAT also map to different chromosomes in Drosophila (Clark, 1994, Tiong et al., 1989, Zalkin, 1993). Therefore, it is unlikely that the PRAT and FGARAT genes are in close proximity to each other in the CHO cell genome, allowing both to be inactivated by a cis-acting mutation. These data suggest that there is a third genetic locus acting in trans involved in encoding or regulating these two steps, and it is this locus that is affected in the AdePAB mutants. This locus could, for example, encode a protein that binds to both PRAT and FGARAT and is required for both activities or, alternatively, causes an interaction directly between PRAT and FGARAT that is required for activity. Assessment of these possibilities will be aided greatly by isolation of human FGARAT cDNA and genomic clones.
With the cloning of FGARAT, human genes encoding all of the known proteins involved in de-novo IMP synthesis have been isolated. Isolation of clones encoding other enzymes of this pathway has been instrumental in determining the multifunctional nature of some of the enzymes in the pathway (Chang et al., 1990, Gnirke et al., 1991, Schild et al., 1990, Zalkin and Dixon, 1992) and in revealing aspects of the possible coordinate regulation of these genes (Brayton et al., 1994, Chen et al., 1997, Gavalas et al., 1993). The two amidotransferases in the pathway, PRAT and FGARAT, are both important from a regulatory point of view and as targets for cancer chemotherapy. Genetic evidence suggests that the regulation of these two loci must be coordinated and involve a third genetic locus (Oates et al., 1980). The isolation of cDNA and genomic clones for FGARAT, along with the availability of clones for all the other steps in the pathway, should enable detailed investigations, previously not possible, of the regulatory mechanisms used by human cells to control the rate of de-novo purine synthesis.

Human phosphoribosylformylglycineamide amidotransferase (FGARAT): regional mapping, complete coding sequence, isolation of a functional genomic clone, and DNA sequence analysis

Abstract
Purines play essential roles in many cellular functions, including DNA replication, transcription, intra- and extra-cellular signaling, energy metabolism, and as coenzymes for many biochemical reactions. The de-novo synthesis of purines requires 10 enzymatic steps for the production of inosine monophosphate (IMP). Defects in purine metabolism are associated with human diseases. Further, many anticancer agents function as inhibitors of the de-novo biosynthetic pathway. Genes or cDNAs for most of the enzymes comprising this pathway have been isolated from humans or other mammals. One notable exception is the phosphoribosylformylglycineamide amidotransferase (FGARAT) gene, which encodes the fourth step of this pathway. This gene has been cloned from numerous microorganisms and from Drosophila melanogaster and C. elegans. We report here the identification of a human cDNA containing the coding region of the FGARAT mRNA and the isolation of a P1 clone that contains an intact human FGARAT gene. The P1 clone corrects the purine auxotrophy and protein deficiency of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell mutants (AdeB) deficient in both the activity and the protein for FGARAT.

The P1 clone was used to regionally map the FGARAT gene to chromosome region 17p13, a location consistent with our prior assignment of this gene to chromosome 17. A comparison of the DNA sequence of the human FGARAT and FGARAT DNA sequence from 17 other organisms is reported. The isolation of this gene means that DNA clones for all the 10 steps of IMP synthesis have been isolated from humans or other mammals.

Keywords
Comparative sequence analysisEnzyme evolutionEnzyme structurePurine synthesis
Abbreviations
CHO, Chinese hamster ovaryCNS, central nervous systemDAPI, 4,6 diamidino-2-phenylindoleFGARAT, phosphoribosylformylglycineamide amidotransferaseFISH, fluorescence in-situ hybridizationHFGARAT, human cDNA encoding FGARATIMP, inosine monophosphateORF, open reading frameTPX, thioredoxin-dependent peroxide reductase gene
1. Introduction
Purines are fundamental biological molecules, serving as components of DNA and RNA, and as neurotransmitters, second messengers, key components of cellular energy metabolism, and coenzymes. Virtually all free-living organisms can synthesize purine nucleotides, either de novo from precursor molecules or from exogenous purine bases (Becker and Roessler, 1995, Rossiter and Caskey, 1995). Mutations in purine nucleotide synthesis lead to severe disease states in humans and animals.

These include Lesch–Nyhan syndrome, immune deficiencies, mental retardation and autism, sensorineural deafness, and gouty arthritis (Becker et al., 1989, Hershfield and Mitchell, 1995, Jaeken and van den Berghe, 1994, Jimenez et al., 1989).
The de-novo biosynthetic pathway consists of 10 enzymatic steps leading to IMP. A critical step to understanding regulation of these genes is the isolation of cDNA and genomic clones encoding the various steps of the pathway. For example, cloning of the genes encoding the first, sixth, and seventh steps of the pathway demonstrated that two genes encode these three enzymatic functions and that these genes are bidirectionally transcribed and share a common promoter region (Brayton et al., 1994, Chen et al., 1997, Gavalas et al., 1993). Cloning of the locus encoding the second, third, and fifth steps of the pathway demonstrated conclusively that a single genetic locus encodes a trifunctional protein carrying out all these steps (Chang et al., 1990, Gnirke et al., 1991, Schild et al., 1990). Presently, cDNAs and genomic clones encoding nine of the 10 committed steps resulting in IMP synthesis have been isolated from human and various other vertebrates (Gnirke et al., 1991, Zalkin and Dixon, 1992, Zalkin, 1993).

The only exception is phosphoribosylformylglycineamide amidotransferase (FGARAT) (EC 6.3.5.3). which encodes step 4.
We report here the identification of a cDNA clone containing the complete sequence of human FGARAT and the isolation of a P1 clone containing the entire human genomic DNA sequence of this locus.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Identification of a human cDNA encoding FGARAT
To identify a human cDNA clone encoding FGARAT, a gapped BLASTP search was carried out using the NCBI's sequence similarity tool (Altschul et al., 1997). The Drosophila melanogaster FGARAT amino acid sequence (Tiong and Nash, 1993; Genbank Accession No. U00683) was the query sequence.
2.2. Isolation of a FGARAT containing P1 clone
The Dupont human P1 library (Shepherd et al., 1994) was screened by PCR as previously described (Brodsky et al., 1997) using primers that amplify nucleotides 938–1109 (5′ primer=gaagtccgattcctacggcctg , 3′ primer=tgcactggacatctcgaatccg) from the human cDNA sequence. To verify the presence of the 5′ and 3′ ends of the gene, the P1 clone, P97A12, was further analyzed using primer sets that amplify nucleotides 42–141 (5′ primer=gcaaaggacacatctctccag, 3′ primer=tggccagagggacgaacatag) and 4751–4980 (5′ primer=gaggcagtctcactctgtcac, 3′ primer=ggcaggcgaatcacttgaggt) of the cDNA, respectively.

To determine the insert size, the clone was digested with NotI and the products were resolved on a CHEF DRII Pulsed Field Gel Electrophoresis apparatus (Biorad).
2.3. Functional complementation of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell FGARAT mutations
P1 clone P97A12 was transfected into AdeB cells using Lipofectamine reagent (Gibco-BRL) according to a standard protocol (Brodsky et al., 1997). Briefly, 4×105 cells per 100 mm dish were plated in Ham's F12 medium supplemented with 5% fetal calf serum. After 24 h, the medium was removed, the plates were rinsed, and 2 μg of NotI-linearized P1 clone DNA in 35 μg Lipofectamine were added to each dish in a minimal volume of F12 without serum. After 24 h, the plates were rinsed with Saline G, and F12 with serum was added for a 24 h. recovery. Finally, the cells were removed from the dish, rinsed, and plated at 5×105 per 100 mm dish in the purine-free growth medium F12D plus 5% of the macromolecular fraction of fetal calf serum. Colonies could be seen after 5–7 days in selective media and were picked into deficient media for further growth and isolation of protein and RNA.

Proteins were isolated from cell cultures, and Western blotting was performed as previously described (Brodsky et al., 1997).
2.4. Chromosomal mapping of FGARAT
The primer sets described above were used to amplify DNA from a panel of somatic cell hybrids as previously described (Berger et al., 1995, Pahl et al., 1995). Confirmation of chromosome assignment was accomplished with all three primer sets described in Section 2.2. Linearized P97A12 DNA was labeled with digoxygenin dUTP (Boehringer-Mannheim) by nick translation and hybridized to metaphase spreads of human chromosomes. The P1 clone probe was detected with fluorscein-conjugated anti-digoxygenin antibodies (Pahl et al, 1995). Chromosomes were counterstained with 4,6 diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) in antifade to produce reverse DAPI banding for chromosome identification.
2.5. Analysis of the human FGARAT mRNA and intron detection
To assess the presence of human FGARAT mRNA in various cell lines, RNA was isolated from human (HeLa), CHO-K1, AdeB, and AdeB transfectant cell lines using an RNA isolation kit from Qiagen according to the manufacturer's directions. The RNA was treated with RNAse-free DNAse. Reverse-transcriptase reactions were performed using random hexamers and murine leukemia virus reverse transcriptase (Perkin-Elmer).

Specific PCR primers for FGARAT amplifying the human cDNA between nucleotides 3288 and 3463 (5′ primer=cccgagtcgccatcttgcgagag, 3′ primer=atctgcatagctgaagccgccca), which span an intron, were then used in a standard PCR reaction with the RT products as templates.
To determine the 5′ end of the FGARAT coding region, three sets of primers between bases 81 and 190 were designed and synthesized to be used for 5′ RACE. The primer sequences were ; SP1, cagtttcccttgcagtttcctc; SP2, atggccagagggacgaacatag; SP3, atctctgcaggtgtcctttgc. RNA isolated from two separate human cell lines was used in duplicate reactions with these primer sets using a 5′ RACE kit from Boehringer according to the manufacturer's protocol. DNA from a clone generated from each RNA was isolated and sequenced.
To examine the human FGARAT gene for the presence of an intron in the region of the junction between the purL and purQ domains (Tiong and Nash, 1993), the primer set spanning bases 3288–3463 in the human cDNA described above was used. This region corresponds to the region in which the second intron is found in the Drosophila gene.

The primer set was used to amplify DNA from the P1 clone and the product size compared to that of the cDNA to assess the presence of an intron. The PCR product was sequenced using an ABI373 automated sequencing system.
3. Results
3.1. Identification a human cDNA encoding FGARAT
The Drosophila melanogaster FGARAT genomic DNA and corresponding genomic clones were previously reported by Tiong and Nash (1993). A BLASTP search of protein sequence databases with the conceptual protein sequence determined from the Drosophila DNA sequence identified a 5338 bp human cDNA clone with an expectation value of 0.0. (Nagase et al., 1997; Accession No. AB002359). This cDNA clone, which was isolated from a human brain cDNA library, was graciously provided to us by Dr Nagase of the Kazusa DNA Research Institute, Japan. The comparison of the human and Drosophila sequences is shown in Fig. 1. The human protein sequence shows 51% identity and 66% similarity with the Drosophila sequence over 1332 amino acids starting at positions 34 and 69 for Drosophila and human, respectively, indicating that a human cDNA encoding FGARAT (hFGARAT) has been identified (Altschul et al., 1997).

A significant sequence homology was also detected with putative FGARAT sequences from 16 additional organisms (Table 1, Table 2).
The hFGARAT cDNA contains an open reading frame (ORF) of 4117 bases or 1371 amino acids. The Drosophila DNA sequence contains an ORF of 4062 bases or 1354 amino acids (Tiong and Nash, 1993). The first methionine of the human ORF is at amino acid 34. Comparison with the Drosophila DNA places this methionine within two positions of the putative initial methionine in the Drosophila DNA (Tiong and Nash, 1993). Assuming that the Drosophila translation start site is as indicated, the positioning of a methionine in the human ORF two positions away indicates that this is the translation start in the human clone. The ORF in the human clone extends 5′ to the start of the insert. The putative translation start of the Drosophila gene was determined by comparison with the E. coli sequence. Interestingly, the Drosophila ORF extends an additional 44 amino acids 5′ of this methionine, but there are no additional methionines. To investigate further whether the entire FGARAT coding sequence is present in the human cDNA clone, we performed 5′ RACE on HeLa cell mRNA.

Sequencing of a RACE clone revealed an in-frame potential coding region of 10 additional non-methionine amino acids and then an in-frame UAA stop codon. Therefore, we suspect that this cDNA clone contains the entire FGARAT protein-coding region.
A BLASTN search using the Drosophila DNA sequence detected hFGARAT, but the homology was extremely limited. Drosophila bases 2840–2883 showed 86% identity to bases 1643–1686 of the human sequence.

The result of this PCR analysis using the primers amplifying bases 938–1109 in the middle region of the human cDNA is shown in Fig. 2.

The amplimer detected is 259 bp in human and hybrid cells and in the FGARAT containing P1 clone (see below, data not shown), indicating that this amplimer spans the intronic DNA sequence. The presence of an 87 bp intron in this clone was confirmed by DNA sequencing of the PCR amplimer. The amplification of intron DNA is evidence that the primers are not detecting a processed pseudogene.

3.3. Isolation of a P1 clone that corrects the defect in FGARAT deficient mutants of CHO-K1 cells
We used the same PCR primers to isolate a P1 clone, P97A12, containing a 68.5 kb insert. Fluorescence in-situ hybridization (FISH) mapping using P97A12 DNA confirmed mapping of the FGARAT gene to chromosome 17 and refined the mapping to chromosome region 17p13 (Fig. 3).

We have previously reported the isolation and characterization of AdeB CHO cell
mutants deficient in FGARAT activity (Barnes et al., 1994, Patterson, 1975).

AdeB cells display 100% plating efficiency in medium containing purines relative to wild-type CHO-K1 cells (approximately 90% of cells give rise to colonies). In the absence of purines, less than one colony per million AdeB cells plated produce colonies. Transfection of AdeB cells with linearized P97A12 DNA allowed clonal growth of 100–300 per 5×105 AdeB cells in the absence of purines. Several clones were isolated and expanded in purine-free medium for analysis. Fig. 4a shows by Western blot analysis that two independent clonally isolated transfectants produce a protein recognized by anti-FGARAT antibody (Barnes et al., 1994) that is not produced in the parental AdeB cells. This protein is the expected size, 145 kDa, for FGARAT.

We then examined the production of human-specific FGARAT mRNA by the same transfectants. Messenger RNA was isolated from human (HeLa), CHO-K1, AdeB, and the transfectants. A reverse transcriptase reaction was performed using random hexamers. The products of the reverse transcriptase reactions were PCR-amplified using the same primers used in Fig. 2 to map the FGARAT gene.

Only reverse transcription products from human cells and the transfectants could be PCR-amplified, and the size of the amplimer is 172 bp, as expected if the amplimer is indeed derived from reverse-transcribed FGARAT mRNA (Fig. 4b). These data provide convincing evidence that P97A12 contains all the information necessary to produce functional human FGARAT.
3.4. Analysis of the human FGARAT gene sequence
In B. subtilis, the activity of FGARAT requires two proteins, the products of the purL and purQ genes. The Drosophila protein resembles a fusion of the B. subtilis purL and purQ proteins (Tiong and Nash, 1993). The Drosophila FGARAT gene is reported to have two introns, one at bp 1091 and one at bp 3444 (Tiong and Nash, 1993). The second intron in the Drosophila gene occurs near the putative site of fusion of the B. subtilis genes. We designed PCR primers flanking the appropriate region in the human sequence, bases 3288–3463 in the human cDNA and analyzed the P1 clone. Instead of the expected 172 bp amplimer, a product of 259 bp is seen.

Sequencing of this PCR product detected an 87 bp intron at a position in the human gene 8 codons 5′ of the location of the intron in the Drosophila locus (Fig. 1).
An additional interesting feature of the DNA sequence of hFGARAT is that the 5′ end of the cDNA contains three copies of a 19 bp direct repeat, at bases 34–52, 54–72, and 74–92 according to the numbering system of the human FGARAT cDNA sequence in GenBank Accession No. AB002359. The repeats end eight bases upstream of the start site. Fig. 5 shows the first 120 bases of the human cDNA sequence with the repeats indicated by underlining. This sequence was analyzed using RepeatMasker (Smit, A.F.A., Green, P. RepeatMasker at HYPERLINK http://ftp.genome.washington.edu/RM/RepeatMasker.html). No repetitive sequences were detected using this program. This includes Alu, short interspersed repeats, long interspersed repeats, MIR, LINE2, retroviral sequences, LINE1 sequences and other repeats. The significance of these repeats is not known.

4. Discussion
4.1. Analysis of the structure of the FGARAT protein
We present here conclusive evidence for the identification and isolation of both a cDNA and a functional, full-length genomic clone encoding the human FGARAT locus.

This evidence includes sequence homology with the Drosophila gene (and 16 other FGARAT genes) (Tiong and Nash, 1993), mapping to human chromosome 17p13, previously shown by us to be the chromosome containing the FGARAT gene by Western blot analysis of a somatic cell hybrid mapping panel using anti-FGARAT antibody (Barnes et al., 1994), and functional complementation of the FGARAT deficiency in AdeB mutants of CHO cells.
Analysis of the amino acid sequence of human FGARAT and comparison with the sequences of other organisms from which the gene has been isolated provide insight into the evolution of the gene and the nature of the enzyme activity. FGARAT coding sequences have been identified for the eukaryotes Drosophila melanogaster, S. cerevisiae, S. pombe, and C. elegans. Additionally, full or partial sequences have been reported for at least 13 bacterial strains including three archaebacteria and 10 eubacteria (Table 1).
FGARAT catalyzes the ATP-dependent transfer of an amino group from glutamine to phosphoribosylformylglycineamide (FGAR), resulting in the production of phosphoribosylformylglycineamidine (FGAM) and ADP.

Therefore, the enzyme would be expected to contain an ATP-binding domain and a glutamine amide transfer domain.
These features of the protein are highly conserved in FGARAT from the eukaryotes and all the bacterial strains. Thus, a glycine-rich putative ATP-binding domain (Andreichuk et al., 1997) at positions 327–338 in the D. melanogaster sequence (numbering according to Fig. 1), indicated by underlining in Fig. 1, is essentially completely conserved in the human and C. elegans protein (11/12 identities, one conserved amino acid). In yeast and all 13 bacterial strains, 8/12 amino acids are identical. Interestingly, it is the same eight amino acids that are conserved in all organisms. Two other positions are highly conserved. Position 336 consists of the related amino acids leucine, valine, or isoleucine in all organisms (Table 2). Position 329 consists of alanine in 14 organisms, threonine in three, and glycine in one. The highly conserved nature of this sequence clearly argues for its functional importance. These relationships are summarized in Table 2.
Ebbole and Zalkin (1987) noted three conserved regions of various glutamine amidotransferases.

Within these regions, a cysteine at position 1180, a histidine at position 1310, and a glutamate at 1312 were hypothesized to be essential for glutamine amide transfer (Ebbole and Zalkin, 1987). All three of these amino acids are conserved in all 18 prokaryotic and eukaryotic FGARAT enzymes studied here. In Fig. 1, the overline above the first of these domains, 1132–1141 in the D. melanogaster protein, indicates the hypothesized first glutamine amide transfer domain amino acids according to Ebbole and Zalkin (1987). Interestingly, the first five of these amino acids are not highly conserved in all FGARATs (Table 2). However, the next three amino acids, FSY, are completely conserved in all organisms with only two exceptions, an A at position 1141 in M. jannaschii and an F at position 1141 in A. aeolius. The R at position 1313 in the third amino acid domain is conserved in all organisms except M. tuberculosis and M. leprae, which have an H at this position. Thus, the conservation of these residues certainly supports their functional importance.

We propose that the FSY sequence at positions 1139–1141 should be considered part of the first of the three glutamine amide transfer domains due to their high conservation. These relationships are also summarized in Table 2.
Previous comparisons of eight FGARAT enzymes revealed a total of 123 invariant amino acid residues (Andreichuk et al., 1997). Since that analysis, FGARAT sequence from 10 additional organisms has become available. Extension of the analysis of Andreichuk et al. (1997) to include these additional FGARAT sequences reveals that 83 of these amino acids remain conserved when the current set of organisms is examined. At least 84% of the 123 amino acids are conserved in each of the organisms studied here, although the exact subset of conserved amino acids is not identical in all organisms. Interestingly, one of the least conserved, at 84%, is C. elegans.
Several investigators have noted that in B. subtilis, two proteins carry out the complete FGARAT reaction, while in E. coli, a single protein carries out both functions. The B. subtilis proteins are designated purL, which corresponds to the amino end of the E. coli enzyme, and purQ, which corresponds to the carboxy domain. By sequence analysis, the E.

coli enzyme resembles a fusion of the domains present in B. subtilis. As shown here, the human enzyme is encoded by a single protein, as are the enzymes from D. melanogaster, C. elegans, S. cerevisiae, S. pombe, E. coli, S. typhimurium, and H. influenzae. In the other 10 bacterial strains, two proteins are required for FGARAT activity. These include all three representatives of the archaebacteria. These observations are consistent with the hypothesis that the most ancient organization of this enzymatic step was as two genes encoding two proteins.
It is interesting to speculate on the observation that FGARAT activity is carried on a single protein in all eukaryotes studied and in certain proteobacteria, whereas all other bacterial organisms require two proteins for this function. As pointed out by Tiong and Nash (1993), it seems unreasonable to assume that the eukaryotes evolved from the proteobacteria. Instead, this may be an example of chimeric evolution of the eukaryotic genome (Bult et al., 1996, Lake et al., 1999, Rivera et al., 1998). In this regard, the grouping of genes into two supergroups, informational and operational, offers a way of thinking about the evolution of the eukaryotic genome.

According to this grouping, informational genes include those involved in transcription, translation, and related processes. Operational genes are those involved in housekeeping functions such as intermediary metabolism or nucleotide synthesis (Bult et al., 1996, Lake et al., 1999, Rivera et al., 1998). Eukaryotes appear to have acquired their informational genes from an archaebacterium-like organism (e.g. M. jannaschii), and their operational genome primarily, but not exclusively, from a proteobacteria-like organism (e.g. E. coli). FGARAT is classified as an operational gene in this scheme (Bult et al., 1996). The finding that FGARAT is a single protein in human and all other eukaryotes so far examined and in all the proteobacteria, but consists of two proteins in eubacteria and archaebacteria, is consistent with this hypothesis (Table 1).
This still leaves open the question of whether the FGARAT gene encoding a single FGARAT protein arose from the two FGARAT genes encoding the two proteins required for FGARAT activity in some organisms, and if so, what caused this change in gene organization. Tiong and Nash (1993) identified residue 1085 as the primary purQ start site in their analysis of the D. melanogaster sequence.

Analysis of the junction between the purL and purQ domains in the organisms containing two proteins indicates that in four, B. subtilis, L. lactis, M. jannaschii, and M. thermoautotrophicum, the purQ protein domain begins in exactly the same site, residue 1085 of the D. melanogaster sequence of Fig. 1, indicated by the designation >purQ; in three, M. tuberculosis, M. leprae, and S. sp, it is two residues away at position 1087; in one, A. fulgidus, it is six residues away at position 1079; and in one, A. aeolicus, it is nine residues away at position 1094. This remarkable consistency of the start site of the purQ domain includes archaebacteria as well as eubacteria.
Tiong and Nash (1993) also identified a presumptive end of the purL homologous region at position 1046. This leaves an inter-domain connecting sequence of 39 amino acids. As discussed above, the D. melanogaster and human FGARAT amino acid sequences overall are 51% identical and 66% similar. The relatedness of the amino acid sequence in the 39 residue connecting sequence is much lower. Only 26% of the amino acid residues are identical, and only 28% are similar.

In addition, none of the residues found to be invariant among all FGARATs is within this region. All the purL domains end well before the inter-domain region.
Analysis of the DNA sequence of the 5′ end of the human FGARAT cDNA indicates that the methionine indicated in Fig. 1 is in fact the start site. There is a G at the −3 position, one of the important features of translation start sites (Kozak, 1996). In addition, 5′ RACE found an in-frame termination codon, UAA, 132 bases upstream of the proposed start site with no methionines between the termination codon and the proposed start site.
FGARAT is one of two amidotransferases in the first 10 steps of IMP synthesis (Zalkin and Dixon, 1992, Zalkin, 1993). The other amidotransferase, amidophosphoribosyltransferase (PRAT), is often considered to be the rate-limiting and regulatory step of the pathway and can be allosterically regulated (Becker et al., 1989, Becker and Roessler, 1995). There is minimal sequence homology between PRAT and FGARAT. Interestingly, we have reported the isolation of mutant CHO cells, AdePAB, which require purines for growth and which are defective in both PRAT and FGARAT glutamine-dependent amidotransferase activities (Oates et al., 1980).

Somatic cell hybrid studies demonstrate that the AdePAB defects cannot be complemented by AdeA mutants, lacking PRAT, or AdeB mutants, lacking FGARAT (Oates et al., 1980). CHO cell mutants lacking any of the other enzyme activities required for de-novo purine synthesis, when hybridized with AdePAB cells, do eliminate their requirement for purines for growth (Oates et al., 1980). Revertants of AdePAB cells that have regained the activities can be isolated; therefore, these mutants cannot be deletions. We and others have regionally mapped the PRAT locus to chromosome 4q12 and FGARAT to chromosome 17p13 in humans (Barton et al., 1991, Stanley and Chu, 1978). PRAT and FGARAT also map to different chromosomes in Drosophila (Clark, 1994, Tiong et al., 1989, Zalkin, 1993). Therefore, it is unlikely that the PRAT and FGARAT genes are in close proximity to each other in the CHO cell genome, allowing both to be inactivated by a cis-acting mutation. These data suggest that there is a third genetic locus acting in trans involved in encoding or regulating these two steps, and it is this locus that is affected in the AdePAB mutants.

This locus could, for example, encode a protein that binds to both PRAT and FGARAT and is required for both activities or, alternatively, causes an interaction directly between PRAT and FGARAT that is required for activity. Assessment of these possibilities will be aided greatly by isolation of human FGARAT cDNA and genomic clones.
With the cloning of FGARAT, human genes encoding all of the known proteins involved in de-novo IMP synthesis have been isolated. Isolation of clones encoding other enzymes of this pathway has been instrumental in determining the multifunctional nature of some of the enzymes in the pathway (Chang et al., 1990, Gnirke et al., 1991, Schild et al., 1990, Zalkin and Dixon, 1992) and in revealing aspects of the possible coordinate regulation of these genes (Brayton et al., 1994, Chen et al., 1997, Gavalas et al., 1993). The two amidotransferases in the pathway, PRAT and FGARAT, are both important from a regulatory point of view and as targets for cancer chemotherapy. Genetic evidence suggests that the regulation of these two loci must be coordinated and involve a third genetic locus (Oates et al., 1980).

The isolation of cDNA and genomic clones for FGARAT, along with the availability of clones for all the other steps in the pathway, should enable detailed investigations, previously not possible, of the regulatory mechanisms used by human cells to control the rate of de-novo purine synthesis.
