HUMAN 6-PYRUVOYLTETRAHYDROPTERINSYNTHASE: cDNA CLONING AND HETEROLOGOUS EXPRESSION OF THE RECOMBINANT ENZYME*

6-Pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase(PTPS) is involved in the biosynthesis of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH,), an essential cofactor for enzymes such as the hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase. BH, deficiency causes malignant hyperphenylalaninemia. We cloned the human liver cDNA encoding PTPS. The coding region for PTPS contains 145 amino acids and predicts a polypeptide of 16’387 Da. The human amino acid sequence showed a 82% identity with the rat liver sequence. Expression of the cDNA in E. coli yielded the active enzyme and showed immunoreactivity with antibodies against the rat liver PTPS. This is the basis for the molecular understanding of BH, deficiency in patients suffering from a defect in PTPS activity.

Tetrahydrobiopterin(BH,) is the essential cofactor of the aromatic amino acid hydroxylases(I), the glycerol ether monooxygenase(2) and the arginine utilizing nitric oxide synthase(3,4). Either a deficiency in the pterin moiety, or a defect in the phenylalanine hydroxylase leads to hyperphenylalaninemia, a disorder accompanied by severe progressive mental retardation(5). BH, biosynthesis requires at least three successive enzymatic steps carried out by the enzymes guanosine triphosphate cyclohydrolase I, 6-pyruvoyl tetrahydropterin synthase (PTPS), sepiapterin reductase, and probably, aldose reductase(6). Most of the patients suffering from BH, deficiency described so far have been shown to bear a defect in the second enzymatic step in the biosynthetic pathway, the PTPS, which catalyzes the conversion of 7,8-dihydroneopterin triphosphate to 6-pyruvoyl tetrahydropterin, thereby eliminating the triphosphate residue.

As a first step towards a detailed understanding of the genetic nature of the defects caused by PTPS deficiency, we were interested in the molecular cloning of the corresponding human cDNA. Since the molecular cloning of the rat liver enzyme was published recently(7), we used this information for reisolating the rat cDNA. With the rat probe, we screened a human fetal liver cDNA library and isolated a human clone encoding the PTPS. Expression of the recombinant protein in E. coli proved the cloning of the correct human cDNA. This is the basis for future molecular analysis of BH, deficiency due to defects in PTPS activity.

Materials and Methods

Oligonucleotides and general methods
Oligonucleotides were synthesized on a Gene Assembler Plus DNA synthesizer (Pharmacia LKB). Oligonucleotides used to isolate the rat cDNA for PTPS by PCR are based on the published sequence (see Fig. 6 in Ref. 7): 
PTPS1 (nt position 1-18; 5'-CGGAATTCATGAACGCGGCGGTTGGC-3') 
PTPSB (nt position 411-432; 5'-CGGGATCCTTCTCCTTTGTAGACCACAATG-3').

Two specific primers were synthesized to isolate the 5'-end of the human PTPS cDNA (Fig. 1):
PTPS7 (5'-GGCACATCCATATCCAG-3')
and PTPSS (5'-CGGGATCCGGGGCTGCATAATCGCCTCC-3'). 

For overexpression of the recombinant enzyme, the following primers were used (nt positions refer to Fig. 1):
PTPS12 (nt 447-465; 5'-CGGAATTCCAATGCTAACCCCAATAGC-3') 
and PTPS13 (nt 10-29; 5'-TCCCCCGGGrrGATTTAAATAAGGAGGAGGAATATGAGCACGGAAGGTGGTGG-3').

DNA hybridizations, cDNA synthesis, PCR, and λ-phage handling were performed according to standard protocols (8).

Isolation of the rat gene for PTPS
Total RNA was isolated from 1 g of frozen rat liver following the protocol by Chirgwin et al. (9). This yielded approximately 74 µg RNA, from which 2 µg was incubated with M-MLV reverse transcriptase (BRL) together with oligodeoxythymidine as a primer to produce cDNA. This cDNA pool was the template for PCR using the oligonucleotides PTPS1 and PTPSB in a standard reaction. The PCR product was cloned into pUC18 to generate pRSY1, and subsequently sequenced. The DNA sequence was identical to the published sequence, with the exception of a guanine instead of an adenine at position 110 (Fig. 6 in Ref. 7).

Construction of a PTPS-overproducing plasmid and protein expression
The complete cDNA encoding the human PTPS was the template for PCR using the primers PTPS12 and PTPS13. Primer PTPS13 contained a SmaI restriction site at the 5'-end for cloning, followed by several stop codons and a 'Shine-Dalgarno' sequence (Fig. 3A; 10). The PCR product was digested with SmaI and EcoRI, and subsequently cloned into the expression vector PING-1 (11) to generate pHSY10. The PTPS-overproducing strain E. coli MC1061 (12), harboring plasmid pHSY10, was grown at 37°C in LB medium (8) containing 40 µg/ml ampicillin to an OD at 600 nm of 0.45. Overproduction of PTPS was achieved in 2.5 h with the addition of 0.75% L-(+)-arabinose (Fluka). The cells were collected by centrifugation, resuspended in buffer A (20 mM Tris-HCl buffer, pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride, 2 mM 1,4-dithioerythritol, 10% glycerol, 5 µg/ml leupeptin, 0.1% NP40) and frozen in liquid nitrogen.

Lysozyme was added (to 0.4 mg/ml) to the thawed E. coli cells, and subsequently incubated for 1 min at 37°C followed by 30 min at 4°C. Freezing in liquid nitrogen and thawing at 8°C followed by 40 min centrifugation at 40,000 rpm (Sorvall T-1270 rotor), resulted in the crude protein fraction. Aliquots were stored frozen in liquid nitrogen and later used for directly assaying PTPS activity.

Assay for PTPS activity in E. coli extracts and identification of immunoreactive PTPS
Human PTPS activity was assayed as described (13). Immunoreactive PTPS was identified by Western blot analysis using a rabbit anti-rat PTPS antibody raised against the enzyme purified from an E. coli strain overexpressing the recombinant rat PTPS (unpublished). Following 7-18% SDS-polyacrylamide gradient gel electrophoresis (Multiphor II handbook, Pharmacia LKB) of whole E. coli extracts and transfer to nitrocellulose, standard antibody reaction was done as described (14). For visualization, a goat anti-rabbit antibody conjugated with alkaline phosphatase was used (BioRad).

RESULTS and DISCUSSION

Isolation of the human cDNA for PTPS using the isolated rat cDNA
The rat PTPS cDNA cloned in pRSY1 was labelled with ³²P and used for screening a λgt11-vector-derived human fetal liver cDNA library (Clontech). Approximately 5 x 10⁵ phage clones were screened. After rescreening, Southern hybridization, and DNA sequence analysis, only one λ-clone, λHSY2, was found to be coding for PTPS. Subcloning and DNA sequence analysis of λHSY2 revealed an insert fragment of approximately 2 kb, harboring at one end the cDNA encoding part of the putative human PTPS cDNA (position 46 to 662 in Fig. 1). The other end of the insert fragment (approx. 1.3 kb) of clone λHSY2 contained the partial coding region for the human complement protein C8 (β subunit), starting from the EcoRI restriction site (nt position 701 in Ref. 15). The 3'-end of this gene contained a polyA stretch of 31 adenines followed by the partial coding region for the PTPS, reading in the same direction. The isolation of a clone harboring two completely different fused reading frames separated by a polyA stretch was most probably due to a cloning artefact, whereby two randomly ligated cDNA fragments were inserted into the λgt11 vector.

PCR screening was applied to isolate a different cDNA clone harboring the complete 5'-coding sequence for the human PTPS. To this end, the λgt11-specific primers (λgt11-forward and λgt11-reverse, Biolabs) together with two human PTPS-specific primers (PTPS7 and PTPSS; see Fig. 1) were used to amplify a potential cDNA fragment encoding the 5'-portion of PTPS. As a template, a pool of approximately 10⁶ λ clones was mixed to perform a first round of amplification with either the primers PTPS7 and λgt11-forward, or PTPS7 and λgt11-reverse. A second round of amplification was done with a 1:50 dilution from the first reaction mixture, now using the oligonucleotide PTPSS and the same λ-specific primer. From the different DNA fragments amplified, the largest was cloned. DNA sequence analysis revealed the putative 5'-end of the coding region for the human PTPS plus additional 9 bp upstream of the ATG (see Fig. 1). We believe that the ATG at bp position 10 in Fig. 1 is the translation start site for the human PTPS, due to the following reasons (see also below):(i) Although the homology in the N-terminal region between the human and the rat sequence is significantly lower compared to the rest of the protein, the length, which differs only in one amino acid between the two proteins, argues for the correct start site at nt position 10. (ii) Expression of this recombinant polypeptide in E. coli revealed an active enzyme.

The inserts of the two overlapping cDNA clones were ligated together using the single NcoI restriction site in the coding region for PTPS to generate a complete coding sequence.

DNA sequence analysis and comparison of its deduced amino acid sequence to other PTPS sequences
The complete cDNA sequence for the human PTPS is shown in Fig. 1. An open reading frame starts with ATG at position 10 and extends to bp 444, thus coding for a polypeptide of 145 amino acids. The stop codon is followed by an 198 bp untranslated region and an adjacent stretch of 17 adenines, probably derived from the polyadenylated 3'-end of the mRNA. The deduced molecular mass of the complete predicted polypeptide for the human PTPS subunit is 16,387 Da. This is in good agreement with the value obtained from SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis of the human pituitary gland subunit (16.5 kDa; 16).

A comparison of the amino acid sequences between the human, the rat, and the only partially available salmon PTPS is given in Fig. 2. Extensive homology between the three polypeptides can be found almost throughout the entire sequences. The unprocessed human and rat sequences differ only in one amino acid in length. The two proteins show 82% identity, whereby the only significant difference (more than two consecutive amino acid differences) between all three proteins is located in the amino terminal end. The rat enzyme has been reported to be modified by a posttranslational proteolytic removal of the first four residues (7).

For the salmon enzyme, two different amine termini were found by a combination of Edman degradation and mass spectrometry, indicating the presence of similar, but N-terminally different isoforms (17). Since we have no N-terminal amino acid sequence information, we do not know the mature amine terminus of the human enzyme. Interestingly, the human enzyme has a cysteine residue at position 10, which is missing in the rat and in the salmon proteins. However, the salmon PTPS has a cysteine at position 20 in Fig. 2. A second cysteine in the sequence is conserved in both rat and human enzymes (amino acid 43 in the human sequence), whereas the sequence for salmon in this region is unknown. The rat enzyme has been described as having a strong homology to a potential ATPase activity site of large T antigens from different polyoma viruses (7). This site, indicated in Fig. 2 with residues 70-94, appears to be highly conserved in all three proteins. Only defined structural and functional analysis of PTPS, e.g., using the recombinant enzyme (see below), will show a potential involvement of this particular site in the elimination of triphosphate of the dihydroneopterin triphosphate substrate.

Heterologous expression of the human PTPS in E. coli
For overexpression of the human PTPS cDNA in E. coli we used the two-cistronic expression vector PING-1, harboring an inducible arabinose-responding promoter (11). The full-length human PTPS coding region was cloned into this vector to generate pHSY10 (see Fig. 3 A). Upon induction of E. coli cells harboring either PING-1 or pHSY10, the prepared extracts showed an additional band of 16.5 kDa only when PTPS cDNA was present on the expression vector (pHSY10, Fig. 3 B). This 16.5 kDa polypeptide, the putative PTPS subunit, was clearly immunoreactive when analyzed in the corresponding Western blot using polyclonal antibodies raised against the purified rat PTPS (Fig. 3 C). Additional immunoreactive material present in E. coli/pHSY10 (approximately 41 kDa and 65 kDa) might be due to homo-multimer formation, because these bands were also observed when purified rat PTPS was incubated with the same antiserum on a Western blot (unpublished observation).

Recombinant PTPS activity was measured in a standard enzyme assay by following the production of BH4 (Fig. 4). No activity was detected in extracts of E. coli/PING-1. A crude extract harboring the cDNA for the human PTPS had a specific activity of 1.32 nmol of BH4 formed per mg protein per min. This activity is 1914-fold higher than the activity reported in crude extracts of human liver (13).

This work provides the basis for purification of human PTPS in the large quantities needed to perform defined biochemical and biophysical studies. In addition, the cloned cDNA will allow to isolate the corresponding genomic gene(s), and to study the genes from patients suffering from BH4 deficiency due to a defect in PTPS activity.

HUMAN 6-PYRUVOYLTETRAHYDROPTERINSYNTHASE: cDNA CLONING AND HETEROLOGOUS EXPRESSION OF THE RECOMBINANT ENZYME*

6-Pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase(PTPS) is involved in the biosynthesis of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH,), an essential cofactor for enzymes such as the hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase. BH, deficiency causes malignant hyperphenylalaninemia. We cloned the human liver cDNA encoding PTPS. The coding region for PTPS contains 145 amino acids and predicts a polypeptide of 16’387 Da. The human amino acid sequence showed a 82% identity with the rat liver sequence. Expression of the cDNA in E. coli yielded the active enzyme and showed immunoreactivity with antibodies against the rat liver PTPS. This is the basis for the molecular understanding of BH, deficiency in patients suffering from a defect in PTPS activity.

Tetrahydrobiopterin(BH,) is the essential cofactor of the aromatic amino acid hydroxylases(I), the glycerol ether monooxygenase(2) and the arginine utilizing nitric oxide synthase(3,4). Either a deficiency in the pterin moiety, or a defect in the phenylalanine hydroxylase leads to hyperphenylalaninemia, a disorder accompanied by severe progressive mental retardation(5). BH, biosynthesis requires at least three successive enzymatic steps carried out by the enzymes guanosine triphosphate cyclohydrolase I, 6-pyruvoyl tetrahydropterin synthase (PTPS), sepiapterin reductase, and probably, aldose reductase(6).

Most of the patients suffering from BH, deficiency described so far have been shown to bear a defect in the second enzymatic step in the biosynthetic pathway, the PTPS, which catalyzes the conversion of 7,8-dihydroneopterin triphosphate to 6-pyruvoyl tetrahydropterin, thereby eliminating the triphosphate residue.

As a first step towards a detailed understanding of the genetic nature of the defects caused by PTPS deficiency, we were interested in the molecular cloning of the corresponding human cDNA. Since the molecular cloning of the rat liver enzyme was published recently(7), we used this information for reisolating the rat cDNA. With the rat probe, we screened a human fetal liver cDNA library and isolated a human clone encoding the PTPS. Expression of the recombinant protein in E. coli proved the cloning of the correct human cDNA. This is the basis for future molecular analysis of BH, deficiency due to defects in PTPS activity.

Materials and Methods

Oligonucleotides and general methods
Oligonucleotides were synthesized on a Gene Assembler Plus DNA synthesizer (Pharmacia LKB). Oligonucleotides used to isolate the rat cDNA for PTPS by PCR are based on the published sequence (see Fig. 6 in Ref.

7): 
PTPS1 (nt position 1-18; 5'-CGGAATTCATGAACGCGGCGGTTGGC-3') 
PTPSB (nt position 411-432; 5'-CGGGATCCTTCTCCTTTGTAGACCACAATG-3').

Two specific primers were synthesized to isolate the 5'-end of the human PTPS cDNA (Fig. 1):
PTPS7 (5'-GGCACATCCATATCCAG-3')
and PTPSS (5'-CGGGATCCGGGGCTGCATAATCGCCTCC-3'). 

For overexpression of the recombinant enzyme, the following primers were used (nt positions refer to Fig. 1):
PTPS12 (nt 447-465; 5'-CGGAATTCCAATGCTAACCCCAATAGC-3') 
and PTPS13 (nt 10-29; 5'-TCCCCCGGGrrGATTTAAATAAGGAGGAGGAATATGAGCACGGAAGGTGGTGG-3').

DNA hybridizations, cDNA synthesis, PCR, and λ-phage handling were performed according to standard protocols (8).

Isolation of the rat gene for PTPS
Total RNA was isolated from 1 g of frozen rat liver following the protocol by Chirgwin et al. (9). This yielded approximately 74 µg RNA, from which 2 µg was incubated with M-MLV reverse transcriptase (BRL) together with oligodeoxythymidine as a primer to produce cDNA. This cDNA pool was the template for PCR using the oligonucleotides PTPS1 and PTPSB in a standard reaction. The PCR product was cloned into pUC18 to generate pRSY1, and subsequently sequenced. The DNA sequence was identical to the published sequence, with the exception of a guanine instead of an adenine at position 110 (Fig. 6 in Ref.

7).

Construction of a PTPS-overproducing plasmid and protein expression
The complete cDNA encoding the human PTPS was the template for PCR using the primers PTPS12 and PTPS13. Primer PTPS13 contained a SmaI restriction site at the 5'-end for cloning, followed by several stop codons and a 'Shine-Dalgarno' sequence (Fig. 3A; 10). The PCR product was digested with SmaI and EcoRI, and subsequently cloned into the expression vector PING-1 (11) to generate pHSY10. The PTPS-overproducing strain E. coli MC1061 (12), harboring plasmid pHSY10, was grown at 37°C in LB medium (8) containing 40 µg/ml ampicillin to an OD at 600 nm of 0.45. Overproduction of PTPS was achieved in 2.5 h with the addition of 0.75% L-(+)-arabinose (Fluka). The cells were collected by centrifugation, resuspended in buffer A (20 mM Tris-HCl buffer, pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride, 2 mM 1,4-dithioerythritol, 10% glycerol, 5 µg/ml leupeptin, 0.1% NP40) and frozen in liquid nitrogen.

Lysozyme was added (to 0.4 mg/ml) to the thawed E. coli cells, and subsequently incubated for 1 min at 37°C followed by 30 min at 4°C.

Freezing in liquid nitrogen and thawing at 8°C followed by 40 min centrifugation at 40,000 rpm (Sorvall T-1270 rotor), resulted in the crude protein fraction. Aliquots were stored frozen in liquid nitrogen and later used for directly assaying PTPS activity.

Assay for PTPS activity in E. coli extracts and identification of immunoreactive PTPS
Human PTPS activity was assayed as described (13). Immunoreactive PTPS was identified by Western blot analysis using a rabbit anti-rat PTPS antibody raised against the enzyme purified from an E. coli strain overexpressing the recombinant rat PTPS (unpublished). Following 7-18% SDS-polyacrylamide gradient gel electrophoresis (Multiphor II handbook, Pharmacia LKB) of whole E. coli extracts and transfer to nitrocellulose, standard antibody reaction was done as described (14). For visualization, a goat anti-rabbit antibody conjugated with alkaline phosphatase was used (BioRad).

RESULTS and DISCUSSION

Isolation of the human cDNA for PTPS using the isolated rat cDNA
The rat PTPS cDNA cloned in pRSY1 was labelled with ³²P and used for screening a λgt11-vector-derived human fetal liver cDNA library (Clontech). Approximately 5 x 10⁵ phage clones were screened. After rescreening, Southern hybridization, and DNA sequence analysis, only one λ-clone, λHSY2, was found to be coding for PTPS.

Subcloning and DNA sequence analysis of λHSY2 revealed an insert fragment of approximately 2 kb, harboring at one end the cDNA encoding part of the putative human PTPS cDNA (position 46 to 662 in Fig. 1). The other end of the insert fragment (approx. 1.3 kb) of clone λHSY2 contained the partial coding region for the human complement protein C8 (β subunit), starting from the EcoRI restriction site (nt position 701 in Ref. 15). The 3'-end of this gene contained a polyA stretch of 31 adenines followed by the partial coding region for the PTPS, reading in the same direction. The isolation of a clone harboring two completely different fused reading frames separated by a polyA stretch was most probably due to a cloning artefact, whereby two randomly ligated cDNA fragments were inserted into the λgt11 vector.

PCR screening was applied to isolate a different cDNA clone harboring the complete 5'-coding sequence for the human PTPS. To this end, the λgt11-specific primers (λgt11-forward and λgt11-reverse, Biolabs) together with two human PTPS-specific primers (PTPS7 and PTPSS; see Fig. 1) were used to amplify a potential cDNA fragment encoding the 5'-portion of PTPS.

As a template, a pool of approximately 10⁶ λ clones was mixed to perform a first round of amplification with either the primers PTPS7 and λgt11-forward, or PTPS7 and λgt11-reverse. A second round of amplification was done with a 1:50 dilution from the first reaction mixture, now using the oligonucleotide PTPSS and the same λ-specific primer. From the different DNA fragments amplified, the largest was cloned. DNA sequence analysis revealed the putative 5'-end of the coding region for the human PTPS plus additional 9 bp upstream of the ATG (see Fig. 1). We believe that the ATG at bp position 10 in Fig. 1 is the translation start site for the human PTPS, due to the following reasons (see also below):(i) Although the homology in the N-terminal region between the human and the rat sequence is significantly lower compared to the rest of the protein, the length, which differs only in one amino acid between the two proteins, argues for the correct start site at nt position 10. (ii) Expression of this recombinant polypeptide in E.

coli revealed an active enzyme.

The inserts of the two overlapping cDNA clones were ligated together using the single NcoI restriction site in the coding region for PTPS to generate a complete coding sequence.

DNA sequence analysis and comparison of its deduced amino acid sequence to other PTPS sequences
The complete cDNA sequence for the human PTPS is shown in Fig. 1. An open reading frame starts with ATG at position 10 and extends to bp 444, thus coding for a polypeptide of 145 amino acids. The stop codon is followed by an 198 bp untranslated region and an adjacent stretch of 17 adenines, probably derived from the polyadenylated 3'-end of the mRNA. The deduced molecular mass of the complete predicted polypeptide for the human PTPS subunit is 16,387 Da. This is in good agreement with the value obtained from SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis of the human pituitary gland subunit (16.5 kDa; 16).

A comparison of the amino acid sequences between the human, the rat, and the only partially available salmon PTPS is given in Fig. 2. Extensive homology between the three polypeptides can be found almost throughout the entire sequences.

The unprocessed human and rat sequences differ only in one amino acid in length. The two proteins show 82% identity, whereby the only significant difference (more than two consecutive amino acid differences) between all three proteins is located in the amino terminal end. The rat enzyme has been reported to be modified by a posttranslational proteolytic removal of the first four residues (7).

For the salmon enzyme, two different amine termini were found by a combination of Edman degradation and mass spectrometry, indicating the presence of similar, but N-terminally different isoforms (17). Since we have no N-terminal amino acid sequence information, we do not know the mature amine terminus of the human enzyme. Interestingly, the human enzyme has a cysteine residue at position 10, which is missing in the rat and in the salmon proteins. However, the salmon PTPS has a cysteine at position 20 in Fig. 2. A second cysteine in the sequence is conserved in both rat and human enzymes (amino acid 43 in the human sequence), whereas the sequence for salmon in this region is unknown.

The rat enzyme has been described as having a strong homology to a potential ATPase activity site of large T antigens from different polyoma viruses (7). This site, indicated in Fig. 2 with residues 70-94, appears to be highly conserved in all three proteins. Only defined structural and functional analysis of PTPS, e.g., using the recombinant enzyme (see below), will show a potential involvement of this particular site in the elimination of triphosphate of the dihydroneopterin triphosphate substrate.

Heterologous expression of the human PTPS in E. coli
For overexpression of the human PTPS cDNA in E. coli we used the two-cistronic expression vector PING-1, harboring an inducible arabinose-responding promoter (11). The full-length human PTPS coding region was cloned into this vector to generate pHSY10 (see Fig. 3 A). Upon induction of E. coli cells harboring either PING-1 or pHSY10, the prepared extracts showed an additional band of 16.5 kDa only when PTPS cDNA was present on the expression vector (pHSY10, Fig. 3 B). This 16.5 kDa polypeptide, the putative PTPS subunit, was clearly immunoreactive when analyzed in the corresponding Western blot using polyclonal antibodies raised against the purified rat PTPS (Fig. 3 C). Additional immunoreactive material present in E.

coli/pHSY10 (approximately 41 kDa and 65 kDa) might be due to homo-multimer formation, because these bands were also observed when purified rat PTPS was incubated with the same antiserum on a Western blot (unpublished observation).

Recombinant PTPS activity was measured in a standard enzyme assay by following the production of BH4 (Fig. 4). No activity was detected in extracts of E. coli/PING-1. A crude extract harboring the cDNA for the human PTPS had a specific activity of 1.32 nmol of BH4 formed per mg protein per min. This activity is 1914-fold higher than the activity reported in crude extracts of human liver (13).

This work provides the basis for purification of human PTPS in the large quantities needed to perform defined biochemical and biophysical studies. In addition, the cloned cDNA will allow to isolate the corresponding genomic gene(s), and to study the genes from patients suffering from BH4 deficiency due to a defect in PTPS activity.
