1. Introduction
The amino acid 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC) is a key metabolic intermediate in the biosynthesis of the plant hormone ethylene. This gaseous hormone is a vital signaling molecule that regulates many facets of plant growth and development (Abeles et al., 1992). ACC synthase (ACS) (methylthioadenosine lyase EC 4.4.1.14) catalyzes the penultimate and rate-determining step of ethylene biosynthesis, which is the conversion of S-adenosyl-l-methionine (SAM) to 5′-methylthioadenosine (MTA) and ACC (Fig. 1A). Ethylene is subsequently produced by ACC oxidase.
The biosynthesis and utilization of ACC appear to be limited to plants and microorganisms. There are currently only three known metabolic fates for ACC within these organisms. In plants, ACC is either oxidized to form ethylene by ACC oxidase or it is covalently modified by malonylation at the α-amino group as a mechanism for controlling the amount of ACC available for ethylene biosynthesis (Hoffman et al., 1982). The third metabolic fate of ACC occurs in microorganisms where it is converted to α-ketobutyrate and ammonia by the action of ACC deaminase (Honma, 1985).
Although ACC has been used in pharmacological studies of the mammalian N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor (i.e. Nahum-Levy et al., 1999), there is no evidence that ACC is produced in animals. The recent report describing the identification of a gene encoding a putative ACS in Japanese pufferfish (Fugu rubripes) (Peixoto et al., 2000), and the corresponding gene for a potential human orthologue located on the short arm of chromosome 11 (11p11), raises the intriguing possibility that ACC may be synthesized in animals. The mRNA for each of these genes was shown to be present in tissues from their respective organisms, demonstrating that these genes are expressed.
If ACC were produced in humans and other animals, the possible biosynthesis of the important plant regulatory hormone, ethylene, would have important physiological consequences. To date, however, there have been no reports of animal genes that would encode homologues of the three known enzymes that act on ACC. Thus, the metabolic fate of nascent ACC, if formed in animals, can not be deduced. We describe here the cloning of a cDNA encoding the putative human ACS (PHACS) and the characterization of the expressed and purified 58 kDa recombinant protein.

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
SAM was purchased from Calbiochem (La Jolla, CA). Bovine liver l-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH Type VI, G2009), l-vinylglycine (l-VG), and other amino acids used were from Sigma (St. Louis, MO). Ni-NTA Superflow resin was purchased from Qiagen (Valencia, CA). IMAGE EST clone 3632065 was obtained from Incyte Genomics Inc. (St. Louis, MO). Synthetic oligonucleotides were purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies (Coralville, IA). Other reagents were of the highest quality available.
2.2. Cloning the PHACS cDNA
Rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE) was employed to obtain the 5′ and 3′ ends of the full-length PHACS cDNA from a human prostate Marathon-Ready cDNA library (Clontech, Palo Alto, CA) using the manufacturer's Advantage 2 polymerase mixture and recommended PCR conditions. The gene-specific primers used for RACE were based on the human prostate EST clone (GenBank, AI676022), which displays homology to the apple ACS open reading frame. These primers are HACS1 (5′-CGT GGG GCT GGC TTC TTC ATC TGG GTT G-3′), HACS2 (5′-CCC AGG CAA AGC CGG TGG ACC TGG TCT G-3′), and the nested primers NHACS1 (5′-CTT GAG AAA GTA CCT GCC CAA GGG CAC C-3′) and NHACS2 (5′-AGA AGA CAA AGC GAA ACC AAC CAG GCT C-3′). The 5′ and 3′ fragments of the PHACS open reading frame were joined by recombinant PCR using outside primers BNHACS (5′-GCG GGA TCC CAT ATG TTC ACC CTT CCT CAA AAG GAC T-3′) and hHIS (5′-ATA AGA ATG CGG CCG CTT AGT GAT GGT GAT GGT GAT GCC TGC GTT-3′), which introduce a His6-tag at the carboxy-terminus of the PHACS protein. A carboxy-terminal His6-tag has been shown not to impair the catalytic function of either apple ACS or E. coli aspartate aminotransferase (Feng and Kirsch, 2000; Koch and Kirsch, unpublished data), which are predicted structural neighbors of PHACS (see Section 3.2). To facilitate cloning, a BamHI restriction endonuclease cleavage site within the PHACS coding region was removed by silent mutagenesis using the primers dbam1 (5′-AGG GCA TTG GGG ATA CCC TTC TTG AGT CGT-3′) and dbam2 (5′-CAC GAC TCA AGA AGG GTA TCC CCA ATG CCC-3′). The PHACS open reading frame was cloned into the BamHI and NotI sites of the Pichia pastoris expression plasmid pPIC3 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA). The DNA sequence of the final clone was verified.
2.3. Bioinformatics
BLAST searches of the human EST database identified several ESTs that display homology to plant ACSs with apple ACS (SwissProt, p37821) as the query. Multiple sequence alignments were produced with ClustalW using the default settings within MacVector 6.0.1 software (Oxford Molecular, Beaverton, OR). A search for conserved protein domains was performed with PFAM (Bateman et al., 2000) (http://www.sanger.ac.uk/Software/Pfam/index.shtml). The three-dimensional structure prediction algorithms/structural neighbor search methods of Fischer and Eisenberg (1996) (http://fold.doe-mbi.ucla.edu/), 3D-PSSM (Kelley et al., 2000) (http://www.bmm.icnet.uk/~3dpssm/), and FFAS (Rychlewski et al., 2000) (http://bioinformatics.burnham-inst.org/FFAS/) were used to identify probable structural neighbors of PHACS.
2.4. Expression and purification
Recombinant His6-tagged PHACS was expressed in P. pastoris strain GS115 and purified by Ni-NTA chromatography as described for His6-tagged apple ACS (Feng and Kirsch, 2000). The concentration of purified PHACS was determined from the calculated extinction coefficient (ε280nm=7.87×104 M−1 cm−1; http://expasy.cbr.nrc.ca/tools/protparam.html) (Gill and von Hippel, 1989).
2.5. Kinetic analysis
The ACS-catalyzed conversion of SAM to ACC and MTA (Fig. 1A) was monitored by an adenosine deaminase coupled enzyme assay (White et al., 1994). Deamination of l-VG (Fig. 1B) by PHACS was assessed by monitoring the formation of ammonia using the glutamate dehydrogenase coupled assay described previously (Feng and Kirsch, 2000). Single-turnover aminotransferase experiments were performed by analyzing the shift in pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) absorbance maxima from 422 to 320 nm which accompanies the reductive amination of PLP during the first half of the transamination reaction (Feng et al., 2000).
2.6. Homology model of PHACS
A structural model of the PHACS protein was generated from the 1b8g apple ACS dimer structure (Capitani et al., 1999). A pairwise alignment between the apple ACS and PHACS sequences provided the input data for the MODELLER 4.0 program (Sali and Blundell, 1993). The alignment was improved stepwise based on the MODELLER output and on a multiple sequence alignment of 38 plant ACS sequences. Using the improved alignment, 100 ‘candidate’ models of PHACS were generated and filtered according to their stereochemical quality. The best model was chosen for subsequent energy minimization and constant temperature torsion angle dynamics with X-PLOR 3.85 (Brünger, 1992). The geometry of the internal aldimine linkage was optimized in this phase. The model was validated with the WHAT_CHECK server, which reported no major problems.

3. Results
3.1. Cloning of the PHACS cDNA
The cloned PHACS cDNA encodes a 501 amino acid protein (Fig. 2) with a calculated molecular weight of 58 kDa. The 3′ end of the cDNA, derived from 3′-RACE, contains untranslated sequences that include a putative polyadenylation signal. The 5′ end of the PHACS cDNA was deduced from the DNA sequences of several cloned 5′-RACE products, a human uterus EST (GenBank, BE393764; IMAGE clone 3632065), and the genomic DNA sequence harboring the PHACS gene (GenBank, U73628). It is noteworthy that there is a one base discrepancy between the reported DNA sequence of IMAGE clone 3632065 and the corresponding genomic DNA sequence encoding the 5′ UTR of PHACS. There is an in-frame TAG stop codon 378 bp upstream of the initiator methionine ATG codon in the genomic DNA sequence that is absent in the reported sequence for the IMAGE clone. We re-sequenced the IMAGE clone and found that the reported DNA sequence is off by one base and therefore the PHACS 5′ UTR contains an in-frame stop codon. The PHACS coding sequence used for expression of the recombinant protein was constructed by recombinant PCR using 5′-RACE and 3′-RACE products (Higuchi, 1990). The exon arrangement within this portion of the PHACS cDNA was independently verified by sequencing direct amplification PCR products from the Marathon-Ready cDNA library. The PHACS coding sequence and 3′ UTR are derived from 14 exons, with an additional exon encompassing the 5′ UTR. The genomic organization of splice site junctions for the 14 exon–exon boundaries within the PHACS coding sequence from 5′ to 3′ are type 0, 0, 0, II, 0, I, 0, 0, II, II, 0, I, 0, and I, respectively (Fig. 3) (Sharp, 1981). It is important to note that this is the exact order of splice site types found in the predicted coding sequence for the putative Fugu ACS. All of the splice sites within the PHACS cDNA contain ‘GT’ splice donor and ‘AG’ splice acceptor consensus sequences (Fig. 3) (Jackson, 1991).
3.2. Bioinformatic analysis of PHACS
BLAST searches of the GenBank non-redundant database reveal that ACSs are the most homologous enzymes to PHACS. The putative Fugu ACS tops the list (58% identity over 417 residues; E-value=10−142), followed by several plant ACSs with the most homologous isoform from papaya (30% identity over 396 residues; E-value=2×10−58). A multiple sequence alignment of PHACS with the putative Fugu ACS (GenBank, AAD20564), papaya ACS (GenBank, AAC98809), Arabidopsis thaliana ACS (SwissProt, q06402), and apple ACS (SwissProt, p37821) is shown in Fig. 4. Ten residues are completely conserved in all ACSs and aminotransferases within the Aminotransferase I subfamily of the α-family of PLP-dependent enzymes (Tyr70, Asn194, Pro195, Gly197, Asp222, Tyr225, Lys258, Arg266, Gly268 and Arg386: pig cytosolic aspartate aminotransferase (AAT) numbering) (Jensen and Gu, 1996). Additionally, Gly110 is strongly conserved in this subfamily, but not in the ACSs. Interestingly, the putative Fugu ACS is reported to have alanine at the equivalent position of the invariant Gly197 residue. This is likely to be a sequencing error, because Gly197 is one of four totally conserved residues in the Aminotransferase subfamilies I, II and IV of PLP-dependent enzymes that include plant ACSs (Jensen and Gu, 1996). Moreover, the expected Gly197 is present in the PHACS sequence. Nine of the ten conserved residues (Asn194, Pro195, Gly197, Asp222, Tyr225, Lys258, Arg266, Gly268 and Arg386) are present in PHACS.
The evolutionary relatedness of ACSs to other PLP-dependent enzymes was established by the amino acid sequence and structure-based bioinformatic analysis of apple ACS (Capitani et al., 1999, Feng et al., 2000). To gain a better understanding of the relationship of PHACS to other PLP-dependent enzymes, structural prediction and search algorithms were applied to identify potential structural neighbors (Table 1). Each of the three methods employed uses a different approach to identify structurally related proteins. The 3D-PSSM procedure (Kelley et al., 2000) uses structural alignments of homologous proteins that have similar three-dimensional structures, within the Structural Classification of Proteins (SCOP) database (Lo Conte et al., 2000). A multiple sequence alignment including the query is generated by standard search methods, and is adjusted to conserve secondary structure. The position-specific scoring matrix that is formed from this multiple sequence alignment allows the identification of potential structural neighbors. Four significant putative structural neighbors of PHACS were identified by 3D-PSSM, with apple ACS having the highest score (Protein Data Bank (PDB), 1b8g; Capitani et al., 1999). The three other significant matches are all α-family PLP-dependent enzymes, each of which was previously identified as a structural neighbor of apple ACS (Capitani et al., 1999). The Function and Fold Assignment System (FFAS) (Rychlewski et al., 2000) generates a profile (amino acid substitution matrix) based on a multiple sequence alignment obtained from a BLAST search of the query. This profile is compared to existing ones obtained from proteins in the PDB to identify related structures. FFAS gave similar results to 3D-PSSM within the top five matches, with the exception of cystalysin. Finally, the method of Fischer and Eisenberg (1996), which predicts the secondary structure of the query and compares this prediction to known three-dimensional structures within the PDB, was applied. While these results differ from the first two, a common theme emerges among the structural neighbors identified by all three methods: with the exception of apple ACS, all of the predicted structural neighbors are either aminotransferases (aspartate aminotransferase and tyrosine aminotransferase) or enzymes that catalyze β-elimination reactions on amino acids (MalY, cystalysin, tryptophanase and tyrosine phenol-lyase). Consistent with this observation, a search for conserved functional domains using PFAM (Bateman et al., 2000) identified overlapping Aminotransferase I and β-eliminating lyase domains in PHACS.
The tissue distribution of PHACS expression, based on reported human ESTs, includes liver (GenBank, AV654561, AV649108, AV648628, AV649030, AV649079, AV648689, and AV64909), liver/spleen (GenBank, T87253 and H47556), stomach (GenBank, AW817658, AW817617, and AW817734), breast (GenBank, AW998352), breast tumor (GenBank, AW939274), brain (GenBank, AA224259), uterus (GenBank, AW874412 and BE393764), prostate (GenBank, AI676022, AW451890, and BE856140), colon (GenBank, AI802784, AW968101, and AW968108), lung/testes/B-cell (GenBank, AA968591), and B-cell germinal centers (GenBank, AA256057 and AA286896). Moreover, based on the presence of ESTs that encode peptides with a high degree of similarity to PHACS (generally >80% similarity over ∼100 amino acids), it is evident that orthologues exist in Bos taurus (GenBank, BE682983, BF705787, AW430553, AW353498, BF600864, AW485201, and AW356136), Mus musculus (GenBank, BE287848, AI663771, and BF144812), Rattus norvegicus (GenBank, AW916488, BF396113, and BF552546), and Sus scrofa (GenBank, AW436114). The apparent lack of PHACS or Fugu ACS orthologues in the Drosophila, yeast, or C. elegans genomes implies that the function of these enzymes is specific to vertebrates.
3.3. Expression and purification of recombinant PHACS
Pichia pastoris is the current organism of choice for the heterologous expression of apple ACS (Feng and Kirsch, 2000), and was therefore used for the expression of PHACS. Approximately 5 mg of pure recombinant PHACS protein was isolated from a 1 l culture of P. pastoris harboring the integrated pPIC3-PHACS plasmid. Purified PHACS is homogenous by SDS-PAGE (data not shown), and exhibits the characteristic PLP-absorption maximum at 422 nm (Feng and Kirsch, 2000).
3.4. Comparison of kinetic parameters between PHACS and the apple ACS enzymes
Although the physiological role of apple ACS is to convert SAM to ACC and MTA (formally an α,γ-elimination reaction) (Fig. 1A), the enzyme also slowly catalyzes the inappropriate β,γ-elimination reaction yielding MTA and enzyme bound l-VG. l-VG is a mechanism-based inactivator of ACS (Satoh and Yang, 1989) and other PLP-dependent enzymes. Apple ACS does, however, catalyze the deamination of l-VG to form α-ketobutyrate and ammonia (Fig. 1B) (Feng and Kirsch, 2000), providing substantial protection to the enzyme against inactivation. The inactivation event occurs once every 500 catalytic turnovers of l-VG (Feng and Kirsch, 2000).
The kinetics describing the reaction of PHACS with SAM and l-VG are compared with those of the apple enzyme in Table 2. There is no detectable PHACS-catalyzed conversion of SAM to ACC under a variety of conditions. The limits of detection give an upper limit estimate that the human enzyme has <0.12% of the specific activity of the apple enzyme (White et al., 1994). Interestingly, PHACS catalyzes the deamination of l-VG with a specificity constant (kcat/Km) that is only 30-fold less than that of apple ACS (Feng and Kirsch, 2000). The latter result proves that the enzyme, as isolated, is active.
The closest phylogenetic neighbors, other than plant ACSs, to PHACS are aminotransferases from the α-family of PLP-dependent enzymes (Table 1); therefore, PHACS was reacted with several amino acids under single-turnover conditions to enhance sensitivity. PHACS does slowly convert l-Ala to pyruvate (kcat/Km ∼2.8×10−4 M−1 s−1), but this rate constant is too low for the enzyme to be a physiologically relevant aminotransferase. No detectable aminotransferase activity was observed during 5 min assays with the following amino acids: SAM (200 mM), l-Asp (20 mM), l-Arg (20 mM), l-Thr (50 mM) and l-Phe (50 mM). The putative PHACS structural neighbors cystalysin, MalY, tryptophanase, and tyrosine-phenol lyase catalyze the α,β-elimination of an amino acid side chain substituent from their respective substrates. All of these enzymes yield pyruvate and ammonia as two of their products, which allows coupling of each reaction to the glutamate dehydrogenase ammonia assay. No detectable ammonia was found upon incubation of PHACS for 5 min with l-cystathionine (5 mM), l-Met (15 mM), l-Tyr (110 μM), and l-Trp (5 mM).
3.5. Model quality and spatial distribution of the conserved PHACS residues
The PHACS and apple ACS sequences share a high degree of similarity, with 140 completely conserved and 87 partially conserved out of 510 residues. As a consequence, the homology model of PHACS (Fig. 5A), based on the apple ACS structure, exhibits very good geometric and stereochemical quality. The PHACS model encompasses residues 79–479 of the PHACS sequence which has 84% of its residues in the most favored regions of the Ramachandran plot, 15.2% in the additionally allowed regions and 0.8% in the generously allowed regions. No residues are found in disallowed regions. These values compare favorably with those expected for a refined crystal structure at moderate resolution (∼3.0 Å).
The completely conserved residues are distributed throughout the PHACS structure, and are not clustered at the dimer interface. Although the active site region (Fig. 5B) is largely conserved, two key active site residues are not conserved between PHACS and apple ACS. Trp135 replaces a catalytically important Tyr85 of the plant ACSs, and Ala133 replaces Gln83.

4. Discussion
The large group of PLP-dependent enzymes has been subdivided into four families of related enzymes (Mehta and Christen, 2000): the α-, β-, d-alanine aminotransferase, and alanine racemase families. The members of each family share common structural features, but generally catalyze different reactions. The α-family is the largest and the most catalytically diverse of the four subdivisions of PLP-dependent enzymes. It was previously referred to as the α-family/γ-family (Alexander et al., 1994, Mehta and Christen, 1994, Mehta et al., 1993, Sandmeier et al., 1994), the Fold Type I family (Grishin et al., 1995), and the aspartate aminotransferase family (Jansonius, 1998). The three-dimensional structure of apple ACS confirmed that it is also a member of the α-family (Capitani et al., 1999). Apple ACS is a homodimeric enzyme whose subunits are comprised of two domains. The larger is derived from the central amino acids of the primary sequence (residues 50–332), and contains the PLP cofactor. The smaller one is constructed from both the amino- and carboxy-termini. Each domain contributes functional active site residues.
A model of SAM bound to the active site of the apple ACS (G. Capitani, data not shown) suggests that Tyr85 (Tyr70 equivalent; large domain) is involved in substrate binding by stacking with the adenine ring of SAM. In aspartate aminotransferase (AATase), Tyr70 forms a hydrogen bond with the phosphate of PLP. Mutation of Tyr70 to phenylalanine results in a dramatic loss of catalytic activity (Toney and Kirsch, 1991), indicating that the hydrogen bond is more critical than the aromatic nature of this residue in AATase. In contrast, the closest distance between Tyr85 (-OH) and the phosphate of PLP in apple ACS is 7.0 Å, which is too large for a hydrogen bond to form (Capitani et al., 1999). The proposed role of Tyr85 in base stacking with the adenine ring of SAM suggests that the aromatic nature of this residue is critical. Consistent with this hypothesis, a mutation of this residue in tomato ACS (Tyr92) to phenylalanine results in a modest three-fold decrease in specific activity, while the more structurally perturbing mutations Y92L and Y92W reduce the specific activity by 132- and 20-fold, respectively (Tarun and Theologis, 1998). The presence of tryptophan at this position in both PHACS and the putative Fugu ACS may partly explain the lack of observable ACS activity.
Gln83 is a second active site residue that is not conserved in PHACS. The amide side chain of Gln83 is <4 Å from the positively charged sulfonium pole of SAM in the model of SAM bound to the apple ACS active site. The equivalent residue in both PHACS and the putative Fugu ACS is alanine. The Q83A mutation in apple ACS obliterates ACS activity (Koch and Kirsch, unpublished data), and may further explain the inability of PHACS to catalyze the ACS reaction.
Several observations suggest that the putative Fugu ACS, like PHACS, is not a functional ACS. First, the high degree of amino acid sequence identity between the Fugu ACS and PHACS proteins indicates that they are more closely related to each other than they are to the plant ACSs. Second, a high degree of synteny between the chromosomal regions surrounding the genes for each putative ACS has been reported (Peixoto et al., 2000), which implies a conservation of function between PHACS and the Fugu ACS. Third, the conservation of splice site junction type and order between the Fugu and human genes also shows the close evolutionary relationship. Finally, the putative human and Fugu ACSs contain the same deleterious amino acid substitutions at two active site positions (Gln83 and Tyr85) that are known to be critical for ACS activity. These observations taken together with the fact that none of the sequences for enzymes known to act on the product ACC (see Section 1) are present in the vertebrate databases argue that the definition of the Fugu protein as a ACS, as it is currently annotated in GenBank (AAD20564), is incorrect. The results of this study serve additionally to emphasize the caution that must be exercised in assigning a function to a newly identified gene solely on the basis of homology to genes of known function. We propose that the PHACS gene retain its acronym, but be referred to as pseudo human ACS rather than putative.

1. Introduction
The amino acid 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC) is a key metabolic intermediate in the biosynthesis of the plant hormone ethylene. This gaseous hormone is a vital signaling molecule that regulates many facets of plant growth and development (Abeles et al., 1992). ACC synthase (ACS) (methylthioadenosine lyase EC 4.4.1.14) catalyzes the penultimate and rate-determining step of ethylene biosynthesis, which is the conversion of S-adenosyl-l-methionine (SAM) to 5′-methylthioadenosine (MTA) and ACC (Fig. 1A). Ethylene is subsequently produced by ACC oxidase.
The biosynthesis and utilization of ACC appear to be limited to plants and microorganisms. There are currently only three known metabolic fates for ACC within these organisms. In plants, ACC is either oxidized to form ethylene by ACC oxidase or it is covalently modified by malonylation at the α-amino group as a mechanism for controlling the amount of ACC available for ethylene biosynthesis (Hoffman et al., 1982).

The third metabolic fate of ACC occurs in microorganisms where it is converted to α-ketobutyrate and ammonia by the action of ACC deaminase (Honma, 1985).
Although ACC has been used in pharmacological studies of the mammalian N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor (i.e. Nahum-Levy et al., 1999), there is no evidence that ACC is produced in animals. The recent report describing the identification of a gene encoding a putative ACS in Japanese pufferfish (Fugu rubripes) (Peixoto et al., 2000), and the corresponding gene for a potential human orthologue located on the short arm of chromosome 11 (11p11), raises the intriguing possibility that ACC may be synthesized in animals. The mRNA for each of these genes was shown to be present in tissues from their respective organisms, demonstrating that these genes are expressed.
If ACC were produced in humans and other animals, the possible biosynthesis of the important plant regulatory hormone, ethylene, would have important physiological consequences. To date, however, there have been no reports of animal genes that would encode homologues of the three known enzymes that act on ACC. Thus, the metabolic fate of nascent ACC, if formed in animals, can not be deduced.

We describe here the cloning of a cDNA encoding the putative human ACS (PHACS) and the characterization of the expressed and purified 58 kDa recombinant protein.

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
SAM was purchased from Calbiochem (La Jolla, CA). Bovine liver l-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH Type VI, G2009), l-vinylglycine (l-VG), and other amino acids used were from Sigma (St. Louis, MO). Ni-NTA Superflow resin was purchased from Qiagen (Valencia, CA). IMAGE EST clone 3632065 was obtained from Incyte Genomics Inc. (St. Louis, MO). Synthetic oligonucleotides were purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies (Coralville, IA). Other reagents were of the highest quality available.
2.2. Cloning the PHACS cDNA
Rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE) was employed to obtain the 5′ and 3′ ends of the full-length PHACS cDNA from a human prostate Marathon-Ready cDNA library (Clontech, Palo Alto, CA) using the manufacturer's Advantage 2 polymerase mixture and recommended PCR conditions. The gene-specific primers used for RACE were based on the human prostate EST clone (GenBank, AI676022), which displays homology to the apple ACS open reading frame.

These primers are HACS1 (5′-CGT GGG GCT GGC TTC TTC ATC TGG GTT G-3′), HACS2 (5′-CCC AGG CAA AGC CGG TGG ACC TGG TCT G-3′), and the nested primers NHACS1 (5′-CTT GAG AAA GTA CCT GCC CAA GGG CAC C-3′) and NHACS2 (5′-AGA AGA CAA AGC GAA ACC AAC CAG GCT C-3′). The 5′ and 3′ fragments of the PHACS open reading frame were joined by recombinant PCR using outside primers BNHACS (5′-GCG GGA TCC CAT ATG TTC ACC CTT CCT CAA AAG GAC T-3′) and hHIS (5′-ATA AGA ATG CGG CCG CTT AGT GAT GGT GAT GGT GAT GCC TGC GTT-3′), which introduce a His6-tag at the carboxy-terminus of the PHACS protein. A carboxy-terminal His6-tag has been shown not to impair the catalytic function of either apple ACS or E. coli aspartate aminotransferase (Feng and Kirsch, 2000; Koch and Kirsch, unpublished data), which are predicted structural neighbors of PHACS (see Section 3.2). To facilitate cloning, a BamHI restriction endonuclease cleavage site within the PHACS coding region was removed by silent mutagenesis using the primers dbam1 (5′-AGG GCA TTG GGG ATA CCC TTC TTG AGT CGT-3′) and dbam2 (5′-CAC GAC TCA AGA AGG GTA TCC CCA ATG CCC-3′).

The PHACS open reading frame was cloned into the BamHI and NotI sites of the Pichia pastoris expression plasmid pPIC3 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA). The DNA sequence of the final clone was verified.
2.3. Bioinformatics
BLAST searches of the human EST database identified several ESTs that display homology to plant ACSs with apple ACS (SwissProt, p37821) as the query. Multiple sequence alignments were produced with ClustalW using the default settings within MacVector 6.0.1 software (Oxford Molecular, Beaverton, OR). A search for conserved protein domains was performed with PFAM (Bateman et al., 2000) (http://www.sanger.ac.uk/Software/Pfam/index.shtml). The three-dimensional structure prediction algorithms/structural neighbor search methods of Fischer and Eisenberg (1996) (http://fold.doe-mbi.ucla.edu/), 3D-PSSM (Kelley et al., 2000) (http://www.bmm.icnet.uk/~3dpssm/), and FFAS (Rychlewski et al., 2000) (http://bioinformatics.burnham-inst.org/FFAS/) were used to identify probable structural neighbors of PHACS.
2.4. Expression and purification
Recombinant His6-tagged PHACS was expressed in P. pastoris strain GS115 and purified by Ni-NTA chromatography as described for His6-tagged apple ACS (Feng and Kirsch, 2000). The concentration of purified PHACS was determined from the calculated extinction coefficient (ε280nm=7.87×104 M−1 cm−1; http://expasy.cbr.nrc.ca/tools/protparam.html) (Gill and von Hippel, 1989).
2.5. Kinetic analysis
The ACS-catalyzed conversion of SAM to ACC and MTA (Fig.

1A) was monitored by an adenosine deaminase coupled enzyme assay (White et al., 1994). Deamination of l-VG (Fig. 1B) by PHACS was assessed by monitoring the formation of ammonia using the glutamate dehydrogenase coupled assay described previously (Feng and Kirsch, 2000). Single-turnover aminotransferase experiments were performed by analyzing the shift in pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) absorbance maxima from 422 to 320 nm which accompanies the reductive amination of PLP during the first half of the transamination reaction (Feng et al., 2000).
2.6. Homology model of PHACS
A structural model of the PHACS protein was generated from the 1b8g apple ACS dimer structure (Capitani et al., 1999). A pairwise alignment between the apple ACS and PHACS sequences provided the input data for the MODELLER 4.0 program (Sali and Blundell, 1993). The alignment was improved stepwise based on the MODELLER output and on a multiple sequence alignment of 38 plant ACS sequences. Using the improved alignment, 100 ‘candidate’ models of PHACS were generated and filtered according to their stereochemical quality. The best model was chosen for subsequent energy minimization and constant temperature torsion angle dynamics with X-PLOR 3.85 (Brünger, 1992). The geometry of the internal aldimine linkage was optimized in this phase.

The model was validated with the WHAT_CHECK server, which reported no major problems.

3. Results
3.1. Cloning of the PHACS cDNA
The cloned PHACS cDNA encodes a 501 amino acid protein (Fig. 2) with a calculated molecular weight of 58 kDa. The 3′ end of the cDNA, derived from 3′-RACE, contains untranslated sequences that include a putative polyadenylation signal. The 5′ end of the PHACS cDNA was deduced from the DNA sequences of several cloned 5′-RACE products, a human uterus EST (GenBank, BE393764; IMAGE clone 3632065), and the genomic DNA sequence harboring the PHACS gene (GenBank, U73628). It is noteworthy that there is a one base discrepancy between the reported DNA sequence of IMAGE clone 3632065 and the corresponding genomic DNA sequence encoding the 5′ UTR of PHACS. There is an in-frame TAG stop codon 378 bp upstream of the initiator methionine ATG codon in the genomic DNA sequence that is absent in the reported sequence for the IMAGE clone. We re-sequenced the IMAGE clone and found that the reported DNA sequence is off by one base and therefore the PHACS 5′ UTR contains an in-frame stop codon.

The PHACS coding sequence used for expression of the recombinant protein was constructed by recombinant PCR using 5′-RACE and 3′-RACE products (Higuchi, 1990). The exon arrangement within this portion of the PHACS cDNA was independently verified by sequencing direct amplification PCR products from the Marathon-Ready cDNA library. The PHACS coding sequence and 3′ UTR are derived from 14 exons, with an additional exon encompassing the 5′ UTR. The genomic organization of splice site junctions for the 14 exon–exon boundaries within the PHACS coding sequence from 5′ to 3′ are type 0, 0, 0, II, 0, I, 0, 0, II, II, 0, I, 0, and I, respectively (Fig. 3) (Sharp, 1981). It is important to note that this is the exact order of splice site types found in the predicted coding sequence for the putative Fugu ACS. All of the splice sites within the PHACS cDNA contain ‘GT’ splice donor and ‘AG’ splice acceptor consensus sequences (Fig. 3) (Jackson, 1991).
3.2. Bioinformatic analysis of PHACS
BLAST searches of the GenBank non-redundant database reveal that ACSs are the most homologous enzymes to PHACS.

The putative Fugu ACS tops the list (58% identity over 417 residues; E-value=10−142), followed by several plant ACSs with the most homologous isoform from papaya (30% identity over 396 residues; E-value=2×10−58). A multiple sequence alignment of PHACS with the putative Fugu ACS (GenBank, AAD20564), papaya ACS (GenBank, AAC98809), Arabidopsis thaliana ACS (SwissProt, q06402), and apple ACS (SwissProt, p37821) is shown in Fig. 4. Ten residues are completely conserved in all ACSs and aminotransferases within the Aminotransferase I subfamily of the α-family of PLP-dependent enzymes (Tyr70, Asn194, Pro195, Gly197, Asp222, Tyr225, Lys258, Arg266, Gly268 and Arg386: pig cytosolic aspartate aminotransferase (AAT) numbering) (Jensen and Gu, 1996). Additionally, Gly110 is strongly conserved in this subfamily, but not in the ACSs. Interestingly, the putative Fugu ACS is reported to have alanine at the equivalent position of the invariant Gly197 residue. This is likely to be a sequencing error, because Gly197 is one of four totally conserved residues in the Aminotransferase subfamilies I, II and IV of PLP-dependent enzymes that include plant ACSs (Jensen and Gu, 1996). Moreover, the expected Gly197 is present in the PHACS sequence.

Nine of the ten conserved residues (Asn194, Pro195, Gly197, Asp222, Tyr225, Lys258, Arg266, Gly268 and Arg386) are present in PHACS.
The evolutionary relatedness of ACSs to other PLP-dependent enzymes was established by the amino acid sequence and structure-based bioinformatic analysis of apple ACS (Capitani et al., 1999, Feng et al., 2000). To gain a better understanding of the relationship of PHACS to other PLP-dependent enzymes, structural prediction and search algorithms were applied to identify potential structural neighbors (Table 1). Each of the three methods employed uses a different approach to identify structurally related proteins. The 3D-PSSM procedure (Kelley et al., 2000) uses structural alignments of homologous proteins that have similar three-dimensional structures, within the Structural Classification of Proteins (SCOP) database (Lo Conte et al., 2000). A multiple sequence alignment including the query is generated by standard search methods, and is adjusted to conserve secondary structure. The position-specific scoring matrix that is formed from this multiple sequence alignment allows the identification of potential structural neighbors. Four significant putative structural neighbors of PHACS were identified by 3D-PSSM, with apple ACS having the highest score (Protein Data Bank (PDB), 1b8g; Capitani et al., 1999).

The three other significant matches are all α-family PLP-dependent enzymes, each of which was previously identified as a structural neighbor of apple ACS (Capitani et al., 1999). The Function and Fold Assignment System (FFAS) (Rychlewski et al., 2000) generates a profile (amino acid substitution matrix) based on a multiple sequence alignment obtained from a BLAST search of the query. This profile is compared to existing ones obtained from proteins in the PDB to identify related structures. FFAS gave similar results to 3D-PSSM within the top five matches, with the exception of cystalysin. Finally, the method of Fischer and Eisenberg (1996), which predicts the secondary structure of the query and compares this prediction to known three-dimensional structures within the PDB, was applied. While these results differ from the first two, a common theme emerges among the structural neighbors identified by all three methods: with the exception of apple ACS, all of the predicted structural neighbors are either aminotransferases (aspartate aminotransferase and tyrosine aminotransferase) or enzymes that catalyze β-elimination reactions on amino acids (MalY, cystalysin, tryptophanase and tyrosine phenol-lyase).

Consistent with this observation, a search for conserved functional domains using PFAM (Bateman et al., 2000) identified overlapping Aminotransferase I and β-eliminating lyase domains in PHACS.
The tissue distribution of PHACS expression, based on reported human ESTs, includes liver (GenBank, AV654561, AV649108, AV648628, AV649030, AV649079, AV648689, and AV64909), liver/spleen (GenBank, T87253 and H47556), stomach (GenBank, AW817658, AW817617, and AW817734), breast (GenBank, AW998352), breast tumor (GenBank, AW939274), brain (GenBank, AA224259), uterus (GenBank, AW874412 and BE393764), prostate (GenBank, AI676022, AW451890, and BE856140), colon (GenBank, AI802784, AW968101, and AW968108), lung/testes/B-cell (GenBank, AA968591), and B-cell germinal centers (GenBank, AA256057 and AA286896). Moreover, based on the presence of ESTs that encode peptides with a high degree of similarity to PHACS (generally >80% similarity over ∼100 amino acids), it is evident that orthologues exist in Bos taurus (GenBank, BE682983, BF705787, AW430553, AW353498, BF600864, AW485201, and AW356136), Mus musculus (GenBank, BE287848, AI663771, and BF144812), Rattus norvegicus (GenBank, AW916488, BF396113, and BF552546), and Sus scrofa (GenBank, AW436114). The apparent lack of PHACS or Fugu ACS orthologues in the Drosophila, yeast, or C. elegans genomes implies that the function of these enzymes is specific to vertebrates.
3.3.

Expression and purification of recombinant PHACS
Pichia pastoris is the current organism of choice for the heterologous expression of apple ACS (Feng and Kirsch, 2000), and was therefore used for the expression of PHACS. Approximately 5 mg of pure recombinant PHACS protein was isolated from a 1 l culture of P. pastoris harboring the integrated pPIC3-PHACS plasmid. Purified PHACS is homogenous by SDS-PAGE (data not shown), and exhibits the characteristic PLP-absorption maximum at 422 nm (Feng and Kirsch, 2000).
3.4. Comparison of kinetic parameters between PHACS and the apple ACS enzymes
Although the physiological role of apple ACS is to convert SAM to ACC and MTA (formally an α,γ-elimination reaction) (Fig. 1A), the enzyme also slowly catalyzes the inappropriate β,γ-elimination reaction yielding MTA and enzyme bound l-VG. l-VG is a mechanism-based inactivator of ACS (Satoh and Yang, 1989) and other PLP-dependent enzymes. Apple ACS does, however, catalyze the deamination of l-VG to form α-ketobutyrate and ammonia (Fig. 1B) (Feng and Kirsch, 2000), providing substantial protection to the enzyme against inactivation.

The inactivation event occurs once every 500 catalytic turnovers of l-VG (Feng and Kirsch, 2000).
The kinetics describing the reaction of PHACS with SAM and l-VG are compared with those of the apple enzyme in Table 2. There is no detectable PHACS-catalyzed conversion of SAM to ACC under a variety of conditions. The limits of detection give an upper limit estimate that the human enzyme has <0.12% of the specific activity of the apple enzyme (White et al., 1994). Interestingly, PHACS catalyzes the deamination of l-VG with a specificity constant (kcat/Km) that is only 30-fold less than that of apple ACS (Feng and Kirsch, 2000). The latter result proves that the enzyme, as isolated, is active.
The closest phylogenetic neighbors, other than plant ACSs, to PHACS are aminotransferases from the α-family of PLP-dependent enzymes (Table 1); therefore, PHACS was reacted with several amino acids under single-turnover conditions to enhance sensitivity. PHACS does slowly convert l-Ala to pyruvate (kcat/Km ∼2.8×10−4 M−1 s−1), but this rate constant is too low for the enzyme to be a physiologically relevant aminotransferase.

No detectable aminotransferase activity was observed during 5 min assays with the following amino acids: SAM (200 mM), l-Asp (20 mM), l-Arg (20 mM), l-Thr (50 mM) and l-Phe (50 mM). The putative PHACS structural neighbors cystalysin, MalY, tryptophanase, and tyrosine-phenol lyase catalyze the α,β-elimination of an amino acid side chain substituent from their respective substrates. All of these enzymes yield pyruvate and ammonia as two of their products, which allows coupling of each reaction to the glutamate dehydrogenase ammonia assay. No detectable ammonia was found upon incubation of PHACS for 5 min with l-cystathionine (5 mM), l-Met (15 mM), l-Tyr (110 μM), and l-Trp (5 mM).
3.5. Model quality and spatial distribution of the conserved PHACS residues
The PHACS and apple ACS sequences share a high degree of similarity, with 140 completely conserved and 87 partially conserved out of 510 residues. As a consequence, the homology model of PHACS (Fig. 5A), based on the apple ACS structure, exhibits very good geometric and stereochemical quality.

The PHACS model encompasses residues 79–479 of the PHACS sequence which has 84% of its residues in the most favored regions of the Ramachandran plot, 15.2% in the additionally allowed regions and 0.8% in the generously allowed regions. No residues are found in disallowed regions. These values compare favorably with those expected for a refined crystal structure at moderate resolution (∼3.0 Å).
The completely conserved residues are distributed throughout the PHACS structure, and are not clustered at the dimer interface. Although the active site region (Fig. 5B) is largely conserved, two key active site residues are not conserved between PHACS and apple ACS. Trp135 replaces a catalytically important Tyr85 of the plant ACSs, and Ala133 replaces Gln83.

4. Discussion
The large group of PLP-dependent enzymes has been subdivided into four families of related enzymes (Mehta and Christen, 2000): the α-, β-, d-alanine aminotransferase, and alanine racemase families. The members of each family share common structural features, but generally catalyze different reactions. The α-family is the largest and the most catalytically diverse of the four subdivisions of PLP-dependent enzymes.

It was previously referred to as the α-family/γ-family (Alexander et al., 1994, Mehta and Christen, 1994, Mehta et al., 1993, Sandmeier et al., 1994), the Fold Type I family (Grishin et al., 1995), and the aspartate aminotransferase family (Jansonius, 1998). The three-dimensional structure of apple ACS confirmed that it is also a member of the α-family (Capitani et al., 1999). Apple ACS is a homodimeric enzyme whose subunits are comprised of two domains. The larger is derived from the central amino acids of the primary sequence (residues 50–332), and contains the PLP cofactor. The smaller one is constructed from both the amino- and carboxy-termini. Each domain contributes functional active site residues.
A model of SAM bound to the active site of the apple ACS (G. Capitani, data not shown) suggests that Tyr85 (Tyr70 equivalent; large domain) is involved in substrate binding by stacking with the adenine ring of SAM. In aspartate aminotransferase (AATase), Tyr70 forms a hydrogen bond with the phosphate of PLP. Mutation of Tyr70 to phenylalanine results in a dramatic loss of catalytic activity (Toney and Kirsch, 1991), indicating that the hydrogen bond is more critical than the aromatic nature of this residue in AATase.

In contrast, the closest distance between Tyr85 (-OH) and the phosphate of PLP in apple ACS is 7.0 Å, which is too large for a hydrogen bond to form (Capitani et al., 1999). The proposed role of Tyr85 in base stacking with the adenine ring of SAM suggests that the aromatic nature of this residue is critical. Consistent with this hypothesis, a mutation of this residue in tomato ACS (Tyr92) to phenylalanine results in a modest three-fold decrease in specific activity, while the more structurally perturbing mutations Y92L and Y92W reduce the specific activity by 132- and 20-fold, respectively (Tarun and Theologis, 1998). The presence of tryptophan at this position in both PHACS and the putative Fugu ACS may partly explain the lack of observable ACS activity.
Gln83 is a second active site residue that is not conserved in PHACS. The amide side chain of Gln83 is <4 Å from the positively charged sulfonium pole of SAM in the model of SAM bound to the apple ACS active site. The equivalent residue in both PHACS and the putative Fugu ACS is alanine.

The Q83A mutation in apple ACS obliterates ACS activity (Koch and Kirsch, unpublished data), and may further explain the inability of PHACS to catalyze the ACS reaction.
Several observations suggest that the putative Fugu ACS, like PHACS, is not a functional ACS. First, the high degree of amino acid sequence identity between the Fugu ACS and PHACS proteins indicates that they are more closely related to each other than they are to the plant ACSs. Second, a high degree of synteny between the chromosomal regions surrounding the genes for each putative ACS has been reported (Peixoto et al., 2000), which implies a conservation of function between PHACS and the Fugu ACS. Third, the conservation of splice site junction type and order between the Fugu and human genes also shows the close evolutionary relationship. Finally, the putative human and Fugu ACSs contain the same deleterious amino acid substitutions at two active site positions (Gln83 and Tyr85) that are known to be critical for ACS activity.

These observations taken together with the fact that none of the sequences for enzymes known to act on the product ACC (see Section 1) are present in the vertebrate databases argue that the definition of the Fugu protein as a ACS, as it is currently annotated in GenBank (AAD20564), is incorrect. The results of this study serve additionally to emphasize the caution that must be exercised in assigning a function to a newly identified gene solely on the basis of homology to genes of known function. We propose that the PHACS gene retain its acronym, but be referred to as pseudo human ACS rather than putative.
