Ketimine reductases specifically catalyse the reduction of imine bonds using either NADH or NADPH as cofactor. They include the previously partially characterised Δ1-piperideine-2-carboxylate (P2C)/Δ1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate (Pyr2C) reductase (E.C. 1.5.1.21) isolated from porcine kidney (Petrakis and Greenberg 1965) and Pseudomonas putida (Payton and Chang 1982), and ketimine reductase (E.C. 1.5.1.25) isolated from bovine cerebellum (Nardini et al. 1988b) and porcine kidney (Nardini et al. 1988a). Two different ketimine reductases have previously been partially purified from bovine cerebellum (Nardini et al. 1988b) and porcine kidney cortex (Nardini et al. 1988a), and partly characterised. No sequence data were obtained, and as a result no gene assignments are currently available for these reductases.

Ketimine reductase substrates include the sulphur-containing cyclic ketimines S-(2-aminoethyl)-l-cysteine ketimine (AECK), lanthionine ketimine (LK) and cystathionine ketimine (CysK) (Fig. 1). These originate from sulphur-containing amino acids such as cysteine and homocysteine, which are converted to the cyclic sulphur-containing amino acid precursors by cystathionine β-synthase (Cavallini et al. 1991). These precursors are then transaminated by glutamine transaminase K [GTK; also known as kynurenine aminotransferase isozyme I (KAT1)] (Cooper 2004), or possibly oxidised by l-amino acid oxidase, to form the corresponding α-keto acids, which non-enzymatically cyclise to form the cyclic ketimines (Cavallini et al. 1991) (Fig. 2).

Δ1-Piperideine-2-carboxylate and Δ1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate (Fig. 1) are also ketimine reductase substrates. P2C is derived from lysine catabolism from the pipecolic acid pathway. In mammals, lysine is metabolised by two main pathways – the saccharopine pathway and the pipecolic acid pathway. The saccharopine pathway predominates in extracerebral tissues, whereas the pipecolic acid pathway is the main route for lysine catabolism in the adult brain (Garweg et al. 1980). In the pipecolic acid pathway, oxidation of l-lysine at the α-carbon results in the formation of an α-keto acid that cyclises to P2C (Garweg et al. 1980). Pyr2C arises from the oxidation of d-proline by d-amino acid oxidase. Ketimine reductases catalyse its reduction to l-proline (Petrakis and Greenberg 1965).

Cystathionine ketimine and LK have been reported to be present in human cerebral cortex, AECK and CysK in bovine brain, and CysK and LK in human urine (Cavallini et al. 1991). The reduced enzyme products of AECK, LK and CysK, namely 1,4-thiomorpholine-3-carboxylic acid (TMA), 1,4-thiomorpholine-3,5-dicarboxylic acid and cyclothionine, respectively, have been reported to be present in bovine brain and in human urine (Cavallini et al. 1991).

Biological activity that could affect neurological function has been demonstrated for the sulphur-containing cyclic ketimines. LK is known to bind strongly to isolated brain membranes, resulting in significant increases of cAMP. This binding was found to be saturable, reversible and specific. Specific binding was shown by the fact that LK could only be displaced by other ketimines, AECK and CysK, and catecholamines (Dupre et al. 1993). AECK is a strong competitive inhibitor of d-amino acid oxidase (Ricci et al. 1983), and may act as an endogenous regulator of glutamate NMDA receptor activity through modulation of d-serine levels. This implies a specific neuromodulator/transmitter role for the ketimines with particular importance in the brain. In contrast, little is known regarding the biological functions of P2C or Pyr2C. l-Pipecolic acid, derived from the reduction of P2C by ketimine reductase, has been shown to be a weak inhibitory neurotransmitter (Charles 1986). No other biological functions have been reported for P2C or Pyr2C and their reduced products.

Cyclic ketimines are present in solution as an equilibrium mixture of cyclic enaminic, cyclic ketiminic, and open-chain forms, with cyclic forms predominating under physiological conditions (Cavallini et al. 1991). However, ketimine reductases appear to only catalyse the reduction of the ketiminic form as: when assayed at pH 5 some substrates, such as CysK, do not exist as enamines (Nardini et al. 1988a); the ketimine reductase product using AECK as substrate is the cyclic amino acid TMA (Nardini et al. 1988a), which cannot arise from reduction of the open chain form.

Here, we report the purification of a ketimine reductase from lamb cerebral cortex and the identification of the lamb and human enzyme as the protein μ-crystallin (CRYM), for which an enzymatic function had not previously been determined. We also report the strong competitive enzyme inhibition by the thyroid hormone 3,5,3′-l-triiodothyronine (T3). This new role for T3 in regulation of cyclic ketimine levels represents an important new mechanism in our understanding of the biochemical actions of T3, and is an important addition to our understanding of the neurochemical role of thyroid hormones.

Materials and methods
Materials and assays
All chemicals and reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (Sydney, Australia) unless stated otherwise. AECK and CysK were synthesized as per the protocols of Cavallini et al. (1983), and P2C by the protocol of Meister (1954). The full length human CRYM ORF bacterial expression clone (product # I0311) was purchased from GeneCopoeia (Rockville, MD, USA). All chromatographic media and columns were purchased from GE Healthcare (Sydney, Australia) and Bio-Rad (Sydney, Australia).

Ketimine reductase assays were performed in a similar manner to those previously reported (Nardini et al. 1988a,b), using a standard mixture in 100 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5) at 37°C. One unit of enzyme activity is defined as the amount of enzyme that catalyses the oxidation of 1 μmol of NADH per minute at 37°C in a standard reaction mixture.

For enzyme kinetic measurements, assays were adapted to microtiter plates using a BMG Fluostar Galaxy (Offenburg, Germany) and were performed in a total volume of 200 μL of buffer containing 20% w/v glycerol, 100 mM sodium acetate (pH 5) with variable concentrations of substrates at 37°C. The reaction was initiated by the addition of enzyme which had been diluted in assay buffer. Fluorescence detection, excitation wavelength of 360 nm and emission wavelength of 460 nm, was used instead of UV absorbance for monitoring the conversion of NADH or NADPH to NAD or NADP, respectively. Standard curves were generated with varying concentrations of NADH and NADPH. The non-enzymatic decrease in fluorescence of NADH or NADPH, because of the acidic assay conditions, was compensated for by running a blank simultaneously containing all assay components except for the ketimine substrate. The reduction product of AECK was identified as the cyclic amino acid TMA (Fig. 1) by the procedure of Nardini et al. (1988a).

Inhibition studies involving T3 were carried out at pH 5 and also at pH 7 (100 mM potassium phosphate buffer). A stock solution of T3 was made up in dimethylsulfoxide and varying amounts added to the reaction mixture. In a separate experiment, it was determined that the amount of dimethylsulfoxide in the reaction mixture resulting from addition of T3 stock solutions did not inhibit the enzyme activity.

Enzyme kinetic data were globally fitted and analysed using GraphPad Prism 5 software (GraphPad software Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) using non-linear regression.

Purification protocol
Potassium phosphate buffer [10 mM, pH 7, 10% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT)] was used in all protocols unless otherwise specified. All purification protocols were performed at 4°C. Brain ketimine reductase was purified from lamb frontal cortical sections using multiple chromatography columns, and purified to apparent homogeneity by tracking enzyme activity using AECK (1 mM) and NADH (0.2 mM) as substrates. A Bio-Rad Biologic HR chromatography worksystem was used for purification steps. Sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) was used to monitor the purification. Pall, Inc. concentrating membranes (Port Washington, NY, USA) with a cut-off of 30 kDa were used, except in the case of the final purification step where a 10 kDa membrane was used.

Preparation of lamb brains
Lamb brains were purchased from a local abattoir, chilled on ice within 30 min of slaughter, and stored within 2 h at −80°C. Enzyme activity was found to be stable for prolonged periods in the frozen brain at this temperature. Thawed frontal cortex sections (250 g wet weight in total) were added to 700 mL of ice-cold potassium phosphate buffer, and homogenised in a Waring blender (Torrington, CT, USA) at high speed for 2 min. The homogenate was centrifuged for 60 min in a Beckman centrifuge (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA), at 30 000 g using a JA-20 rotor.

Anion exchange chromatography
As per the protocol of Nardini et al. (1988a), the supernatant (650 mL) was immediately applied to a 100 mL XK50/20 column containing DEAE fast Sepharose weak anion exchanger (GE Healthcare) equilibrated with potassium phosphate buffer. The supernatant was pumped onto the column at 8 mL/min. The DEAE column was washed with 95 mM KCl in phosphate buffer until the absorbance at 280 nm was less than 0.1, and protein was then eluted at 6 mL/min with 165 mM KCl in phosphate buffer. Active fractions were pooled and solid ammonium sulphate (AS) was immediately added to a final concentration of 700 mM.

Hydrophobic interaction chromatography
The pooled active fractions were then pumped onto an XK16/20 column containing 12 mL of phenyl sepharose HP (GE Healthcare) at 6 mL/min. The column was previously equilibrated with phosphate buffer containing 700 mM AS. The column was then washed with the same concentration of AS in phosphate buffer, until the UV absorbance at 280 nm was less than 0.02, then protein was eluted at 6 mL/min with a 100-0%. AS gradient of 12 column volumes followed by 5 column volumes of phosphate buffer. Active fractions eluted in a single peak and were collected, concentrated to 12 mL, and buffer exchanged to 20 mM phosphate buffer a using Sephadex G-25 column.

Flow-through protocol
In preliminary experiments, ketimine reductase was found not to bind to either hydroxylapatite or heparin sulphate in the presence of phosphate buffer at 20 mM. Thus, a flow-through protocol using these two matrices, together with a HiTrap Blue column, was used to quickly remove many protein contaminants. The flow-through protocol made use of a ceramic 10-mL hydroxylapatite column (80 μm ceramic beads), 10-mL heparin sulphate fast flow, and 1-mL HiTrap Blue connected in series. The columns were equilibrated with 20 mM phosphate buffer. After the sample from the previous purification step was injected onto the columns and washed with 35 mL of buffer at 1 mL/min, the hydroxylapatite column and heparin columns were disconnected. The HiTrap Blue column was washed with 10 column volumes of 20 mM phosphate buffer, and the protein samples eluted using 1 μM NADPH directly onto a pre-equilibrated 1-mL Resource Q strong anion exchange column. The column was washed with 10 column volumes of 20 mM phosphate buffer containing 20% (v/v) glycerol and eluted with a 0–500 mM KCl gradient, in 20 mM phosphate buffer, over 12 column volumes at 1 mL/min. A single peak was collected and the pooled samples concentrated to 110 μL. Protein samples in 5-μL aliquots were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C.

Sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis
Bio-Rad 5× loading dye, containing bromophenol blue dye and β-mercaptoethanol (200 mM) were added to protein samples in 1.5-mL Eppendorf tubes, which were then heated for 2 min in a boiling water bath. SDS–PAGE was performed using NuSep (Sydney, Australia) 10-well Tris–Gly 4–20% LongLife gels. Bio-Rad Broad Range molecular mass markers were added to the first lane (200, 116, 97, 66, 45, 31, 21.5, 14.4, 6.5 kDa). SDS–PAGE conditions: 55 min at 155 V using a Bio-Rad power source until the bromophenol blue dye front had reached the base of the gel. The gels were stained with colloidal Coomassie Blue stain/methanol (4 : 1) overnight. The gels were then destained with 20% methanol, after which they were washed and analysed.

Protein identification by MS/MS
Gel bands were excised after their positions were revealed by staining. The protein in each band was reduced with DTT, alkylated with iodoacetamide, and digested in-gel with trypsin (Haynes et al. 1998). Extracted peptides were subjected to nanoLC-MS/MS (mass spectrometry) (Lee et al. 2009). Briefly, peptides were separated by reversed-phase chromatography and eluted directly into a Thermo LTQ-XL ion trap mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The six most abundant peptides detected in a survey scan of 400–1500 amu were subjected to collision induced dissociation. Raw files were converted to mzxml format and spectra were searched against the bovine sequence database (release date 13 April 2010) using the XTandem algorithm running under The Global Proteome Machine interface (Craig et al. 2004). The peptide mass tolerance was set at 2 Da, fragment ion mass tolerance at 0.2 Da, cysteine was considered to be modified with iodoacetamide and methionine was considered to be variably modified by S oxidation. Spectra were also searched against a reversed database to estimate false discovery rates, and using minimum criteria of three peptides identified and a log (e) score of <−10. With these search criteria no proteins were identified in the reversed database searches.

Expression and purification of recombinant proteins in Escherichia coli
The full length human CRYM ORF bacterial expression clone (Entrez gene ID: 1428 transcript variant 1, longer isoform) contained an N-His6 tag and T7 promoter in a pReceiver-B01 vector, and ampicillin selectivity. It was transformed into E. coli (Fusion Blue cells) and E. coli BL21 (DE3)STAR (Inoue et al. 1990). For production of the CRYM the transformed E. coli BL21 (DE3)STAR was streaked onto Luria-Bertani agar plates containing ampicillin (100 μg/mL). The plates were incubated overnight at 37°C and a single colony was picked and cultured in 1 L of Luria-Bertani medium with 1 mM ampicillin at 37°C and with constant shaking on an orbital shaker until the OD600 reached 0.5. Recombinant protein expression was induced with 1 mM isopropyl-β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation overnight at 18°C with constant shaking. The culture was then centrifuged at 6000 g for 20 min at 4°C, and the pellet resuspended in 20 mL of binding buffer [Tris buffer (20 mM, pH 7.9) containing NaCl (500 mM) and imidazole (5 mM)]. The cell suspension was lysed using three passes of a French press at 10 000 psi. Further centrifuging at 20 000 g resulted in the isolation of a soluble protein-containing supernatant. The supernatant was applied to a nickel-charged His-Trap affinity column (1 mL). The column was pre-equilibrated with cold binding buffer. After binding of the protein to the column, the column was successively washed with (i) 5 column volumes of binding buffer, (ii) 5 volumes of Tris buffer (20 mM, pH 7.9) containing NaCl (500 mM) and imidazole (60 mM). The CRYM protein was then eluted with Tris buffer (20 mM, pH 7.9) containing NaCl (500 mM) and imidazole (500 mM), and collected in 0.5 mL fractions. Most of the protein and ketimine reductase activity was found to be in three consecutive fractions totalling 1.5 mL. These were combined and desalted using a 5-mL desalting column equilibrated with 10 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7) containing 20% (v/v) glycerol and 1 mM DTT. Aliquots (15 μL) were flash-frozen in 500 μL Eppendorf tubes and stored at −80°C. Protein concentration was determined using a Bio-Rad Bradford assay with bovine serum albumin as a standard and was determined to be 8 mg/mL. Protein purity was determined by SDS–PAGE and MS/MS protein identification, with only one major band on SDS–PAGE and only one major protein detected by MS/MS.

Gel filtration
A Superdex 200HR gel filtration column (GE Healthcare) was used to check the apparent Mr. The column was eluted at 0.5 mL/min using 150 mM NaCl in 10 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7). The column was calibrated with GE Healthcare Protein standards (ferritin, 440 kDa; aldolase, 158 kDa; ovalbumin, 43 kDa; and ribonuclease, 13.7 kDa).

Data presentation
All data are presented as the mean ± SE.

Results
Purification of lamb brain ketimine reductase and identification as CRYM by MS/MS.

Lamb forebrain ketimine reductase was purified ∼ 470 fold to apparent homogeneity with a yield of 0.2% by utilizing four different chromatographic steps (Fig. 3). The purified enzyme was found to have a specific activity of 15 U/mg. There was a low recovery of protein after the final step (24 μg), but a marked gain in specific activity (Fig. 3). The enzyme was found to be highly unstable and prone to oxidation as was found by earlier researchers (Nardini et al. 1988a,b). A single protein band at ∼ 35 kDa on SDS–PAGE was observed (Fig. 3). The purified protein was trypsin-digested and identified by MS/MS. The highest ranking protein identification was bovine μ-crystallin (CRYM) with a log (e) score of −869, 1429 total peptides, 68 unique peptides identified, and 75% coverage. Identified peptides covered all exons (Fig. 4) corresponding to the full-length 314 amino acid bovine CRYM isoform, GenBank Accession NP_001039379, and the bovine CRYM has 91% identity to the human CRYM, Accession number NP_001879.1 (Fig. 4). A minor contaminant was identified as pyridoxal phosphate phosphatase with a log (e) score of −22 with only four total peptides and three unique peptides identified, and 10% coverage.

Identification of recombinant human CRYM as ketimine reductase
The recombinant human CRYM orthologue of the full-length 314 amino acid bovine CRYM isoform was heterologously expressed in E. coli to conclusively confirm the identity of the ketimine reductase. HisTrap-purified recombinant human CRYM was subjected to SDS–PAGE, and displayed a single band at ∼ 35 kDa (Fig. 3). The purified human enzyme eluted from a Superdex 200 HR column with an apparent Mr of ∼ 70 000, confirming its native form as a homodimer. It had a maximum specific activity as a ketimine reductase of 9.6 U/mg using AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor. The pH optimum was found to be identical to that of porcine ketimine reductase (Nardini et al. 1988a) at pH 4.5 under the same reaction conditions, and similar to that found for bovine cerebellum ketimine reductase (pH 5) (Nardini et al. 1988b). The reaction rate exhibited with NADPH is 40% that exhibited with NADH when AECK is the co-substrate.

For comparison purposes with previous research, various potential substrates for lamb ketimine reductase were tested (Table 1). Similar assay conditions and substrate concentrations were used as in previous studies (Nardini et al. 1988a,b). Assays using 0.2 mM NADH or NADPH in sodium acetate buffer (100 mM, pH 5) were performed. Maximal activity with lamb ketimine reductase was found using AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor. This substrate specificity is similar to that found previously for porcine kidney ketimine reductase (Nardini et al. 1988a). In comparison, the best substrate for bovine cerebellum ketimine reductase was found to be P2C with NADPH as cofactor (Nardini et al. 1988b).

Michaelis-Menten kinetics
A double reciprocal plot of kinetic data indicated that human recombinant CRYM catalyses a sequential mechanism (Fig. 5). Thus, kinetic data were globally fitted to the equation for a bi-bi sequential mechanism using non-linear regression:

where [A] represents AECK substrate concentration and [B] represents NADH concentration. In the presence of 0.053 μg of enzyme, a Km of 47 ± 10 μM and Vmax of 9.6 ± 0.3 μmol/min/mg was determined using varying NADH concentrations and AECK as substrate (Fig. 5). A Km of 3.6 ± 1.4 μM was determined for NADH under the same conditions. These results compare favourably to those documented previously for porcine kidney ketimine reductase, where the Km values obtained under similar conditions for AECK and NADH were found to be 77 μM and 27 μM, respectively (Nardini et al. 1988a).
Inhibition studies
Previous reports indicated that 3,5,3′-l-triodothyronine (T3) strongly binds to CRYM in the presence of NADPH (Vie et al. 1997), with the strength of binding in the order: d-T3 ≈ l-T3 > l-thyroxine (T4) > reverse T3 (Beslin et al. 1995). Assays were therefore conducted to investigate whether T3 inhibits the ketimine reductase activity of human recombinant CRYM. Inhibitory data were recorded using 0.13 μg enzyme in each assay mixture. Assays were conducted at varying concentrations of T3, AECK, and NADH. Global non-linear regression analysis of all data revealed that the equation for competitive inhibition was the best fit:

At neutral pH the inhibition was far stronger, but it was not possible to accurately determine a Ki value using AECK as substrate, as the inhibition no longer fitted any of the classical equations (Fig. 7). This is because of the reported very low KD for T3 at neutral pH of 0.31 nM (Beslin et al. 1995). The assays in Fig. 7 were done at an enzyme concentration of 44.5 nM as at neutral pH enzyme activity with AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor is 25% that at pH 5. The curves at different T3 concentrations have a calculated Vmax that would be expected if the concentration of enzyme were equal to (44.5-[T3]). This inhibitory effect is consistent with inhibition of enzyme activity by T3 and the 0.31 nM KD for T3 binding (Beslin et al. 1995) to CRYM. This type of inhibition by T3 is almost equivalent to an irreversible inhibitor in enzyme kinetic terms and it effectively means that ketimine reductase activity would be negligible when T3 is in excess of CRYM in vivo.

Discussion
Lamb forebrain ketimine reductase was purified to apparent homogeneity using a rapid purification protocol, identified as CRYM by MS/MS, and the identification confirmed by assaying recombinantly expressed human CRYM. The enzymatic function of CRYM has remained elusive in spite of research efforts spanning more than 20 years. It is a homologue of a number of prokaryote enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism, including ornithine cyclodeaminase (Goodman et al. 2004) and lysine cyclodeaminase (Tsotsou and Barbirato 2007), although CRYM has previously been shown to have no cyclodeaminase activity (Goodman et al. 2004). CRYM has been shown to be a major cytosolic T3 binding protein and a key redox-dependent regulator of intracellular T3 bioavailability and transactivation to the nucleus (Mori et al. 2002). CRYM mRNA expression is also down-regulated by follicle stimulating hormone in mammalian ovary and it may play an important regulatory role in steroidogenesis (Ko et al. 2003). A direct role of CRYM/ketimine reductase enzyme substrates as regulators of steroidogenesis cannot be ruled out. CRYM has also been shown to be the most abundantly expressed protein in the lens of diurnal marsupials (Segovia et al. 1997). Our data clearly identify CRYM as a ketimine reductase in lamb brain and show that human CRYM has similar reductase activity (Fig. 4). This research is the first to conclusively demonstrate an enzyme function for CRYM. The strong inhibition of enzyme activity by T3 is a unique finding defining it as a key regulator of amino acid metabolism, especially as it would be a key regulator of the pipecolic acid pathway, which is the predominant lysine catabolic pathway in adult mammalian brain. The ketimine reductase activity of CRYM and the potent inhibition of activity by T3 suggest that in vivo concentrations of T3 and CRYM, as well as activities of associated enzymes supplying ketimine substrates to CRYM, can be expected to have a profound effect on the intracellular concentrations of ketimines. In addition, our findings suggest a reciprocal role of ketimine reductase enzyme activity in regulation of T3 transactivation to the nucleus.

The X-ray crystal structure of human CRYM was solved in 2007, but with no bound ligand apart from the cofactor NADPH, as its enzyme role was not known prior to the present research (Cheng et al. 2007). The X-ray crystal structure of P. syringae P2C/Pyr2C reductase was solved in 2005 (Goto et al. 2005). The enzyme was shown to belong to a new family of oxidoreductases and is not a structural homologue of CRYM, even though it catalyses similar reactions. Thus, bacterial P2C reductase and mammalian CRYM represent good examples of convergent evolution.

Ketimine reductase previously purified from porcine kidney was reported to have an apparent Mr of 73 000 using gel filtration, but no data on the subunit composition were presented (Nardini et al. 1988a). Nevertheless, this finding compares favourably with the Mr of the recombinant homodimeric lamb forebrain ketimine reductase determined in the present work to be ∼ 70 000. Moreover, the reaction rate data are similar in the two studies. Taken together the evidence suggests that the porcine kidney ketimine reductase and lamb forebrain ketimine reductase are orthologues. However, the partially purified bovine cerebellar enzyme was reported to be a homodimer with a Mr of ∼ 100 000 (Nardini et al. 1988b). Thus, it is possible that the lamb forebrain ketimine reductase and the bovine cerebellar reductase are not orthologues, but rather different enzymes. Of note was our inability to purify ketimine reductase from lamb cerebellum using the reported purification protocols, which would be consistent with findings that CRYM concentrations in cerebellum are markedly reduced in comparison with cerebral levels (Suzuki et al. 1991). The presence of the reported bovine cerebellum ketimine reductase suggests the possibility that more than one ketimine reductase is present in the brain.

μ-Crystallin expression has been found to be significantly altered in a number of neurological and psychiatric disorders including familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Fukada et al. 2007), facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (Reed et al. 2007), multiple sclerosis (Avasarala et al. 2008), schizophrenia (Middleton et al. 2002), and Alzheimer disease (George et al. 2009). In addition, there are two known point mutations of human CRYM, both of which are associated with non-syndromal deafness (Abe et al. 2003). The effects of these mutations on enzyme activity must now be evaluated. The inference is that levels of CRYM/ketimine reductase substrates are important determinants in hearing as CRYM mRNA is highly expressed in human inner ear (Aoki et al. 2000). Altered CRYM expression has also been reported in various cancers such as non-small-cell lung cancer (Chong et al. 2006), glioblastoma (Khalil 2007), and prostate cancer (Malinowska et al. 2009). CRYM is also suspected of playing a role in diabetes as hyperglycaemia has been shown to elevate expression of this protein in vivo and in vitro (Al-Kafaji and Malik 2009). These findings related to CRYM should be re-evaluated in the context of its ketimine reductase activity and the role that CRYM substrates may play in these pathologies.

As there is likely more than one ketimine reductase in the brain we are currently intensively concentrating our research efforts to purify other ketimine reductases from mammalian brain. Enzyme assays of the known CRYM/ketimine reductase mutants would also be beneficial in clarifying their role in enzyme activity in relation to disease phenotypes. Our findings of T3 regulation of CRYM/ketimine reductase enzyme activity define a new direct role in metabolic regulation for T3. Thyroid hormones are known to have profound effects on neurotransmission (Vara et al. 2002), brain development (Bernal 2005), and neural plasticity (Vallortigara et al. 2008). The ketimine reductase inhibition by T3, thus raises an interesting question as to what role the accumulation of CRYM enzyme substrates have in these processes. T3 control of levels of ketimines, which are considered putative neurotransmitters/neuromodulators, adds a new layer to the complexity of neurochemistry, suggesting subtle interactions among the endocrine system, amino acid metabolism and neurotransmission.

Mammalian forebrain ketimine reductase identified as μ-crystallin; potential regulation by thyroid hormones

Abstract
J. Neurochem. (2011) 118, 379–387.

Ketimine reductase (E.C. 1.5.1.25) was purified to apparent homogeneity from lamb forebrain by means of a rapid multi-step chromatography protocol. The purified enzyme was identified by MS/MS (mass spectrometry) as μ-crystallin. The identity was confirmed by heterologously expressing human μ-crystallin in Escherichia coli and subsequent chromatographic purification of the protein. The purified human μ-crystallin was confirmed to have ketimine reductase activity with a maximum specific activity similar to that of native ovine ketimine reductase, and was found to catalyse a sequential reaction. The enzyme substrates are putative neuromodulator/transmitters. The thyroid hormone 3,5,3′-l-triiodothyronine (T3) was found to be a strong reversible competitive inhibitor, and may have a novel role in regulating their concentrations. μ-Crystallin is also involved in intracellular T3 storage and transport. This research is the first to demonstrate an enzyme function for μ-crystallin.

This newly demonstrated enzymatic activity identifies a new role for thyroid hormones in regulating mammalian amino acid metabolism, and a possible reciprocal role of enzyme activity regulating bioavailability of intracellular T3.

Ketimine reductases specifically catalyse the reduction of imine bonds using either NADH or NADPH as cofactor. They include the previously partially characterised Δ1-piperideine-2-carboxylate (P2C)/Δ1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate (Pyr2C) reductase (E.C. 1.5.1.21) isolated from porcine kidney (Petrakis and Greenberg 1965) and Pseudomonas putida (Payton and Chang 1982), and ketimine reductase (E.C. 1.5.1.25) isolated from bovine cerebellum (Nardini et al. 1988b) and porcine kidney (Nardini et al. 1988a). Two different ketimine reductases have previously been partially purified from bovine cerebellum (Nardini et al. 1988b) and porcine kidney cortex (Nardini et al. 1988a), and partly characterised. No sequence data were obtained, and as a result no gene assignments are currently available for these reductases.

Ketimine reductase substrates include the sulphur-containing cyclic ketimines S-(2-aminoethyl)-l-cysteine ketimine (AECK), lanthionine ketimine (LK) and cystathionine ketimine (CysK) (Fig. 1).

These originate from sulphur-containing amino acids such as cysteine and homocysteine, which are converted to the cyclic sulphur-containing amino acid precursors by cystathionine β-synthase (Cavallini et al. 1991). These precursors are then transaminated by glutamine transaminase K [GTK; also known as kynurenine aminotransferase isozyme I (KAT1)] (Cooper 2004), or possibly oxidised by l-amino acid oxidase, to form the corresponding α-keto acids, which non-enzymatically cyclise to form the cyclic ketimines (Cavallini et al. 1991) (Fig. 2).

Δ1-Piperideine-2-carboxylate and Δ1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate (Fig. 1) are also ketimine reductase substrates. P2C is derived from lysine catabolism from the pipecolic acid pathway. In mammals, lysine is metabolised by two main pathways – the saccharopine pathway and the pipecolic acid pathway. The saccharopine pathway predominates in extracerebral tissues, whereas the pipecolic acid pathway is the main route for lysine catabolism in the adult brain (Garweg et al. 1980). In the pipecolic acid pathway, oxidation of l-lysine at the α-carbon results in the formation of an α-keto acid that cyclises to P2C (Garweg et al. 1980). Pyr2C arises from the oxidation of d-proline by d-amino acid oxidase.

Ketimine reductases catalyse its reduction to l-proline (Petrakis and Greenberg 1965).

Cystathionine ketimine and LK have been reported to be present in human cerebral cortex, AECK and CysK in bovine brain, and CysK and LK in human urine (Cavallini et al. 1991). The reduced enzyme products of AECK, LK and CysK, namely 1,4-thiomorpholine-3-carboxylic acid (TMA), 1,4-thiomorpholine-3,5-dicarboxylic acid and cyclothionine, respectively, have been reported to be present in bovine brain and in human urine (Cavallini et al. 1991).

Biological activity that could affect neurological function has been demonstrated for the sulphur-containing cyclic ketimines. LK is known to bind strongly to isolated brain membranes, resulting in significant increases of cAMP. This binding was found to be saturable, reversible and specific. Specific binding was shown by the fact that LK could only be displaced by other ketimines, AECK and CysK, and catecholamines (Dupre et al. 1993). AECK is a strong competitive inhibitor of d-amino acid oxidase (Ricci et al. 1983), and may act as an endogenous regulator of glutamate NMDA receptor activity through modulation of d-serine levels. This implies a specific neuromodulator/transmitter role for the ketimines with particular importance in the brain.

In contrast, little is known regarding the biological functions of P2C or Pyr2C. l-Pipecolic acid, derived from the reduction of P2C by ketimine reductase, has been shown to be a weak inhibitory neurotransmitter (Charles 1986). No other biological functions have been reported for P2C or Pyr2C and their reduced products.

Cyclic ketimines are present in solution as an equilibrium mixture of cyclic enaminic, cyclic ketiminic, and open-chain forms, with cyclic forms predominating under physiological conditions (Cavallini et al. 1991). However, ketimine reductases appear to only catalyse the reduction of the ketiminic form as: when assayed at pH 5 some substrates, such as CysK, do not exist as enamines (Nardini et al. 1988a); the ketimine reductase product using AECK as substrate is the cyclic amino acid TMA (Nardini et al. 1988a), which cannot arise from reduction of the open chain form.

Here, we report the purification of a ketimine reductase from lamb cerebral cortex and the identification of the lamb and human enzyme as the protein μ-crystallin (CRYM), for which an enzymatic function had not previously been determined. We also report the strong competitive enzyme inhibition by the thyroid hormone 3,5,3′-l-triiodothyronine (T3).

This new role for T3 in regulation of cyclic ketimine levels represents an important new mechanism in our understanding of the biochemical actions of T3, and is an important addition to our understanding of the neurochemical role of thyroid hormones.

Materials and methods
Materials and assays
All chemicals and reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (Sydney, Australia) unless stated otherwise. AECK and CysK were synthesized as per the protocols of Cavallini et al. (1983), and P2C by the protocol of Meister (1954). The full length human CRYM ORF bacterial expression clone (product # I0311) was purchased from GeneCopoeia (Rockville, MD, USA). All chromatographic media and columns were purchased from GE Healthcare (Sydney, Australia) and Bio-Rad (Sydney, Australia).

Ketimine reductase assays were performed in a similar manner to those previously reported (Nardini et al. 1988a,b), using a standard mixture in 100 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5) at 37°C.

One unit of enzyme activity is defined as the amount of enzyme that catalyses the oxidation of 1 μmol of NADH per minute at 37°C in a standard reaction mixture.

For enzyme kinetic measurements, assays were adapted to microtiter plates using a BMG Fluostar Galaxy (Offenburg, Germany) and were performed in a total volume of 200 μL of buffer containing 20% w/v glycerol, 100 mM sodium acetate (pH 5) with variable concentrations of substrates at 37°C. The reaction was initiated by the addition of enzyme which had been diluted in assay buffer. Fluorescence detection, excitation wavelength of 360 nm and emission wavelength of 460 nm, was used instead of UV absorbance for monitoring the conversion of NADH or NADPH to NAD or NADP, respectively. Standard curves were generated with varying concentrations of NADH and NADPH. The non-enzymatic decrease in fluorescence of NADH or NADPH, because of the acidic assay conditions, was compensated for by running a blank simultaneously containing all assay components except for the ketimine substrate. The reduction product of AECK was identified as the cyclic amino acid TMA (Fig. 1) by the procedure of Nardini et al.

(1988a).

Inhibition studies involving T3 were carried out at pH 5 and also at pH 7 (100 mM potassium phosphate buffer). A stock solution of T3 was made up in dimethylsulfoxide and varying amounts added to the reaction mixture. In a separate experiment, it was determined that the amount of dimethylsulfoxide in the reaction mixture resulting from addition of T3 stock solutions did not inhibit the enzyme activity.

Enzyme kinetic data were globally fitted and analysed using GraphPad Prism 5 software (GraphPad software Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) using non-linear regression.

Purification protocol
Potassium phosphate buffer [10 mM, pH 7, 10% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT)] was used in all protocols unless otherwise specified. All purification protocols were performed at 4°C. Brain ketimine reductase was purified from lamb frontal cortical sections using multiple chromatography columns, and purified to apparent homogeneity by tracking enzyme activity using AECK (1 mM) and NADH (0.2 mM) as substrates. A Bio-Rad Biologic HR chromatography worksystem was used for purification steps. Sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) was used to monitor the purification. Pall, Inc.

concentrating membranes (Port Washington, NY, USA) with a cut-off of 30 kDa were used, except in the case of the final purification step where a 10 kDa membrane was used.

Preparation of lamb brains
Lamb brains were purchased from a local abattoir, chilled on ice within 30 min of slaughter, and stored within 2 h at −80°C. Enzyme activity was found to be stable for prolonged periods in the frozen brain at this temperature. Thawed frontal cortex sections (250 g wet weight in total) were added to 700 mL of ice-cold potassium phosphate buffer, and homogenised in a Waring blender (Torrington, CT, USA) at high speed for 2 min. The homogenate was centrifuged for 60 min in a Beckman centrifuge (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA), at 30 000 g using a JA-20 rotor.

Anion exchange chromatography
As per the protocol of Nardini et al. (1988a), the supernatant (650 mL) was immediately applied to a 100 mL XK50/20 column containing DEAE fast Sepharose weak anion exchanger (GE Healthcare) equilibrated with potassium phosphate buffer. The supernatant was pumped onto the column at 8 mL/min.

The DEAE column was washed with 95 mM KCl in phosphate buffer until the absorbance at 280 nm was less than 0.1, and protein was then eluted at 6 mL/min with 165 mM KCl in phosphate buffer. Active fractions were pooled and solid ammonium sulphate (AS) was immediately added to a final concentration of 700 mM.

Hydrophobic interaction chromatography
The pooled active fractions were then pumped onto an XK16/20 column containing 12 mL of phenyl sepharose HP (GE Healthcare) at 6 mL/min. The column was previously equilibrated with phosphate buffer containing 700 mM AS. The column was then washed with the same concentration of AS in phosphate buffer, until the UV absorbance at 280 nm was less than 0.02, then protein was eluted at 6 mL/min with a 100-0%. AS gradient of 12 column volumes followed by 5 column volumes of phosphate buffer. Active fractions eluted in a single peak and were collected, concentrated to 12 mL, and buffer exchanged to 20 mM phosphate buffer a using Sephadex G-25 column.

Flow-through protocol
In preliminary experiments, ketimine reductase was found not to bind to either hydroxylapatite or heparin sulphate in the presence of phosphate buffer at 20 mM.

Thus, a flow-through protocol using these two matrices, together with a HiTrap Blue column, was used to quickly remove many protein contaminants. The flow-through protocol made use of a ceramic 10-mL hydroxylapatite column (80 μm ceramic beads), 10-mL heparin sulphate fast flow, and 1-mL HiTrap Blue connected in series. The columns were equilibrated with 20 mM phosphate buffer. After the sample from the previous purification step was injected onto the columns and washed with 35 mL of buffer at 1 mL/min, the hydroxylapatite column and heparin columns were disconnected. The HiTrap Blue column was washed with 10 column volumes of 20 mM phosphate buffer, and the protein samples eluted using 1 μM NADPH directly onto a pre-equilibrated 1-mL Resource Q strong anion exchange column. The column was washed with 10 column volumes of 20 mM phosphate buffer containing 20% (v/v) glycerol and eluted with a 0–500 mM KCl gradient, in 20 mM phosphate buffer, over 12 column volumes at 1 mL/min. A single peak was collected and the pooled samples concentrated to 110 μL.

Protein samples in 5-μL aliquots were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C.

Sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis
Bio-Rad 5× loading dye, containing bromophenol blue dye and β-mercaptoethanol (200 mM) were added to protein samples in 1.5-mL Eppendorf tubes, which were then heated for 2 min in a boiling water bath. SDS–PAGE was performed using NuSep (Sydney, Australia) 10-well Tris–Gly 4–20% LongLife gels. Bio-Rad Broad Range molecular mass markers were added to the first lane (200, 116, 97, 66, 45, 31, 21.5, 14.4, 6.5 kDa). SDS–PAGE conditions: 55 min at 155 V using a Bio-Rad power source until the bromophenol blue dye front had reached the base of the gel. The gels were stained with colloidal Coomassie Blue stain/methanol (4 : 1) overnight. The gels were then destained with 20% methanol, after which they were washed and analysed.

Protein identification by MS/MS
Gel bands were excised after their positions were revealed by staining. The protein in each band was reduced with DTT, alkylated with iodoacetamide, and digested in-gel with trypsin (Haynes et al. 1998). Extracted peptides were subjected to nanoLC-MS/MS (mass spectrometry) (Lee et al. 2009).

Briefly, peptides were separated by reversed-phase chromatography and eluted directly into a Thermo LTQ-XL ion trap mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The six most abundant peptides detected in a survey scan of 400–1500 amu were subjected to collision induced dissociation. Raw files were converted to mzxml format and spectra were searched against the bovine sequence database (release date 13 April 2010) using the XTandem algorithm running under The Global Proteome Machine interface (Craig et al. 2004). The peptide mass tolerance was set at 2 Da, fragment ion mass tolerance at 0.2 Da, cysteine was considered to be modified with iodoacetamide and methionine was considered to be variably modified by S oxidation. Spectra were also searched against a reversed database to estimate false discovery rates, and using minimum criteria of three peptides identified and a log (e) score of <−10. With these search criteria no proteins were identified in the reversed database searches.

Expression and purification of recombinant proteins in Escherichia coli
The full length human CRYM ORF bacterial expression clone (Entrez gene ID: 1428 transcript variant 1, longer isoform) contained an N-His6 tag and T7 promoter in a pReceiver-B01 vector, and ampicillin selectivity. It was transformed into E.

coli (Fusion Blue cells) and E. coli BL21 (DE3)STAR (Inoue et al. 1990). For production of the CRYM the transformed E. coli BL21 (DE3)STAR was streaked onto Luria-Bertani agar plates containing ampicillin (100 μg/mL). The plates were incubated overnight at 37°C and a single colony was picked and cultured in 1 L of Luria-Bertani medium with 1 mM ampicillin at 37°C and with constant shaking on an orbital shaker until the OD600 reached 0.5. Recombinant protein expression was induced with 1 mM isopropyl-β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation overnight at 18°C with constant shaking. The culture was then centrifuged at 6000 g for 20 min at 4°C, and the pellet resuspended in 20 mL of binding buffer [Tris buffer (20 mM, pH 7.9) containing NaCl (500 mM) and imidazole (5 mM)]. The cell suspension was lysed using three passes of a French press at 10 000 psi. Further centrifuging at 20 000 g resulted in the isolation of a soluble protein-containing supernatant. The supernatant was applied to a nickel-charged His-Trap affinity column (1 mL). The column was pre-equilibrated with cold binding buffer.

After binding of the protein to the column, the column was successively washed with (i) 5 column volumes of binding buffer, (ii) 5 volumes of Tris buffer (20 mM, pH 7.9) containing NaCl (500 mM) and imidazole (60 mM). The CRYM protein was then eluted with Tris buffer (20 mM, pH 7.9) containing NaCl (500 mM) and imidazole (500 mM), and collected in 0.5 mL fractions. Most of the protein and ketimine reductase activity was found to be in three consecutive fractions totalling 1.5 mL. These were combined and desalted using a 5-mL desalting column equilibrated with 10 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7) containing 20% (v/v) glycerol and 1 mM DTT. Aliquots (15 μL) were flash-frozen in 500 μL Eppendorf tubes and stored at −80°C. Protein concentration was determined using a Bio-Rad Bradford assay with bovine serum albumin as a standard and was determined to be 8 mg/mL. Protein purity was determined by SDS–PAGE and MS/MS protein identification, with only one major band on SDS–PAGE and only one major protein detected by MS/MS.

Gel filtration
A Superdex 200HR gel filtration column (GE Healthcare) was used to check the apparent Mr.

The column was eluted at 0.5 mL/min using 150 mM NaCl in 10 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7). The column was calibrated with GE Healthcare Protein standards (ferritin, 440 kDa; aldolase, 158 kDa; ovalbumin, 43 kDa; and ribonuclease, 13.7 kDa).

Data presentation
All data are presented as the mean ± SE.

Results
Purification of lamb brain ketimine reductase and identification as CRYM by MS/MS.

Lamb forebrain ketimine reductase was purified ∼ 470 fold to apparent homogeneity with a yield of 0.2% by utilizing four different chromatographic steps (Fig. 3). The purified enzyme was found to have a specific activity of 15 U/mg. There was a low recovery of protein after the final step (24 μg), but a marked gain in specific activity (Fig. 3). The enzyme was found to be highly unstable and prone to oxidation as was found by earlier researchers (Nardini et al. 1988a,b). A single protein band at ∼ 35 kDa on SDS–PAGE was observed (Fig. 3). The purified protein was trypsin-digested and identified by MS/MS. The highest ranking protein identification was bovine μ-crystallin (CRYM) with a log (e) score of −869, 1429 total peptides, 68 unique peptides identified, and 75% coverage.

Identified peptides covered all exons (Fig. 4) corresponding to the full-length 314 amino acid bovine CRYM isoform, GenBank Accession NP_001039379, and the bovine CRYM has 91% identity to the human CRYM, Accession number NP_001879.1 (Fig. 4). A minor contaminant was identified as pyridoxal phosphate phosphatase with a log (e) score of −22 with only four total peptides and three unique peptides identified, and 10% coverage.

Identification of recombinant human CRYM as ketimine reductase
The recombinant human CRYM orthologue of the full-length 314 amino acid bovine CRYM isoform was heterologously expressed in E. coli to conclusively confirm the identity of the ketimine reductase. HisTrap-purified recombinant human CRYM was subjected to SDS–PAGE, and displayed a single band at ∼ 35 kDa (Fig. 3). The purified human enzyme eluted from a Superdex 200 HR column with an apparent Mr of ∼ 70 000, confirming its native form as a homodimer. It had a maximum specific activity as a ketimine reductase of 9.6 U/mg using AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor. The pH optimum was found to be identical to that of porcine ketimine reductase (Nardini et al.

1988a) at pH 4.5 under the same reaction conditions, and similar to that found for bovine cerebellum ketimine reductase (pH 5) (Nardini et al. 1988b). The reaction rate exhibited with NADPH is 40% that exhibited with NADH when AECK is the co-substrate.

For comparison purposes with previous research, various potential substrates for lamb ketimine reductase were tested (Table 1). Similar assay conditions and substrate concentrations were used as in previous studies (Nardini et al. 1988a,b). Assays using 0.2 mM NADH or NADPH in sodium acetate buffer (100 mM, pH 5) were performed. Maximal activity with lamb ketimine reductase was found using AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor. This substrate specificity is similar to that found previously for porcine kidney ketimine reductase (Nardini et al. 1988a). In comparison, the best substrate for bovine cerebellum ketimine reductase was found to be P2C with NADPH as cofactor (Nardini et al. 1988b).

Michaelis-Menten kinetics
A double reciprocal plot of kinetic data indicated that human recombinant CRYM catalyses a sequential mechanism (Fig. 5). Thus, kinetic data were globally fitted to the equation for a bi-bi sequential mechanism using non-linear regression:

where [A] represents AECK substrate concentration and [B] represents NADH concentration.

In the presence of 0.053 μg of enzyme, a Km of 47 ± 10 μM and Vmax of 9.6 ± 0.3 μmol/min/mg was determined using varying NADH concentrations and AECK as substrate (Fig. 5). A Km of 3.6 ± 1.4 μM was determined for NADH under the same conditions. These results compare favourably to those documented previously for porcine kidney ketimine reductase, where the Km values obtained under similar conditions for AECK and NADH were found to be 77 μM and 27 μM, respectively (Nardini et al. 1988a).
Inhibition studies
Previous reports indicated that 3,5,3′-l-triodothyronine (T3) strongly binds to CRYM in the presence of NADPH (Vie et al. 1997), with the strength of binding in the order: d-T3 ≈ l-T3 > l-thyroxine (T4) > reverse T3 (Beslin et al. 1995). Assays were therefore conducted to investigate whether T3 inhibits the ketimine reductase activity of human recombinant CRYM. Inhibitory data were recorded using 0.13 μg enzyme in each assay mixture. Assays were conducted at varying concentrations of T3, AECK, and NADH.

Global non-linear regression analysis of all data revealed that the equation for competitive inhibition was the best fit:

At neutral pH the inhibition was far stronger, but it was not possible to accurately determine a Ki value using AECK as substrate, as the inhibition no longer fitted any of the classical equations (Fig. 7). This is because of the reported very low KD for T3 at neutral pH of 0.31 nM (Beslin et al. 1995). The assays in Fig. 7 were done at an enzyme concentration of 44.5 nM as at neutral pH enzyme activity with AECK as substrate and NADH as cofactor is 25% that at pH 5. The curves at different T3 concentrations have a calculated Vmax that would be expected if the concentration of enzyme were equal to (44.5-[T3]). This inhibitory effect is consistent with inhibition of enzyme activity by T3 and the 0.31 nM KD for T3 binding (Beslin et al. 1995) to CRYM.

This type of inhibition by T3 is almost equivalent to an irreversible inhibitor in enzyme kinetic terms and it effectively means that ketimine reductase activity would be negligible when T3 is in excess of CRYM in vivo.

Discussion
Lamb forebrain ketimine reductase was purified to apparent homogeneity using a rapid purification protocol, identified as CRYM by MS/MS, and the identification confirmed by assaying recombinantly expressed human CRYM. The enzymatic function of CRYM has remained elusive in spite of research efforts spanning more than 20 years. It is a homologue of a number of prokaryote enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism, including ornithine cyclodeaminase (Goodman et al. 2004) and lysine cyclodeaminase (Tsotsou and Barbirato 2007), although CRYM has previously been shown to have no cyclodeaminase activity (Goodman et al. 2004). CRYM has been shown to be a major cytosolic T3 binding protein and a key redox-dependent regulator of intracellular T3 bioavailability and transactivation to the nucleus (Mori et al. 2002). CRYM mRNA expression is also down-regulated by follicle stimulating hormone in mammalian ovary and it may play an important regulatory role in steroidogenesis (Ko et al. 2003).

A direct role of CRYM/ketimine reductase enzyme substrates as regulators of steroidogenesis cannot be ruled out. CRYM has also been shown to be the most abundantly expressed protein in the lens of diurnal marsupials (Segovia et al. 1997). Our data clearly identify CRYM as a ketimine reductase in lamb brain and show that human CRYM has similar reductase activity (Fig. 4). This research is the first to conclusively demonstrate an enzyme function for CRYM. The strong inhibition of enzyme activity by T3 is a unique finding defining it as a key regulator of amino acid metabolism, especially as it would be a key regulator of the pipecolic acid pathway, which is the predominant lysine catabolic pathway in adult mammalian brain. The ketimine reductase activity of CRYM and the potent inhibition of activity by T3 suggest that in vivo concentrations of T3 and CRYM, as well as activities of associated enzymes supplying ketimine substrates to CRYM, can be expected to have a profound effect on the intracellular concentrations of ketimines.

In addition, our findings suggest a reciprocal role of ketimine reductase enzyme activity in regulation of T3 transactivation to the nucleus.

The X-ray crystal structure of human CRYM was solved in 2007, but with no bound ligand apart from the cofactor NADPH, as its enzyme role was not known prior to the present research (Cheng et al. 2007). The X-ray crystal structure of P. syringae P2C/Pyr2C reductase was solved in 2005 (Goto et al. 2005). The enzyme was shown to belong to a new family of oxidoreductases and is not a structural homologue of CRYM, even though it catalyses similar reactions. Thus, bacterial P2C reductase and mammalian CRYM represent good examples of convergent evolution.

Ketimine reductase previously purified from porcine kidney was reported to have an apparent Mr of 73 000 using gel filtration, but no data on the subunit composition were presented (Nardini et al. 1988a). Nevertheless, this finding compares favourably with the Mr of the recombinant homodimeric lamb forebrain ketimine reductase determined in the present work to be ∼ 70 000. Moreover, the reaction rate data are similar in the two studies.

Taken together the evidence suggests that the porcine kidney ketimine reductase and lamb forebrain ketimine reductase are orthologues. However, the partially purified bovine cerebellar enzyme was reported to be a homodimer with a Mr of ∼ 100 000 (Nardini et al. 1988b). Thus, it is possible that the lamb forebrain ketimine reductase and the bovine cerebellar reductase are not orthologues, but rather different enzymes. Of note was our inability to purify ketimine reductase from lamb cerebellum using the reported purification protocols, which would be consistent with findings that CRYM concentrations in cerebellum are markedly reduced in comparison with cerebral levels (Suzuki et al. 1991). The presence of the reported bovine cerebellum ketimine reductase suggests the possibility that more than one ketimine reductase is present in the brain.

μ-Crystallin expression has been found to be significantly altered in a number of neurological and psychiatric disorders including familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Fukada et al. 2007), facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (Reed et al. 2007), multiple sclerosis (Avasarala et al. 2008), schizophrenia (Middleton et al. 2002), and Alzheimer disease (George et al. 2009). In addition, there are two known point mutations of human CRYM, both of which are associated with non-syndromal deafness (Abe et al.

2003). The effects of these mutations on enzyme activity must now be evaluated. The inference is that levels of CRYM/ketimine reductase substrates are important determinants in hearing as CRYM mRNA is highly expressed in human inner ear (Aoki et al. 2000). Altered CRYM expression has also been reported in various cancers such as non-small-cell lung cancer (Chong et al. 2006), glioblastoma (Khalil 2007), and prostate cancer (Malinowska et al. 2009). CRYM is also suspected of playing a role in diabetes as hyperglycaemia has been shown to elevate expression of this protein in vivo and in vitro (Al-Kafaji and Malik 2009). These findings related to CRYM should be re-evaluated in the context of its ketimine reductase activity and the role that CRYM substrates may play in these pathologies.

As there is likely more than one ketimine reductase in the brain we are currently intensively concentrating our research efforts to purify other ketimine reductases from mammalian brain. Enzyme assays of the known CRYM/ketimine reductase mutants would also be beneficial in clarifying their role in enzyme activity in relation to disease phenotypes. Our findings of T3 regulation of CRYM/ketimine reductase enzyme activity define a new direct role in metabolic regulation for T3.

Thyroid hormones are known to have profound effects on neurotransmission (Vara et al. 2002), brain development (Bernal 2005), and neural plasticity (Vallortigara et al. 2008). The ketimine reductase inhibition by T3, thus raises an interesting question as to what role the accumulation of CRYM enzyme substrates have in these processes. T3 control of levels of ketimines, which are considered putative neurotransmitters/neuromodulators, adds a new layer to the complexity of neurochemistry, suggesting subtle interactions among the endocrine system, amino acid metabolism and neurotransmission.
