Introduction
The glycine cleavage system is a mitochondrial multienzyme system composed of four proteins termed P, H, T and L-protein, and catalyzes the reversible oxidation of glycine yielding carbon dioxide, ammonia, 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate (5,10-CH2-H4folate), and reduced pyridine nucleotide. T-protein (aminomethyltransferase EC 2.1.2.10) is a folate-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the release of ammonia and the transfer of the methylene carbon unit (C1 unit) to tetrahydrofolate (H4folate) from the aminomethyl intermediate attached to the lipoate cofactor of H-protein. The aminomethyl intermediate is the product of the decarboxylation of glycine catalyzed by P-protein.1 In the absence of H4folate, formaldehyde is produced instead of 5,10-CH2-H4folate,2 although toxic formaldehyde is not the physiological product in the cell. In the reverse reaction, T-protein catalyzes the formation of the H-protein-bound aminomethyl lipoate intermediate from 5,10-CH2-H4folate, ammonia, and reduced H-protein via an ordered Ter Bi mechanism, in which reduced H-protein is the first substrate to bind followed by 5,10-CH2-H4folate and ammonia.3
Non-ketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH), an inborn error of metabolism inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, is characterized by a massive accumulation of glycine in plasma and cerebrospinal fluids with severe neurological symptoms. It is caused by mutations in the genes encoding the components of the glycine cleavage system. More than 85% of the patients are deficient in P-protein activity, whereas the remaining patients are deficient in T-protein activity.4 We previously identified three mutations in T-protein causing NKH5 and so far a total of 12 mutations linked to NKH have been reported in the T-protein gene. They result in nine amino acid substitutions; G19R (numbering based on mature human T-protein (huT)), G241D, R292H,5 D248H,6 H14R,7 V184A, Y197C, R268H8 and N117I;9 a one-base deletion, 183delC;6 a premature stop codon, Q192X,10 and a splice site mutation IVS7-1G>A†. The homozygous or heterozygous combinations of these mutations result in the severe neonatal type or the late-onset mild type NKH. E183K, a rare polymorphism occurring in only 2% of control alleles, was also found in the patients with the R292H mutation.8 Most of the residues concerned with the missense mutation are well conserved in T-protein from many species, although little is known about their effects in terms of the molecular basis of these mutations.
We have found that lysine residues of Escherichia coli T-protein (ecT) at positions 78, 81 and 352 are involved in the interaction with the polyglutamate moiety of 5,10-methylenetetrahydropteroyltetraglutamate (5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4).11 Kinetic analysis with single and multiple substitution mutants for these lysine residues postulated that Lys352 interacts with the α-carboxylate of the first glutamate residue nearest the p-aminobenzoic acid ring of 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4 and that Lys81 interacts with the α-carboxylate of the second glutamate residue. Furthermore, a cross-linking study12 revealed that the interaction of E. coli H-protein (ecH) with ecT causes a conformational change of ecT resulting in an intramolecular contact between Asp34 and Lys216 of ecT. Intermolecular contact between Lys288 of ecT and Asp43 of ecH was also identified, providing the information to depict the ecT–ecH complex. The N-terminal region of ecT is essential for the interaction with ecH12 and for holding ecT in a compact form.13
Here, we have determined the crystal structure of mature form huT to gain insights into the reaction site, the catalytic mechanism, and the role of the NKH-causing residues at the molecular level. huT monomer consists of three domains arranged in a cloverleaf-like structure with the central cavity, which 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-CH3-H4folate), an analog of folate substrate, occupies with extensive hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts. The obtained structure allows us to describe not only the mechanistic details of the mode for transfer of C1 unit from the aminomethyl lipoate arm to H4folate, but also the coupling model of T and H-protein for the destabilization and release of the arm from the binding cleft of H-protein. Furthermore, the structure of human enzyme as well as the mutation analysis provided detailed molecular bases for understanding the cause of NKH.

Results and Discussion
Overall and monomer structures
The crystal structure of mature huT was solved using single-wavelength anomalous diffraction data for a heavy-atom variant. The electron density map was of sufficient quality to allow tracing of most residues in the structure. The model was subsequently refined to 2.0 Å with an Rcryst of 16.0% and Rfree of 19.5% (Table 1). The final model contains two huT monomers related by a non-crystallographic 2-fold axis, 1176 water molecules, and 11 molecules of sulfate ion in an asymmetric unit. Several dimeric interactions are observed among the residues on the N-terminal loop, on α-helix D, and the flank on either side of β-strand 8 of the two monomers. However, since the interface is not very extensive, burying 637.1 Å2 (4.3%) of solvent-accessible surface per monomer, and since only the monomeric form is detected in the size exclusion experiment (data not shown), the dimer formation is probably a consequence of crystal contacts. The N-terminal three residues (Ala1–Glu3) (mature huT numbering) and C-terminal Lys375 of each monomer are missing because of structural disorder.
The huT monomer consists of nine α-helices, 19 β-strands and three 310-helices, forming three domains (1, 2 and 3) arranged in a cloverleaf-like structure with the central cavity, where folates bind (Figure 1, Figure 2). Domain 1 (residues 4–56 and 147–239) is made up of two and five-stranded antiparallel β-sheets, five α-helices (αA, αB, αF, αE and αG) and a β-strand (β13). The domain seems to play a critical role in maintaining the entire molecular folding, because the single mutation of Leu6 of ecT (corresponding to Leu10 in huT) (Figure 2(a)) to alanine resulted in high susceptibility to trypsin, leading to the instant cleavage at Arg16 and the consequent rapid degradation of the resulting C-terminal fragment, in contrast to the high resistant nature of wild-type ecT.13 The hydrophobic interaction among Leu10, Val213 and Phe13 might contribute to the folding. Domain 2 (residues 57–146) consists of a five-stranded antiparallel β-sheet and two α-helices (αC and αD). This domain bears the putative catalytic center as described below. The domain 3 (residues 240–374) consists of a loop-rich region and a distorted six-stranded jelly-roll that is oriented perpendicular to the β-sheets of domains 1 and 2, closing the ring-like structure of the protein.
The overall structure resembles those of recently reported bacterial T-proteins from Thermotoga maritima (tmT),14 E. coli and Pyrococcus horikoshii OT3 (phT).15 The superimpositions of Cα atoms of huT on those of tmT in the apo form (PDB accession code 1WOS) gave r.m.s. deviation of 1.1 Å (for 346 equivalent Cα positions). The r.m.s. deviations for ecT (325 equivalent Cα positions from 1VLO) and phT (equivalent Cα positions from 1V5V) were 1.3 Å. The overall structure of huT also resembles that of the C-terminal region of Arthrobacter globiformis dimethylglycine oxidase (DMGO)16 as discussed below.
Active center and catalytic mechanism of huT
To identify the active center of huT, a substrate, 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4 and a competitive inhibitor, 5-CH3-H4folate3 were used to prepare the ligand-bound crystals by the soaking method, but only the 5-CH3-H4folate-bound crystals were obtained. The clear Fo−Fc electron density for 5-CH3-H4folate was present in the central cavity of each huT monomer, effectively filling the space (Figure 1(b)). Although a mixture of 6R and 6S diastereomers of 5-CH3-H4folate was employed in the soaking experiment, only the naturally occurring 6S form was found in the crystals. The ligand binding led to no significant change in the huT structure except for the changes in the χ1 torsion angles of Leu88 and Ile103 of one monomer. Extensive superimposition search indicated that two monomers in an asymmetric unit of the native form are different in the χ1 torsion angles of both Leu88 and Ile103. One monomer is the same as those of the ligand-bound form (Figure 1(b)), and no change occurs by the ligand binding. Leu88 and Ile103 of the other native monomer are rotated 109° in the χ1 torsion angles relative to those of the ligand-bound form, and the angles were converged to the ligand-bound form.
5-CH3-H4folate is bound in a kinked configuration. The pteridine ring is deeply buried in the hydrophobic pocket encircled by Met56, Leu102, Ile103 and Val115 with four hydrogen bonds to the side-chains of Glu204 and Arg233, and the main chain carbonyl of Val115 (Figure 1(b)). A double hydrogen bond, formed between the side-chain of invariant Glu204 and both the 2-amino and 3-imino groups of the pteridine ring, is commonly observed among folate-dependent enzymes such as dimethylglycine oxidase16 and formiminotransferase-cyclodeaminase,17 although the glutamyl residue is occasionally replaced by an aspartyl residue.18 The hydrogen bond between the backbone oxygen of Val115 and the reduced N8 of the pteridine ring is probably responsible for the recognition of the reduced folates as substrate. The p-aminobenzoate moiety, which is oriented almost perpendicular to the pteridine plane, is stacked by the side-chains of Leu88, Tyr197 and Leu242. The glutamyl moiety of 5-CH3-H4folate points to the C-terminal surface. The α-carboxylate links to NH2 group of Arg292 via many water molecules (Figure 1(b)), although the electron densities for these water molecules are weak. The O2 atom of α-carboxylate hydrogen bonds to the side-chain OH group of Tyr371 (2.8 Å), while the γ-carboxylate resides within hydrogen bonding range (3.1 Å) of the backbone nitrogen atom of Leu88 (Figure 1(b)). The model is substantially compatible with our previous prediction that Lys352 and Lys81 of ecT (corresponding to Lys363 and Gln85 of huT, respectively) reside in close proximity to α and γ-carboxylate, respectively, of the bound 5,10-CH2-H4folate glutamate moiety, which is based on a cross-linking experiment using a zero-length cross-linker, 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)carbodiimide.11
The transfer of C1 unit is considered to be initiated by the nucleophilic attack on the methylene carbon of the aminomethyl lipoate arm by the N5 or the N10 atom of the tetrahydrofolate bound to T-protein (Figure 3). The present 5-CH3-H4folate-bound huT crystal structure shows that the Oδ2 atom of strictly conserved Asp101 is to close the N10 atom of 5-CH3-H4folate (3.5 Å). Although the layout of the atoms is not conducive for hydrogen bonding between them in the structure, they will make a hydrogen bond if some conformational changes on the 5-CH3-H4folate occur. On the other hand, the N5 atom of 5-CH3-H4folate is at a distance of 3.9 Å from the Oδ1 atom of Asn117, which is one of the NKH-related residues.8 Asp101 is also involved in the hydrogen bonding network composed of Asn117, Asp100, Ala118 and two water molecules, where Asn117 is the central residue (Figure 5(b)).
To address which atom is responsible for initiating the transfer reaction, we conducted mutation analyses of Asp101 and Asn117. Three mutants employed in our experiment lost the catalytic activity (Table 2), although these mutations did not affect the yields of the mutant proteins overexpressed in E. coli (data not shown). While the D101A mutation seriously disturbs the hydrogen bonding network centered on Asn117, the hydrogen bonding network might remain intact in the D101N mutant. These observations suggest that loss of the oxygen atom able to hydrogen bond to the N10 group leads to loss of the activity and that the transfer reaction would be initiated by the attack on the methylene carbon by the N10 group of the folate substrate. Consistent with this interpretation, the side-chain Oδ2 atom of Asp96 of tmT (corresponding to Asp101 of huT) has been reported to make a hydrogen bond with the N10 group of bound H4folate.14 Furthermore, the C-terminal folate-binding region of DMGO, which is highly similar in primary sequence and catalyzes a reaction homologous to that catalyzed by T-protein, has the Asp552 residue hydrogen bonded to the N10 nitrogen group of folinic acid in the ligand-bound structure.16 Asp552 of DMGO, corresponding to Asp101 of huT in the sequence alignment, is proposed to activate the nucleophilic character of the N10 group to initiate the conversion of the iminium intermediate to sarcosine and 5,10-CH2-H4folate.16 Consequently, the C1 unit transfer reaction is likely to be accomplished by the process outlined in Figure 3, although it needs to be verified by further investigation. The interaction with H-protein may cause the formation of the hydrogen bond between the Oδ2 of Asp101and the N10 atom of the bound folate in huT.
Interaction with H-protein
T-protein forms a complex with H-protein in a 1:1 molar ratio. A graphical coupling of the two proteins was made using pea H-protein (peH) bearing methylamine-loaded lipoate (PDB accession code 1HTP) as a binding partner of huT in the model complex. peH shows a high level of homology (44.6% identical and 67.2% conserved) with human H-protein. The most important prerequisite for the complex formation is the interaction between the lipoate bound to H-protein and the catalytic center of T-protein. It has been reported that the lipoate arms in methylamine-free oxidized or reduced forms are located at the surface of peH in a rather flexible conformation, and following the transfer of methylamine, the cofactor pivots around the lysine linkage and gets locked into the binding cleft of the H-protein.19 The methylamine group at the end of the arm is tightly fixed by ionic bonds to the side-chain carboxyl group of the Glu14, and by hydrogen bonds to the main chain carbonyl groups of Ser12 and Asp67 of peH. Hydrophobic contacts between the long extended chain of carbon atoms of the arm and the hydrophobic residues surrounding the arm also contribute to the fixation. Accordingly, destabilization and release of the arm from the binding cleft are the critical events in the T-protein catalysis and it has been proposed that the β-sheet structure of peH on one side of the lipoyl lysine (β5 and β6 in Figure 4(a)) is collectively destabilized instead of a primary rupture of the methylamine group interaction.20The surface embedding the aminomethy lipoate harbors the protruding side-chain of Glu42 (Figure 4(a)). On the other hand, huT accommodates 5-CH3-H4folate with the N5 and N10 atoms protruding to the N-terminal side at approximately 13–14 Å in depth from the N-terminal surface (Figure 4(b), right). Therefore, the two proteins were put together with these surfaces facing each other, placing the β-sheet of peH (β5 and β6) into the cave under domain 3 of huT. The model predicts a good fitting of the aminomethyl lipoate arm to conserved residues such as Tyr197, Leu230, Arg233, Asp234, Leu244 and Tyr245 of huT. These residues correspond to those interacting with the free form of dihydrolipoic acid in the tmT structure,14 although the interaction may not be the same because the physiologically inactive 6S form of the cofactor21 is incorporated into the structure. Moreover, our complex model may well explain the intramolecular cross-linking between Asp34 and Lys216 of ecT according to the ecH–ecT complex formation.12 Asp39 (Asp34 in ecT) on αB and Lys226 (Lys216 in ecT) on β13 of huT are both positioned at the edge of the domain 1 (Figure 4(a)). The Oδ1 atom of Asp39 is 7.8 Å apart from the NZ atom of Lys226 in the structure. The further approach of peH into the bosom of huT might constrain αB of huT to shift downward or β13 upward, thereby putting Asp39 close to Lys226.
In our complex model, Glu42 of peH is not in the close vicinity of Gly299 of huT. The two residues correspond to Asp43 in ecH and Lys288 in ecT (Figure 2(b)), respectively, that were cross-linked in the ecT–ecH complex.13 However, since the former residue is replaced by serine in animal H-proteins and the sequence around Gly299 is not well conserved among T proteins from various species (Figure 2(a)), the exact positioning of the two residues may not be prerequisite for the complex formation. In the T-H complex model of T. maritima (Tm),14 H-protein bears a protruding lipoate, and the orientation of H-protein against T-protein is quite different from that of our model. Such a protruding structure of the cofactor has not been reported so far even for the methylamine-free form. Consequently, the Tm model seems less rational, since there is no consideration of the destabilization process of the aminomethyl lipoate arm from the binding cleft. Although the crystallographic studies of the complex of T-protein and H-protein with cofactors should give the final answer to the mode of the interaction, our present model can explain not only the structural but also the functional requirements for the catalytic reactions.
Hydrogen bonding networks and structural basis for NKH-causing mutations
Nine residues that on mutation lead to the onset of NKH, as well as a residue showing polymorphism, are mapped in Figure 5(a). Many of them are involved in hydrogen bonding networks surrounding the substrate binding cavity (Figure 5(b)). Asn117 is the central residue of the hydrogen bonding network located in the vicinity of N5/N10 groups of bound folate. The network might participate in the positioning of Asp101 and Val115, the putative enhancer of initiation of the C1 unit transfer and the putative selector of reduced folate, respectively. The NKH-causing mutant, N117I, abolishes the activity (Table 2) probably due to the dysfunction of these residues.
Asp248 forms an extensive hydrogen bonding network with invariant Arg237, Leu244, Thr320 and Ser321, whereas Arg292 forms another hydrogen bonding network adjacent to the former with the backbone carbonyl of Gly258 and Gly241 directly or via an ordered water molecule (Figure 5(b)). Both hydrogen bonding networks contribute not only to supporting the folate-binding space but also to holding the positions and orientations of the αG helix and the following loop (residues 241–246) carrying putative participants in the catalysis. The side-chains of conserved Asp234, Leu244 and Tyr245 form one plane that is parallel with the N-terminal surface, and those of Tyr197 and Leu244 form another plane oriented perpendicular to the former. Either or both planes may function to carry the aminomethyl lipoate arm to the reaction site as discussed above. Based on the tmT structure, Lee et al. predicted the human T-protein structure with the hydrogen bonding network formed between Arg237, Asp248, Arg292, Thr320 and Ser321.14 In our structure, Arg292 is involved in the separate hydrogen bonding network, so that the mutations in Asp248 and Arg292 differently affected the expression and the kinetics. D248H was hardly expressed in E. coli, and only a small amount of the protein was partially purified by affinity chromatography on a Ni2+ column. It gave a specific activity less than 1% of the wild-type (data not shown), suggesting serious alteration of the conformation, probably due to the interruption of the participating hydrogen bonding network. Mutants G241D and R292H were overexpressed in E. coli as soluble proteins comparable to the wild-type enzyme (not shown). The mutant enzymes affinity-purified to almost a single band in SDS-PAGE exhibited specific activities of 12.3% and 1.6%, respectively, of the wild-type (Table 2). These were subjected to detailed kinetic analysis. As shown in Table 3, R292H mutation led to marked increases in the Km for 5,10-CH2-H4folate and 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4 (tenfold and 184-fold, respectively), and resulted in a similar Km value for both substrates. The reduced affinity may be due to the loss of the hydrogen bonding interaction between Arg292 and α-carboxylate or due to the collapse of the glutamyl binding space induced by the disruption of the hydrogen bonds between Arg292 and Asp241. The binding of the α-carboxyl group of the first glutamate residue of the folate polyglutamate may largely contribute to the affinity. In this connection, it should be pointed out that K352E mutation of ecT affects the Km values for 5,10-CH2-H4folate and 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4 less than K81E or K78E mutations.11 Lys352 of ecT is equivalent to Tyr371 of huT whose OH atom also hydrogen bonds to the O2 atom of 5-CH3-H4folat (Figure 1(b)). G241D mutation resulted in four and ninefold increase in the Km value for 5,10-CH2-H4folate and 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4, respectively, suggesting that the side-chain of Gly241 contributes less than Arg292 to the hydrogen bond.
Among other NKH-related residues, His14 and Gly19 are located at the N-terminal side surface of domain 1. We expressed mutants H14R and G19R in E. coli with a His6-tag at the C terminus and they were partially purified by affinity chromatography on a Ni2+ column. Both mutants were poorly expressed as soluble proteins even under co-expression with E. coli chaperones GroEL and GroES (not shown). However, affinity-purified H14R and G19R gave 18% and 61%, respectively, of specific activity relative to the wild-type, suggesting that these residues mainly contribute to the entire folding of huT. The role of both residues could be understood in the context of the N-terminal hasp function.13 The improperly folded mutants may be degraded rapidly in E. coli and in NKH patients.
Glu183 and Val184 are located at the turning point from β10 to β11, which are far from the active center. The E183K mutation was found as a polymorphism that is present in 2/100 normal control alleles, but the co-occurrence with R292H was detected in some NKH patients10 with proposal of a “helper” mutation to produce a more compromised protein function than that of R292H alone.8 The V184A mutation was found in a later onset patient having the heterozygous Y197C mutation. Glu183 hydrogen bonds directly and indirectly to Gly166, Gly186 and Ser188, while Val184 resides in the hydrophobic cluster formed by Leu163, Leu171, Leu174, Met182 and Val192, which contributes to the stacking of these regions. However, the single E183K or V184A mutation might not affect the structure and the activity so greatly. The OH atom of Tyr197 hydrogen bonds to the carbonyl oxygen of Cys243, and plays a critical role in connecting the two highly conserved regions (residues 196–204 and 229–246). Therefore, a patient with the homozygous Y197C mutation might be severely affected.
Comparison with DMGO
DMGO monomer comprises two functional regions, the N-terminal FAD-binding region (residues 1–420) responsible for the oxidation of dimethylglycine, and the C-terminal folate-binding region (residues 421–830) responsible for the formation of 5,10-CH2-H4folate. The primary sequence alignment of huT with the C-terminal folate-binding region of DMGO using CLUSTALW22 gave 22% identity and 42% similarity. The superimposition of Cα atoms of huT (residues 4–374) on those of the C-terminal folate-binding region of folinic acid-bound DMGO (residues 426–830) using LSQMAN23 indicated strong structural similarity (Figure 6(a)) with an r.m.s. deviation of 1.5 Å. Furthermore, the superimposition of the functional residues surrounding the reaction sites demonstrated that all residues involved in binding with the pterin moiety of the respective ligand are conserved in both proteins (Figure 6(b)), except for the corresponding residue to Arg233 that hydrogen bonds to the 4-carbonyl oxygen of 5-CH3-H4folate in huT. The residues involved in the interaction with the glutamate tail cannot be identified in DMGO. The enzyme has a large internal cavity connecting the reaction sites of the N and C-terminal regions, where channeling of the iminium intermediate from the N-terminal reaction site to the C-terminal reaction site is carried out in an intrinsic “unguided” manner.16 The nature of the cavity opening to the outside solution only via the folate-binding funnel ensures sequestration of the reactive iminium intermediate prior to reaction with H4folate to avoid formation of toxic formaldehyde. A similar cavity sequestered from the bulk solvent is likely to be formed by the interaction of H and T-protein. However, in T-protein the aminomethyl head of the lipoate arm should be delivered to the N5/N10 atom positions of H4folate in the narrow tunnel via the ionic and hydrophobic interaction with the residues on the tunnel surface.

Conclusion
We have previously determined the structure and chromosomal localization of the huT gene,24 and identified three missense mutations leading to the onset of NKH.5 The present crystal structure of huT with 5-CH3-H4folate, together with the mutational studies, provides a detailed picture to understand the molecular basis of the disease-causing mutations as well as T-protein catalysis. Most of the disease-related residues cluster around the folate binding cavity forming the extensive hydrogen bonding networks. These networks are essential not only for supporting the folate-binding space but also for holding the positions and orientations of the secondary structural elements surrounding the folate-binding cavity that carry putative participants in the catalysis. Furthermore, the catalytic residues that directly participate in the C1 unit transfer were verified by the mutation analysis. The model of the H and T-protein complex, which is very different from the proposed Tm model, provides a reasonable picture of the catalytic process. First, the aminomethyl lipoate arm will be liberated from the binding cleft in the H-protein surface, and then recruited to the catalytic center without releasing the toxic formaldehyde during the catalysis. The hydrogen bonding networks surrounding the folate-binding cavity play important roles in almost every aspect of the process.
Materials and Methods
Cloning, expression and purification of human T-protein
To construct a full-length coding sequence of huT, an EcoRI-BglII fragment of HT15 insert and a BglII-HindIII fragment of HT24 insert25 were ligated into pTZ19U and resulted in pTZ/HT. For expression of mature form huT lacking the mitochondrial target sequence, an NdeI site was introduced adjacent to the codon for Ala29 residue of the precursor huT cDNA in pTZ/HT by the method described by Kunkel et al.26 using a Bio-Rad kit and the sense oligonucleotide 5′-GTCGTCCACTTCATATGGCACAGGACGT-3′ (the NdeI site is underlined). Creation of a BamHI site placed downstream of the stop codon and deletion of the NdeI site originally present in the coding region without altering the amino acid, were simultaneously carried out with nucleotides 5′-AGTGAAGATGGATCCGGGTGGGGCT-3′ (the BamHI site is underlined) and 5′-GACGTCTCTCACATGCTGCAGAC-3′ (the modified base is shown in boldface), respectively. An NdeI-BamHI fragment of the resulting plasmid was ligated to pET3a. The nucleotide sequence of the construct, pET3/HT, was verified by DNA sequencing.
E. coli BL21(DE3)pLysS cells transformed with pET3/HT were grown in 500 ml of LB medium containing 20 μg/ml of ampicillin and 25 μg/ml of chloramphenicol at 30 °C for 24 hours. Expression was induced by 25 μM isopropyl-d-thiogalactopyranoside added at the start of the incubation. Cell-free extracts were prepared as described,27 with buffer A (50 mM Tricine-NaOH (pH 8.0), 2 mM EDTA, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 10% (v/v) glycerol, 20 μM p-amidinophenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride) and subjected to SP-Sepharose FF column chromatography (Amersham Bioscience). Bound proteins were eluted with a linear gradient of NaCl (0–0.4 M) in buffer A using the P.S.L.C. system (Amersham Bioscience). The peak fractions were pooled, dialyzed, and subjected to hydroxyapatite column chromatography as described. huT obtained from this step gave a single band in SDS-PAGE (not shown). The final preparation was stored on ice in 20 mM sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), 5 mM dithiothreitol, 10% glycerol and concentrated to appropriate concentrations with Microcon-30 before use.
Crystallization and data collection
The huT in free form was crystallized at 25 °C by the hanging-drop, vapor-diffusion method by mixing equal volumes of the protein at 10 mg/ml and a reservoir solution consisting of 2.2 M ammonium sulfate, 0.1 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), and 0.2 M potassium sodium tartrate. Many small crystals in the shape of a thin needle cluster appeared in several days. Microseeding with the crystals of the droplet consisting of equal volumes of the protein solution (8 mg/ml) and a reservoir solution (1.9 M ammonium sulfate, 0.1 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), 0.2 M potassium sodium tartrate) facilitated growth of the needle crystals to the size of 0.02 mm×0.03 mm×0.72 mm. For cryo-crystallography, the crystals were pre-soaked in the stabilization solution (0.1 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), 2.3 M ammonium sulfate, 0.2 M potassium sodium tartrate, 20% glycerol), mounted in nylon loops and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. The data were collected to 2.0 Å resolution at 100 K using synchrotron radiation and an imaging plate detector, DIP6040 (MAC Science/Bruker AXS) on BL44XU at SPring-8 (Hyogo, Japan), and processed using Denzo and Scalepack programs.28 The crystal belongs to the orthorhombic space group P212121 with unit cell parameters of a=54.2 Å, b=128.5 Å, and c=136.2 Å, and has a solvent content of 57.6%.
huT crystals bound to 5-CH3-H4folat were prepared by soaking the native crystals in 2.1 M ammonium sulfate, 0.1 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), 0.2 M potassium sodium tartrate, 20% glycerol, containing 2 mM 5-CH3-H4folat for 24 hours. The data were collected to 2.6 Å resolution as above. Platinum derivative crystals were prepared by soaking the native crystals in the stabilization solution supplemented with 1 mM K2PtCl4 for six hours, followed by a one hour back-soak in the stabilization solution before being flash-frozen and subjected to data collection to 2.7 Å resolution as above.
Structure solution and refinement
The structure was solved using the single-wavelength anomalous dispersion phasing method with platinum derivative data. The initial platinum atom positions were determined from the Bijvoet anomalous difference Patterson map using the program RSPS29 and refined by the program MLPHARE.30 Heavy atom parameter refinement and phase calculation were carried out using the program SHARP,31 and the electron density map was obtained after phase improvement by the program SOLOMON.32 The atomic model was built using the graphics program O.33 The initial map was sufficiently clear, allowing the initial model composed of residues 4–374 of each monomer in the asymmetric unit. Refinement of the model against the 2.0 Å native data set including successive rounds of simulated annealing refinement, individual B-factor refinement, and model rebuilding was carried out with CNS34 resulting in a final Rcryst of 16.0% and Rfree of 19.4%. The native model solved to 2.0 Å resolution was used as a search model to solve the 5-CH3-H4folate-bound huT structure with CNS. Each cycle of refinement was followed by manual fitting with the program O resulting in a final Rcryst of 17.1% and Rfree of 24.5%. The electron density of the ligand was clearly shown in the center of each monomer. Ramachandran analysis using PROCHECK35 indicated 90.7% (native) and 88.6% (ligand-bound) of non-glycine residues were in the most favored regions, and all others were in the additionally allowed regions. The refinement parameters are presented in Table 1.
Secondary structure assignments were carried out using the program DSSP,36 and structure diagrams were drawn with MOLSCRIPT,37 POVScript,38 GRASP,39 MSMS†, and Raster3D.40 The dimer interface area was calculated with Surface Racer.41 Sequence alignment was carried out using CLUSTALW,22 and superimpositions were conducted using LSQMAN.23
Expression and kinetic analysis of mutant huTs
Mutations for G241D and R292H were carried out with the sense oligonucleotides 5′-CTGGAGGCAGACCTCTGCCTG-3′ and 5′-CAGCGGAGGCATGTGGGGTTGAT-3′ (modified bases are shown in boldface letters), respectively, and subcloned into pET3a as described above. The resulting plasmids pET3/HTG241D and pET3/HTR292H as well as pET3/HT were subjected to PCR with 5′-primer, 5′-TAATACGACTCACTATAGGG-3′ (T7 promoter primer), and 3′-primer, 5′-CCAGCTAAGCTTGAGGGTATAGTAGTTTG-3′ (the HindIII site is underlined), and the NdeI-HindIII fragments were ligated into pET23b to create the expression plasmids for huTs His-tagged at the C terminus (pET23/HT, pET23/HTG241D and pET23/HTR292H). For expression of D101A with the C-terminal His6-tag, cDNA fragments with mutations in the unique SfaNI site were generated by PCR using pET23/HT as template. The N-terminal fragment for D101A was amplified with T7 promoter primer as the 5′-primer and the 3′-primer, 5′-AATCAAGGCATCTAAGATGCCTCCAGC-3′ (modified bases are shown in boldface letters and the SfaNI site is underlined). The C-terminal fragment was amplified with 5′-primer, 5′-GGAGGCATCTTAGATGCCTTGATTGTAACCAATACTTCTG-3′ (modified base is shown in boldface and the SfaNI site is underlined) and 3′-primer, 5′-CCAGCTAAGCTTGAGGGTATAGTAGTTTG-3′ (the HindIII site is underlined). The N-terminal NdeI-SfaNI fragment and the C-terminal SfaNI-HindIII fragment were ligated into pET23b. The expression plasmids for D101N and N117I were constructed by the in-fusion cloning method using pET23/HT as a template and the In-Fusion™ PCR Cloning Kit (BD Bioscience) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Mutations were introduced with the following primers; the 5′-primer, 5′-GATAACTTGATTGTAACCAATACTTCTGAGGGCCACCTG-3′ and the 3′-primer, 5′-TACAATCAACTTATCTAAGATGCCTCCAGCTTCGTTGG-3′ (modified bases are shown in boldface) for D101N, and the 5′-primer, GTGTCCATCGCTGGCTGCTGGGAGAAAGATTTGGCC-3′ and 3′-primer, 5′-GCCAGCGATGGACACCACATACAGGTGGCCCTCAG-3′ (modified bases are shown in boldface) for N117I. All constructs were verified by DNA sequencing.
E. coli BL21(DE3)pGroELES cells, which harbor E. coli chaperone genes, were transformed with the constructed expression plasmids and grown in 200 ml of LB medium containing 20 μg/ml of ampicillin and 10 μg/ml of tetracyclin at 22 °C for 48 hours. Expression was induced by 25 μM isopropyl-d-thiogalactopyranoside added at the start of the incubation. Cell-free extracts were prepared as above with buffer B (20 mM potassium phosphate (pH 7.4), 0.3 M NaCl, 0.2 mM dithiothreitol, 10% glycerol, 20 μM p-amidinophenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride) containing 20 mM imidazole, and subjected to affinity chromatography in a Ni2+ column (4 ml, Qiagen). The column was washed with buffer B containing 50 mM imidazole and eluted with buffer B containing 200 mM imidazole. huTs were dialyzed against 20 mM potassium phosphate (pH 7.4), 1 mM dithiothreitol, 10% glycerol, 20 μM p-amidinophenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride, concentrated if necessary, and stored at −80 °C.
Assay of T-protein activity and kinetic analysis were conducted as described,13 except for employment of appropriate concentrations of the enzymes and substrates.
Protein Data Bank accession codes
The atomic coordinates and structure factors have been deposited in the RCSB Protein Data Bank with codes 1WSR (native huT) and 1WSV (5-CH3-H4folate-bound huT).

Crystal Structure of Human T-protein of Glycine Cleavage System at 2.0 Å Resolution and its Implication for Understanding Non-ketotic Hyperglycinemia

T-protein, a component of the glycine cleavage system, catalyzes the formation of ammonia and 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate from the aminomethyl moiety of glycine attached to the lipoate cofactor of H-protein. Several mutations in the human T-protein gene cause non-ketotic hyperglycinemia. To gain insights into the effect of disease-causing mutations and the catalytic mechanism at the molecular level, crystal structures of human T-protein in free form and that bound to 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-CH3-H4folate) have been determined at 2.0 Å and 2.6 Å resolution, respectively. The overall structure consists of three domains arranged in a cloverleaf-like structure with the central cavity, where 5-CH3-H4folate is bound in a kinked shape with the pteridine group deeply buried into the hydrophobic pocket and the glutamyl group pointed to the C-terminal side surface. Most of the disease-related residues cluster around the cavity, forming extensive hydrogen bonding networks. These hydrogen bonding networks are employed in holding not only the folate-binding space but also the positions and the orientations of α-helix G and the following loop in the middle region, which seems to play a pivotal role in the T-protein catalysis.

Structural and mutational analyses demonstrated that Arg292 interacts through water molecules with the folate polyglutamate tail, and that the invariant Asp101, located close to the N10 group of 5-CH3-H4folate, might play a key role in the initiation of the catalysis by increasing the nucleophilic character of the N10 atom of the folate substrate for the nucleophilic attack on the aminomethyl lipoate intermediate. A clever mechanism of recruiting the aminomethyl lipoate arm to the reaction site seems to function as a way of avoiding the release of toxic formaldehyde.

glycine cleavage systemT-proteinnon-ketotic hyperglycinemia5-CH3-H4folateX-ray crystallography

Introduction
The glycine cleavage system is a mitochondrial multienzyme system composed of four proteins termed P, H, T and L-protein, and catalyzes the reversible oxidation of glycine yielding carbon dioxide, ammonia, 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate (5,10-CH2-H4folate), and reduced pyridine nucleotide. T-protein (aminomethyltransferase EC 2.1.2.10) is a folate-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the release of ammonia and the transfer of the methylene carbon unit (C1 unit) to tetrahydrofolate (H4folate) from the aminomethyl intermediate attached to the lipoate cofactor of H-protein.

The aminomethyl intermediate is the product of the decarboxylation of glycine catalyzed by P-protein.1 In the absence of H4folate, formaldehyde is produced instead of 5,10-CH2-H4folate,2 although toxic formaldehyde is not the physiological product in the cell. In the reverse reaction, T-protein catalyzes the formation of the H-protein-bound aminomethyl lipoate intermediate from 5,10-CH2-H4folate, ammonia, and reduced H-protein via an ordered Ter Bi mechanism, in which reduced H-protein is the first substrate to bind followed by 5,10-CH2-H4folate and ammonia.3
Non-ketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH), an inborn error of metabolism inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, is characterized by a massive accumulation of glycine in plasma and cerebrospinal fluids with severe neurological symptoms. It is caused by mutations in the genes encoding the components of the glycine cleavage system. More than 85% of the patients are deficient in P-protein activity, whereas the remaining patients are deficient in T-protein activity.4 We previously identified three mutations in T-protein causing NKH5 and so far a total of 12 mutations linked to NKH have been reported in the T-protein gene.

They result in nine amino acid substitutions; G19R (numbering based on mature human T-protein (huT)), G241D, R292H,5 D248H,6 H14R,7 V184A, Y197C, R268H8 and N117I;9 a one-base deletion, 183delC;6 a premature stop codon, Q192X,10 and a splice site mutation IVS7-1G>A†. The homozygous or heterozygous combinations of these mutations result in the severe neonatal type or the late-onset mild type NKH. E183K, a rare polymorphism occurring in only 2% of control alleles, was also found in the patients with the R292H mutation.8 Most of the residues concerned with the missense mutation are well conserved in T-protein from many species, although little is known about their effects in terms of the molecular basis of these mutations.
We have found that lysine residues of Escherichia coli T-protein (ecT) at positions 78, 81 and 352 are involved in the interaction with the polyglutamate moiety of 5,10-methylenetetrahydropteroyltetraglutamate (5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4).11 Kinetic analysis with single and multiple substitution mutants for these lysine residues postulated that Lys352 interacts with the α-carboxylate of the first glutamate residue nearest the p-aminobenzoic acid ring of 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4 and that Lys81 interacts with the α-carboxylate of the second glutamate residue. Furthermore, a cross-linking study12 revealed that the interaction of E.

coli H-protein (ecH) with ecT causes a conformational change of ecT resulting in an intramolecular contact between Asp34 and Lys216 of ecT. Intermolecular contact between Lys288 of ecT and Asp43 of ecH was also identified, providing the information to depict the ecT–ecH complex. The N-terminal region of ecT is essential for the interaction with ecH12 and for holding ecT in a compact form.13
Here, we have determined the crystal structure of mature form huT to gain insights into the reaction site, the catalytic mechanism, and the role of the NKH-causing residues at the molecular level. huT monomer consists of three domains arranged in a cloverleaf-like structure with the central cavity, which 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-CH3-H4folate), an analog of folate substrate, occupies with extensive hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts. The obtained structure allows us to describe not only the mechanistic details of the mode for transfer of C1 unit from the aminomethyl lipoate arm to H4folate, but also the coupling model of T and H-protein for the destabilization and release of the arm from the binding cleft of H-protein.

Furthermore, the structure of human enzyme as well as the mutation analysis provided detailed molecular bases for understanding the cause of NKH.

Results and Discussion
Overall and monomer structures
The crystal structure of mature huT was solved using single-wavelength anomalous diffraction data for a heavy-atom variant. The electron density map was of sufficient quality to allow tracing of most residues in the structure. The model was subsequently refined to 2.0 Å with an Rcryst of 16.0% and Rfree of 19.5% (Table 1). The final model contains two huT monomers related by a non-crystallographic 2-fold axis, 1176 water molecules, and 11 molecules of sulfate ion in an asymmetric unit. Several dimeric interactions are observed among the residues on the N-terminal loop, on α-helix D, and the flank on either side of β-strand 8 of the two monomers. However, since the interface is not very extensive, burying 637.1 Å2 (4.3%) of solvent-accessible surface per monomer, and since only the monomeric form is detected in the size exclusion experiment (data not shown), the dimer formation is probably a consequence of crystal contacts.

The N-terminal three residues (Ala1–Glu3) (mature huT numbering) and C-terminal Lys375 of each monomer are missing because of structural disorder.
The huT monomer consists of nine α-helices, 19 β-strands and three 310-helices, forming three domains (1, 2 and 3) arranged in a cloverleaf-like structure with the central cavity, where folates bind (Figure 1, Figure 2). Domain 1 (residues 4–56 and 147–239) is made up of two and five-stranded antiparallel β-sheets, five α-helices (αA, αB, αF, αE and αG) and a β-strand (β13). The domain seems to play a critical role in maintaining the entire molecular folding, because the single mutation of Leu6 of ecT (corresponding to Leu10 in huT) (Figure 2(a)) to alanine resulted in high susceptibility to trypsin, leading to the instant cleavage at Arg16 and the consequent rapid degradation of the resulting C-terminal fragment, in contrast to the high resistant nature of wild-type ecT.13 The hydrophobic interaction among Leu10, Val213 and Phe13 might contribute to the folding. Domain 2 (residues 57–146) consists of a five-stranded antiparallel β-sheet and two α-helices (αC and αD). This domain bears the putative catalytic center as described below.

The domain 3 (residues 240–374) consists of a loop-rich region and a distorted six-stranded jelly-roll that is oriented perpendicular to the β-sheets of domains 1 and 2, closing the ring-like structure of the protein.
The overall structure resembles those of recently reported bacterial T-proteins from Thermotoga maritima (tmT),14 E. coli and Pyrococcus horikoshii OT3 (phT).15 The superimpositions of Cα atoms of huT on those of tmT in the apo form (PDB accession code 1WOS) gave r.m.s. deviation of 1.1 Å (for 346 equivalent Cα positions). The r.m.s. deviations for ecT (325 equivalent Cα positions from 1VLO) and phT (equivalent Cα positions from 1V5V) were 1.3 Å. The overall structure of huT also resembles that of the C-terminal region of Arthrobacter globiformis dimethylglycine oxidase (DMGO)16 as discussed below.
Active center and catalytic mechanism of huT
To identify the active center of huT, a substrate, 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4 and a competitive inhibitor, 5-CH3-H4folate3 were used to prepare the ligand-bound crystals by the soaking method, but only the 5-CH3-H4folate-bound crystals were obtained. The clear Fo−Fc electron density for 5-CH3-H4folate was present in the central cavity of each huT monomer, effectively filling the space (Figure 1(b)).

Although a mixture of 6R and 6S diastereomers of 5-CH3-H4folate was employed in the soaking experiment, only the naturally occurring 6S form was found in the crystals. The ligand binding led to no significant change in the huT structure except for the changes in the χ1 torsion angles of Leu88 and Ile103 of one monomer. Extensive superimposition search indicated that two monomers in an asymmetric unit of the native form are different in the χ1 torsion angles of both Leu88 and Ile103. One monomer is the same as those of the ligand-bound form (Figure 1(b)), and no change occurs by the ligand binding. Leu88 and Ile103 of the other native monomer are rotated 109° in the χ1 torsion angles relative to those of the ligand-bound form, and the angles were converged to the ligand-bound form.
5-CH3-H4folate is bound in a kinked configuration. The pteridine ring is deeply buried in the hydrophobic pocket encircled by Met56, Leu102, Ile103 and Val115 with four hydrogen bonds to the side-chains of Glu204 and Arg233, and the main chain carbonyl of Val115 (Figure 1(b)).

A double hydrogen bond, formed between the side-chain of invariant Glu204 and both the 2-amino and 3-imino groups of the pteridine ring, is commonly observed among folate-dependent enzymes such as dimethylglycine oxidase16 and formiminotransferase-cyclodeaminase,17 although the glutamyl residue is occasionally replaced by an aspartyl residue.18 The hydrogen bond between the backbone oxygen of Val115 and the reduced N8 of the pteridine ring is probably responsible for the recognition of the reduced folates as substrate. The p-aminobenzoate moiety, which is oriented almost perpendicular to the pteridine plane, is stacked by the side-chains of Leu88, Tyr197 and Leu242. The glutamyl moiety of 5-CH3-H4folate points to the C-terminal surface. The α-carboxylate links to NH2 group of Arg292 via many water molecules (Figure 1(b)), although the electron densities for these water molecules are weak. The O2 atom of α-carboxylate hydrogen bonds to the side-chain OH group of Tyr371 (2.8 Å), while the γ-carboxylate resides within hydrogen bonding range (3.1 Å) of the backbone nitrogen atom of Leu88 (Figure 1(b)).

The model is substantially compatible with our previous prediction that Lys352 and Lys81 of ecT (corresponding to Lys363 and Gln85 of huT, respectively) reside in close proximity to α and γ-carboxylate, respectively, of the bound 5,10-CH2-H4folate glutamate moiety, which is based on a cross-linking experiment using a zero-length cross-linker, 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)carbodiimide.11
The transfer of C1 unit is considered to be initiated by the nucleophilic attack on the methylene carbon of the aminomethyl lipoate arm by the N5 or the N10 atom of the tetrahydrofolate bound to T-protein (Figure 3). The present 5-CH3-H4folate-bound huT crystal structure shows that the Oδ2 atom of strictly conserved Asp101 is to close the N10 atom of 5-CH3-H4folate (3.5 Å). Although the layout of the atoms is not conducive for hydrogen bonding between them in the structure, they will make a hydrogen bond if some conformational changes on the 5-CH3-H4folate occur.

On the other hand, the N5 atom of 5-CH3-H4folate is at a distance of 3.9 Å from the Oδ1 atom of Asn117, which is one of the NKH-related residues.8 Asp101 is also involved in the hydrogen bonding network composed of Asn117, Asp100, Ala118 and two water molecules, where Asn117 is the central residue (Figure 5(b)).
To address which atom is responsible for initiating the transfer reaction, we conducted mutation analyses of Asp101 and Asn117. Three mutants employed in our experiment lost the catalytic activity (Table 2), although these mutations did not affect the yields of the mutant proteins overexpressed in E. coli (data not shown). While the D101A mutation seriously disturbs the hydrogen bonding network centered on Asn117, the hydrogen bonding network might remain intact in the D101N mutant. These observations suggest that loss of the oxygen atom able to hydrogen bond to the N10 group leads to loss of the activity and that the transfer reaction would be initiated by the attack on the methylene carbon by the N10 group of the folate substrate.

Consistent with this interpretation, the side-chain Oδ2 atom of Asp96 of tmT (corresponding to Asp101 of huT) has been reported to make a hydrogen bond with the N10 group of bound H4folate.14 Furthermore, the C-terminal folate-binding region of DMGO, which is highly similar in primary sequence and catalyzes a reaction homologous to that catalyzed by T-protein, has the Asp552 residue hydrogen bonded to the N10 nitrogen group of folinic acid in the ligand-bound structure.16 Asp552 of DMGO, corresponding to Asp101 of huT in the sequence alignment, is proposed to activate the nucleophilic character of the N10 group to initiate the conversion of the iminium intermediate to sarcosine and 5,10-CH2-H4folate.16 Consequently, the C1 unit transfer reaction is likely to be accomplished by the process outlined in Figure 3, although it needs to be verified by further investigation. The interaction with H-protein may cause the formation of the hydrogen bond between the Oδ2 of Asp101and the N10 atom of the bound folate in huT.
Interaction with H-protein
T-protein forms a complex with H-protein in a 1:1 molar ratio.

A graphical coupling of the two proteins was made using pea H-protein (peH) bearing methylamine-loaded lipoate (PDB accession code 1HTP) as a binding partner of huT in the model complex. peH shows a high level of homology (44.6% identical and 67.2% conserved) with human H-protein. The most important prerequisite for the complex formation is the interaction between the lipoate bound to H-protein and the catalytic center of T-protein. It has been reported that the lipoate arms in methylamine-free oxidized or reduced forms are located at the surface of peH in a rather flexible conformation, and following the transfer of methylamine, the cofactor pivots around the lysine linkage and gets locked into the binding cleft of the H-protein.19 The methylamine group at the end of the arm is tightly fixed by ionic bonds to the side-chain carboxyl group of the Glu14, and by hydrogen bonds to the main chain carbonyl groups of Ser12 and Asp67 of peH. Hydrophobic contacts between the long extended chain of carbon atoms of the arm and the hydrophobic residues surrounding the arm also contribute to the fixation.

Accordingly, destabilization and release of the arm from the binding cleft are the critical events in the T-protein catalysis and it has been proposed that the β-sheet structure of peH on one side of the lipoyl lysine (β5 and β6 in Figure 4(a)) is collectively destabilized instead of a primary rupture of the methylamine group interaction.20The surface embedding the aminomethy lipoate harbors the protruding side-chain of Glu42 (Figure 4(a)). On the other hand, huT accommodates 5-CH3-H4folate with the N5 and N10 atoms protruding to the N-terminal side at approximately 13–14 Å in depth from the N-terminal surface (Figure 4(b), right). Therefore, the two proteins were put together with these surfaces facing each other, placing the β-sheet of peH (β5 and β6) into the cave under domain 3 of huT. The model predicts a good fitting of the aminomethyl lipoate arm to conserved residues such as Tyr197, Leu230, Arg233, Asp234, Leu244 and Tyr245 of huT. These residues correspond to those interacting with the free form of dihydrolipoic acid in the tmT structure,14 although the interaction may not be the same because the physiologically inactive 6S form of the cofactor21 is incorporated into the structure.

Moreover, our complex model may well explain the intramolecular cross-linking between Asp34 and Lys216 of ecT according to the ecH–ecT complex formation.12 Asp39 (Asp34 in ecT) on αB and Lys226 (Lys216 in ecT) on β13 of huT are both positioned at the edge of the domain 1 (Figure 4(a)). The Oδ1 atom of Asp39 is 7.8 Å apart from the NZ atom of Lys226 in the structure. The further approach of peH into the bosom of huT might constrain αB of huT to shift downward or β13 upward, thereby putting Asp39 close to Lys226.
In our complex model, Glu42 of peH is not in the close vicinity of Gly299 of huT. The two residues correspond to Asp43 in ecH and Lys288 in ecT (Figure 2(b)), respectively, that were cross-linked in the ecT–ecH complex.13 However, since the former residue is replaced by serine in animal H-proteins and the sequence around Gly299 is not well conserved among T proteins from various species (Figure 2(a)), the exact positioning of the two residues may not be prerequisite for the complex formation. In the T-H complex model of T.

maritima (Tm),14 H-protein bears a protruding lipoate, and the orientation of H-protein against T-protein is quite different from that of our model. Such a protruding structure of the cofactor has not been reported so far even for the methylamine-free form. Consequently, the Tm model seems less rational, since there is no consideration of the destabilization process of the aminomethyl lipoate arm from the binding cleft. Although the crystallographic studies of the complex of T-protein and H-protein with cofactors should give the final answer to the mode of the interaction, our present model can explain not only the structural but also the functional requirements for the catalytic reactions.
Hydrogen bonding networks and structural basis for NKH-causing mutations
Nine residues that on mutation lead to the onset of NKH, as well as a residue showing polymorphism, are mapped in Figure 5(a). Many of them are involved in hydrogen bonding networks surrounding the substrate binding cavity (Figure 5(b)). Asn117 is the central residue of the hydrogen bonding network located in the vicinity of N5/N10 groups of bound folate.

The network might participate in the positioning of Asp101 and Val115, the putative enhancer of initiation of the C1 unit transfer and the putative selector of reduced folate, respectively. The NKH-causing mutant, N117I, abolishes the activity (Table 2) probably due to the dysfunction of these residues.
Asp248 forms an extensive hydrogen bonding network with invariant Arg237, Leu244, Thr320 and Ser321, whereas Arg292 forms another hydrogen bonding network adjacent to the former with the backbone carbonyl of Gly258 and Gly241 directly or via an ordered water molecule (Figure 5(b)). Both hydrogen bonding networks contribute not only to supporting the folate-binding space but also to holding the positions and orientations of the αG helix and the following loop (residues 241–246) carrying putative participants in the catalysis. The side-chains of conserved Asp234, Leu244 and Tyr245 form one plane that is parallel with the N-terminal surface, and those of Tyr197 and Leu244 form another plane oriented perpendicular to the former. Either or both planes may function to carry the aminomethyl lipoate arm to the reaction site as discussed above. Based on the tmT structure, Lee et al.

predicted the human T-protein structure with the hydrogen bonding network formed between Arg237, Asp248, Arg292, Thr320 and Ser321.14 In our structure, Arg292 is involved in the separate hydrogen bonding network, so that the mutations in Asp248 and Arg292 differently affected the expression and the kinetics. D248H was hardly expressed in E. coli, and only a small amount of the protein was partially purified by affinity chromatography on a Ni2+ column. It gave a specific activity less than 1% of the wild-type (data not shown), suggesting serious alteration of the conformation, probably due to the interruption of the participating hydrogen bonding network. Mutants G241D and R292H were overexpressed in E. coli as soluble proteins comparable to the wild-type enzyme (not shown). The mutant enzymes affinity-purified to almost a single band in SDS-PAGE exhibited specific activities of 12.3% and 1.6%, respectively, of the wild-type (Table 2). These were subjected to detailed kinetic analysis. As shown in Table 3, R292H mutation led to marked increases in the Km for 5,10-CH2-H4folate and 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4 (tenfold and 184-fold, respectively), and resulted in a similar Km value for both substrates.

The reduced affinity may be due to the loss of the hydrogen bonding interaction between Arg292 and α-carboxylate or due to the collapse of the glutamyl binding space induced by the disruption of the hydrogen bonds between Arg292 and Asp241. The binding of the α-carboxyl group of the first glutamate residue of the folate polyglutamate may largely contribute to the affinity. In this connection, it should be pointed out that K352E mutation of ecT affects the Km values for 5,10-CH2-H4folate and 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4 less than K81E or K78E mutations.11 Lys352 of ecT is equivalent to Tyr371 of huT whose OH atom also hydrogen bonds to the O2 atom of 5-CH3-H4folat (Figure 1(b)). G241D mutation resulted in four and ninefold increase in the Km value for 5,10-CH2-H4folate and 5,10-CH2-H4PteGlu4, respectively, suggesting that the side-chain of Gly241 contributes less than Arg292 to the hydrogen bond.
Among other NKH-related residues, His14 and Gly19 are located at the N-terminal side surface of domain 1. We expressed mutants H14R and G19R in E. coli with a His6-tag at the C terminus and they were partially purified by affinity chromatography on a Ni2+ column. Both mutants were poorly expressed as soluble proteins even under co-expression with E.

coli chaperones GroEL and GroES (not shown). However, affinity-purified H14R and G19R gave 18% and 61%, respectively, of specific activity relative to the wild-type, suggesting that these residues mainly contribute to the entire folding of huT. The role of both residues could be understood in the context of the N-terminal hasp function.13 The improperly folded mutants may be degraded rapidly in E. coli and in NKH patients.
Glu183 and Val184 are located at the turning point from β10 to β11, which are far from the active center. The E183K mutation was found as a polymorphism that is present in 2/100 normal control alleles, but the co-occurrence with R292H was detected in some NKH patients10 with proposal of a “helper” mutation to produce a more compromised protein function than that of R292H alone.8 The V184A mutation was found in a later onset patient having the heterozygous Y197C mutation. Glu183 hydrogen bonds directly and indirectly to Gly166, Gly186 and Ser188, while Val184 resides in the hydrophobic cluster formed by Leu163, Leu171, Leu174, Met182 and Val192, which contributes to the stacking of these regions. However, the single E183K or V184A mutation might not affect the structure and the activity so greatly.

The OH atom of Tyr197 hydrogen bonds to the carbonyl oxygen of Cys243, and plays a critical role in connecting the two highly conserved regions (residues 196–204 and 229–246). Therefore, a patient with the homozygous Y197C mutation might be severely affected.
Comparison with DMGO
DMGO monomer comprises two functional regions, the N-terminal FAD-binding region (residues 1–420) responsible for the oxidation of dimethylglycine, and the C-terminal folate-binding region (residues 421–830) responsible for the formation of 5,10-CH2-H4folate. The primary sequence alignment of huT with the C-terminal folate-binding region of DMGO using CLUSTALW22 gave 22% identity and 42% similarity. The superimposition of Cα atoms of huT (residues 4–374) on those of the C-terminal folate-binding region of folinic acid-bound DMGO (residues 426–830) using LSQMAN23 indicated strong structural similarity (Figure 6(a)) with an r.m.s. deviation of 1.5 Å. Furthermore, the superimposition of the functional residues surrounding the reaction sites demonstrated that all residues involved in binding with the pterin moiety of the respective ligand are conserved in both proteins (Figure 6(b)), except for the corresponding residue to Arg233 that hydrogen bonds to the 4-carbonyl oxygen of 5-CH3-H4folate in huT. The residues involved in the interaction with the glutamate tail cannot be identified in DMGO.

The enzyme has a large internal cavity connecting the reaction sites of the N and C-terminal regions, where channeling of the iminium intermediate from the N-terminal reaction site to the C-terminal reaction site is carried out in an intrinsic “unguided” manner.16 The nature of the cavity opening to the outside solution only via the folate-binding funnel ensures sequestration of the reactive iminium intermediate prior to reaction with H4folate to avoid formation of toxic formaldehyde. A similar cavity sequestered from the bulk solvent is likely to be formed by the interaction of H and T-protein. However, in T-protein the aminomethyl head of the lipoate arm should be delivered to the N5/N10 atom positions of H4folate in the narrow tunnel via the ionic and hydrophobic interaction with the residues on the tunnel surface.

Conclusion
We have previously determined the structure and chromosomal localization of the huT gene,24 and identified three missense mutations leading to the onset of NKH.5 The present crystal structure of huT with 5-CH3-H4folate, together with the mutational studies, provides a detailed picture to understand the molecular basis of the disease-causing mutations as well as T-protein catalysis.

Most of the disease-related residues cluster around the folate binding cavity forming the extensive hydrogen bonding networks. These networks are essential not only for supporting the folate-binding space but also for holding the positions and orientations of the secondary structural elements surrounding the folate-binding cavity that carry putative participants in the catalysis. Furthermore, the catalytic residues that directly participate in the C1 unit transfer were verified by the mutation analysis. The model of the H and T-protein complex, which is very different from the proposed Tm model, provides a reasonable picture of the catalytic process. First, the aminomethyl lipoate arm will be liberated from the binding cleft in the H-protein surface, and then recruited to the catalytic center without releasing the toxic formaldehyde during the catalysis. The hydrogen bonding networks surrounding the folate-binding cavity play important roles in almost every aspect of the process.
Materials and Methods
Cloning, expression and purification of human T-protein
To construct a full-length coding sequence of huT, an EcoRI-BglII fragment of HT15 insert and a BglII-HindIII fragment of HT24 insert25 were ligated into pTZ19U and resulted in pTZ/HT.

For expression of mature form huT lacking the mitochondrial target sequence, an NdeI site was introduced adjacent to the codon for Ala29 residue of the precursor huT cDNA in pTZ/HT by the method described by Kunkel et al.26 using a Bio-Rad kit and the sense oligonucleotide 5′-GTCGTCCACTTCATATGGCACAGGACGT-3′ (the NdeI site is underlined). Creation of a BamHI site placed downstream of the stop codon and deletion of the NdeI site originally present in the coding region without altering the amino acid, were simultaneously carried out with nucleotides 5′-AGTGAAGATGGATCCGGGTGGGGCT-3′ (the BamHI site is underlined) and 5′-GACGTCTCTCACATGCTGCAGAC-3′ (the modified base is shown in boldface), respectively. An NdeI-BamHI fragment of the resulting plasmid was ligated to pET3a. The nucleotide sequence of the construct, pET3/HT, was verified by DNA sequencing.
E. coli BL21(DE3)pLysS cells transformed with pET3/HT were grown in 500 ml of LB medium containing 20 μg/ml of ampicillin and 25 μg/ml of chloramphenicol at 30 °C for 24 hours. Expression was induced by 25 μM isopropyl-d-thiogalactopyranoside added at the start of the incubation.

Cell-free extracts were prepared as described,27 with buffer A (50 mM Tricine-NaOH (pH 8.0), 2 mM EDTA, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 10% (v/v) glycerol, 20 μM p-amidinophenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride) and subjected to SP-Sepharose FF column chromatography (Amersham Bioscience). Bound proteins were eluted with a linear gradient of NaCl (0–0.4 M) in buffer A using the P.S.L.C. system (Amersham Bioscience). The peak fractions were pooled, dialyzed, and subjected to hydroxyapatite column chromatography as described. huT obtained from this step gave a single band in SDS-PAGE (not shown). The final preparation was stored on ice in 20 mM sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), 5 mM dithiothreitol, 10% glycerol and concentrated to appropriate concentrations with Microcon-30 before use.
Crystallization and data collection
The huT in free form was crystallized at 25 °C by the hanging-drop, vapor-diffusion method by mixing equal volumes of the protein at 10 mg/ml and a reservoir solution consisting of 2.2 M ammonium sulfate, 0.1 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), and 0.2 M potassium sodium tartrate. Many small crystals in the shape of a thin needle cluster appeared in several days.

Microseeding with the crystals of the droplet consisting of equal volumes of the protein solution (8 mg/ml) and a reservoir solution (1.9 M ammonium sulfate, 0.1 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), 0.2 M potassium sodium tartrate) facilitated growth of the needle crystals to the size of 0.02 mm×0.03 mm×0.72 mm. For cryo-crystallography, the crystals were pre-soaked in the stabilization solution (0.1 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), 2.3 M ammonium sulfate, 0.2 M potassium sodium tartrate, 20% glycerol), mounted in nylon loops and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. The data were collected to 2.0 Å resolution at 100 K using synchrotron radiation and an imaging plate detector, DIP6040 (MAC Science/Bruker AXS) on BL44XU at SPring-8 (Hyogo, Japan), and processed using Denzo and Scalepack programs.28 The crystal belongs to the orthorhombic space group P212121 with unit cell parameters of a=54.2 Å, b=128.5 Å, and c=136.2 Å, and has a solvent content of 57.6%.
huT crystals bound to 5-CH3-H4folat were prepared by soaking the native crystals in 2.1 M ammonium sulfate, 0.1 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.6), 0.2 M potassium sodium tartrate, 20% glycerol, containing 2 mM 5-CH3-H4folat for 24 hours. The data were collected to 2.6 Å resolution as above.

Platinum derivative crystals were prepared by soaking the native crystals in the stabilization solution supplemented with 1 mM K2PtCl4 for six hours, followed by a one hour back-soak in the stabilization solution before being flash-frozen and subjected to data collection to 2.7 Å resolution as above.
Structure solution and refinement
The structure was solved using the single-wavelength anomalous dispersion phasing method with platinum derivative data. The initial platinum atom positions were determined from the Bijvoet anomalous difference Patterson map using the program RSPS29 and refined by the program MLPHARE.30 Heavy atom parameter refinement and phase calculation were carried out using the program SHARP,31 and the electron density map was obtained after phase improvement by the program SOLOMON.32 The atomic model was built using the graphics program O.33 The initial map was sufficiently clear, allowing the initial model composed of residues 4–374 of each monomer in the asymmetric unit. Refinement of the model against the 2.0 Å native data set including successive rounds of simulated annealing refinement, individual B-factor refinement, and model rebuilding was carried out with CNS34 resulting in a final Rcryst of 16.0% and Rfree of 19.4%.

The native model solved to 2.0 Å resolution was used as a search model to solve the 5-CH3-H4folate-bound huT structure with CNS. Each cycle of refinement was followed by manual fitting with the program O resulting in a final Rcryst of 17.1% and Rfree of 24.5%. The electron density of the ligand was clearly shown in the center of each monomer. Ramachandran analysis using PROCHECK35 indicated 90.7% (native) and 88.6% (ligand-bound) of non-glycine residues were in the most favored regions, and all others were in the additionally allowed regions. The refinement parameters are presented in Table 1.
Secondary structure assignments were carried out using the program DSSP,36 and structure diagrams were drawn with MOLSCRIPT,37 POVScript,38 GRASP,39 MSMS†, and Raster3D.40 The dimer interface area was calculated with Surface Racer.41 Sequence alignment was carried out using CLUSTALW,22 and superimpositions were conducted using LSQMAN.23
Expression and kinetic analysis of mutant huTs
Mutations for G241D and R292H were carried out with the sense oligonucleotides 5′-CTGGAGGCAGACCTCTGCCTG-3′ and 5′-CAGCGGAGGCATGTGGGGTTGAT-3′ (modified bases are shown in boldface letters), respectively, and subcloned into pET3a as described above.

The resulting plasmids pET3/HTG241D and pET3/HTR292H as well as pET3/HT were subjected to PCR with 5′-primer, 5′-TAATACGACTCACTATAGGG-3′ (T7 promoter primer), and 3′-primer, 5′-CCAGCTAAGCTTGAGGGTATAGTAGTTTG-3′ (the HindIII site is underlined), and the NdeI-HindIII fragments were ligated into pET23b to create the expression plasmids for huTs His-tagged at the C terminus (pET23/HT, pET23/HTG241D and pET23/HTR292H). For expression of D101A with the C-terminal His6-tag, cDNA fragments with mutations in the unique SfaNI site were generated by PCR using pET23/HT as template. The N-terminal fragment for D101A was amplified with T7 promoter primer as the 5′-primer and the 3′-primer, 5′-AATCAAGGCATCTAAGATGCCTCCAGC-3′ (modified bases are shown in boldface letters and the SfaNI site is underlined). The C-terminal fragment was amplified with 5′-primer, 5′-GGAGGCATCTTAGATGCCTTGATTGTAACCAATACTTCTG-3′ (modified base is shown in boldface and the SfaNI site is underlined) and 3′-primer, 5′-CCAGCTAAGCTTGAGGGTATAGTAGTTTG-3′ (the HindIII site is underlined). The N-terminal NdeI-SfaNI fragment and the C-terminal SfaNI-HindIII fragment were ligated into pET23b. The expression plasmids for D101N and N117I were constructed by the in-fusion cloning method using pET23/HT as a template and the In-Fusion™ PCR Cloning Kit (BD Bioscience) according to the manufacturer's protocol.

Mutations were introduced with the following primers; the 5′-primer, 5′-GATAACTTGATTGTAACCAATACTTCTGAGGGCCACCTG-3′ and the 3′-primer, 5′-TACAATCAACTTATCTAAGATGCCTCCAGCTTCGTTGG-3′ (modified bases are shown in boldface) for D101N, and the 5′-primer, GTGTCCATCGCTGGCTGCTGGGAGAAAGATTTGGCC-3′ and 3′-primer, 5′-GCCAGCGATGGACACCACATACAGGTGGCCCTCAG-3′ (modified bases are shown in boldface) for N117I. All constructs were verified by DNA sequencing.
E. coli BL21(DE3)pGroELES cells, which harbor E. coli chaperone genes, were transformed with the constructed expression plasmids and grown in 200 ml of LB medium containing 20 μg/ml of ampicillin and 10 μg/ml of tetracyclin at 22 °C for 48 hours. Expression was induced by 25 μM isopropyl-d-thiogalactopyranoside added at the start of the incubation. Cell-free extracts were prepared as above with buffer B (20 mM potassium phosphate (pH 7.4), 0.3 M NaCl, 0.2 mM dithiothreitol, 10% glycerol, 20 μM p-amidinophenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride) containing 20 mM imidazole, and subjected to affinity chromatography in a Ni2+ column (4 ml, Qiagen). The column was washed with buffer B containing 50 mM imidazole and eluted with buffer B containing 200 mM imidazole.

huTs were dialyzed against 20 mM potassium phosphate (pH 7.4), 1 mM dithiothreitol, 10% glycerol, 20 μM p-amidinophenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride, concentrated if necessary, and stored at −80 °C.
Assay of T-protein activity and kinetic analysis were conducted as described,13 except for employment of appropriate concentrations of the enzymes and substrates.
Protein Data Bank accession codes
The atomic coordinates and structure factors have been deposited in the RCSB Protein Data Bank with codes 1WSR (native huT) and 1WSV (5-CH3-H4folate-bound huT).
