Human GLYAT showed 39.0% and 40.5% identity to hGLYATL1 and GLYATL2, respectively. Moreover, hGLYATL1 showed 49.0% identity to hGLYATL2. Human GLYAT most closely resembled rat HP33 and bovine glycine acyltransferases (bGLYATs) (Fig. S1).
3.2. Enzyme activity of hGLYAT and hGLYATL1 proteins
Next, the enzyme activities of three affinity-purified recombinant proteins were examined using amino acids (glycine and glutamine) and acyl-CoAs (benzoyl- and phenylacetyl-CoA) as substrates (Table 1). hGLYAT showed the highest activity to benzoyl-CoA as an acyl donor and glycine as acyl acceptor. Moreover, in the case of glutamine as an acceptor, hGLYAT showed favorable catalysis of benzoyl-CoA over phenylacetyl-CoA. These results suggested that hGLYAT is a typical aralkyl transferase.

hGLYATL1 most effectively catalyzed phenylacetyl-CoA and glutamine, indicating that hGLYATL1 is a human arylacetyl transferase [5]. This is the first report to identify a human glutamine N-acyltransferase gene, and this finding is consistent with the coexistence of glycine and glutamine N-acyltransferase activity in the mitochondrial fractions from human and monkey liver [5]. Moreover, these results suggested that glutamine N-acyltransferase evolved from glycine N-acyltransferase by gene duplication and gained glutamine binding affinity through the process of evolution from mammals to primates. GLYATL2 did not show significant enzymatic activity under the conditions used in this study. GLYATL2 also did not show activity with taurine as an acyl acceptor (data not shown). These results were in good agreement with those of Waluk et al. [12] indicating that GLYATL2 mainly catalyzes conjugation with long chain fatty acid-CoA and glycine. The results of multiple alignment analysis (Fig. S1) showed that bGLYAT (glycine acceptor) was more similar to hGLYAT (aralkyl transferase; glycine acceptor) in the 128–178 region than the corresponding region of bGLYATL1 (arylacetyl transferase; glutamine acceptor) at 128–180.

Moreover, bGLYAT (arylacetyl transferase) was irreversibly inhibited by sulfhydryl reagent, while aralkyl bGLYAT was not [4], and the corresponding amino acid residue associated with the enzyme activity to sulfhydryl modification was cysteine at position 130 of arylacetyl bGLYAT. These results suggested that the active center of hGLYAT is localized within aa 128–178, which was important for glycine binding and acyl residue transfer. Moreover, if aa 128–178 of hGLYAT was responsible for glycine binding, the region consisting of aa 128–180 of hGLYATL1 was suggested to be the glutamine binding region.
Based on the sequence identity to hepatocellular carcinoma-related HP33 and enzyme activity for glycine conjugation, we were interested in hGLYAT with regard to its relation with human liver disease.
From the results shown in Table 1, we characterized GLYAT activity with benzoyl-CoA and glycine (Fig. S2). Lineweaver–Burk plot analyses suggested that the Km values for benzoyl-CoA and glycine of hGLYAT were 209 and 26.6 mM, respectively, and the Vm value was 807 nmol/min/mg hGLYAT. The Km for benzoyl-CoA was very smaller to that of hGLYAT purified from the liver (57.9 mM) [16], and Vm was about 1/20th that of hGLYAT from the liver (17.1 μmol/min/mg protein) [16].

The observed Vm was larger than that of bovine liver GLYAT and smaller than that of human liver GLYAT. These differences may be caused by differences in proteins used (recombinant hGLYAT with peptide tag and hGLYAT purified from liver). This enzyme assay indicated that hGLYAT catalyses a sequential bi-bi reaction and not a ping-pong bi-bi reaction.
3.3. Tissue-specific expression of hGLYAT
We performed qRT-PCR analyses to characterize the tissue specificity of hGLYAT gene expression. This tissue specificity was not the same as those of hGLYATL1 and hGLYATL2 [11], [12], and was the same as that reported previously for rat HP33 [14]. Human GLYAT was shown to be expressed predominantly in the liver and kidney (Fig. 1A). Northern blotting analysis indicated that human GLYAT mRNA was about 1.2 kb in length (Fig. S3), which was identical to the length of the cDNA.
3.4. Human GLYAT is localized to mitochondria
GLYAT was shown to function as a glycine acyltransferase in the mitochondria of liver and kidney cells using biochemically purified protein prepared from the tissues.

However, there was no direct evidence for the cellular localization of hGLYAT, and we prepared a specific anti-hGLYAT antibody to analyze the cellular localization of hGLYAT protein (Fig. 1B and C). Anti-hGLYAT antiserum was affinity-purified with recombinant hGLYAT protein after preabsorption with hGLYATL1 and hGLYATL2 proteins (Fig. 1B). Before purification, anti-hGLYAT antiserum showed severe cross-reactivity for hGLYATL1 and hGLYATL2 proteins (Fig. 1B Antiserum). However, after preabsorption and affinity purification, anti-hGLYAT antibody reacted solely with hGLYAT protein (Fig. 1B purified).
The cellular localization of hGLYAT was analyzed in HeLa cells (Fig. 1C). These cells did not show detectable endogenous hGLYAT protein expression on Western blotting analysis (data not shown). Therefore, we performed transient expression of hGLYAT in HeLa cells, followed by immunostaining (Fig. 1C). In the transfected cells, hGLYAT localization was restricted to fibrous structures in the cytosol that were coincident with the mitochondrial space stained with MitoTracker. Moreover, we examined hGLYAT localization by biochemical fractionation (Fig. 1D). Human GLYAT was clearly concentrated in the mitochondrial fraction (Fig. 1D, Mn-SOD) and not in the cytosol (Fig. 1D, β-Actin). These observations were consistent with previous results of the biochemical fractionation of human GLYAT from the liver [5].
3.5.

GLYAT expression was reduced in hepatocellular carcinoma
Previous studies indicated that GLYAT was involved in the metabolic processing of xenobiotics in the liver, and rat HP33, which showed the highest degree of identity to hGLYAT, was induced in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) caused by metabolic intermediates of carcinogens. The results suggested that hGLYAT may be related to human HCC or other liver diseases. Therefore, we investigated hGLYAT expression and localization in specimens from various human diseases, such as HCC and hepatitis of various origins (Fig. 2 and Table 2). Typical hGLYAT expression in HCC tissues indicated that hGLYAT protein was expressed in noncancerous hepatocytes and disappeared in cancerous HCC cells (Fig. 2A upper panel). In noncancerous cells of HCC specimen, hGLYAT was localized in granular structures consistent with the mitochondrial space in the cytosol (Fig. 2A lower left). This observation corresponded to the localization in HeLa cells (Fig. 1C), and hGATF localization was observed in mitochondria in both liver cells and cultured cells. hGLYAT expression was not detected in cancerous cells from the same specimen (Fig. 2A lower right). Moreover, we used 103 specimens of a variety of liver diseases for analyses of hGLYAT expression and localization.

Unexpectedly based on the rat HP33 results, hGLYAT protein was not detected or was detected only weakly in 78% and 22% of 41 HCC specimens, respectively (Table 2). Six samples of colon cancer metastasis (metastatic adenocarcinoma, MAC) to the liver (Fig. 2B) and six samples of cholangiocellular carcinoma (CCC) (Fig. 2C) as control tumors were completely negative for hGLYAT expression (Table 2). The results shown in Fig. 2A–C indicate marked differences in staining at the border between cancerous and noncancerous regions. Cancerous cells showing weak hGLYAT expression were very rare (Fig. S4), and noncancerous cells showed higher levels of hGLYAT expression than cancerous cells in all specimens examined (Table 2). These results indicated that hGLYAT expression was downregulated in all cases of HCC and other liver cancers. To investigate the cause of hGLYAT downregulation in cancerous cells, we performed qRT-PCR to determine hGLYAT expression in noncancerous and cancerous liver cells (Fig. 2D). All cancerous samples examined (HCC, MAC, and CCC) showed marked repression of hGLYAT expression, while all noncancerous samples showed similar and significant hGLYAT expression. Transcriptome analysis of HCC caused by hepatitis B virus infection indicated that hGLYAT expression was depressed in HCC [17].

These results suggested that repression of hGLYAT expression was mainly regulated at the transcriptional level. Moreover, we found no significant relationship between GLYAT expression and the degree of HCC differentiation. Interestingly, GLYAT expression was positive in all of 60 samples from chronic hepatitis patients with various etiologies, such as hepatitis A, B, and C virus infections, alcohol abuse, and autoimmune hepatitis (Table 2). These observations showed that GLYAT was constantly expressed in the noncancerous hepatocytes regardless of their status as normal or hepatitis cells with various origins. GLYAT may be expressed in differentiated hepatocytes and repressed in dedifferentiated cells, such as cancerous cells in the liver. These results strongly suggested that hGLYAT is a good candidate as a novel HCC marker. We propose that hGLYAT may be a key molecule in the transition between differentiation and carcinogenesis of liver cells.

Database linking and accession numbers
Human Glycine N-acyltransferase (GLYAT): GenBank ID: AB665285.
Human GLYATL1: GenBank ID: AB207212 registered as human GATF-C mRNA.
Human GLYATL2: GenBank ID: AB207211 registered as human GATF-B mRNA.

Mammalian Prenylcysteine Carboxyl Methyltransferase Is in the Endoplasmic Reticulum*

Prenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase (pcCMT) is the third of three enzymes that posttranslationally modify C-terminal CAAX motifs and thereby target CAAX proteins to the plasma membrane. Here we report the molecular characterization and subcellular localization of the first mammalian (human myeloid) pcCMT. The deduced amino acid sequence of mammalian pcCMT predicts a multiple membrane-spanning protein with homologies to the yeast pcCMT, STE14 , and the mammalian band 3 anion transporter. The human gene complemented a ste14 mutant. pcCMT mRNAs were ubiquitously expressed in human tissues. An anti-pcCMT antiserum detected a 33-kDa protein in myeloid cell membranes. Ectopically expressed recombinant pcCMT had enzymatic activity identical to that observed in neutrophil membranes. Mammalian pcCMT was not expressed at the plasma membrane but rather restricted to the endoplasmic reticulum. Thus, the final enzyme in the sequence that modifies CAAX motifs is located in membranes topologically removed from the CAAX protein target membrane.

A number of signaling molecules, including Ras and G proteins, are targeted to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane by a sequence of posttranslational modifications of a C-terminal CAAX 1 motif that include prenylation, proteolysis, and carboxyl methylation (1). In some cases palmitoylation of an upstream cysteine is also required (2). These modifications render otherwise hydrophilic proteins hydrophobic, promoting association with membranes. The relative contributions of prenylation, proteolysis, and carboxyl methylation to membrane targeting are not well understood. Whereas neutralization of the negative charge on the α-carboxyl group by methyl esterification adds to overall hydrophobicity, particularly for farnesylated proteins, this modification contributes little to the affinity of geranylgeranylated proteins for membranes (3). Although processed CAAX proteins can associate with phospholipid vesicles in vitro (4), it is not known whether membrane proteins participate in prenylcysteine membrane association in vivo . The Saccharomyces cerevisiae mating pheromone, a-factor, is a CAAX -processed polypeptide, and both its secretion via the Ste6p transporter (5) and its engagement of the Ste3p G protein-linked receptor (6) are dependent on prenylcysteine carboxyl methylation, suggesting a role for this modification in protein-protein interactions. A cycle of prenylcysteine carboxyl methylation is associated with neutrophil activation (7), and inhibitors of this enzyme block signal transduction in neutrophils (7), macrophages (8), and platelets (9), suggesting that, like bacterial chemotaxis (10), some eukaryotic processes may be regulated by reversible carboxyl methylation.
Because prenylcysteine carboxyl methylation cannot be abolished by mutation of the substrate without also eliminating prenylation, elucidation of the role of carboxyl methylation will require characterization and disruption of the methyltransferase. Until recently, the only prenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase (pcCMT) characterized at the molecular level was the STE14 gene product of S. cerevisiae (5). Homologs inSchizosaccharomyces pombe and Xenopus laevis have now been reported (11). Here we report the molecular cloning and preliminary characterization of the first mammalian pcCMT. In addition, using pcCMT tagged with green fluorescent protein (GFP) we show that pcCMT is expressed in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) but excluded from the plasma membrane that is the target of many CAAX proteins, including Ras.
EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES
Molecular Cloning
A text-based search of the expressed sequence tag (EST) data base of the National Center for Biotechnology Information identified a 426-bp partial cDNA from murine placenta (mh77d06.r1) that has amino acid homology to the STE14 gene product of S. cerevisiae . Primers based on this sequence (forward: 5′-GCCGGACTCAACGCGCTGCTGCTGCTACTCTA-3′; reverse: 5′-CGTGTACTCCAGGCTGTGATTCAGGAGGAA-3′) were used to amplify by reverse transcriptase-PCR a 218-bp homologous cDNA fragment from HL60 cells. This fragment was then 32P-labeled and used to screen a unidirectional, size-fractionated HL60 cDNA library constructed in the λZAP system (provided by Dr. Philip Murphy, NIAID). Hybridizations were performed at 56 °C overnight. Of ∼105 recombinant plaques screened, a single doubly positive clone was identified and proved positive on secondary screen. This clone contained a 3.6-kb cDNA insert that was sequenced in both directions.
Northern Blotting
Total RNA (40 μg) from HL60 cells grown with or without 1.25% Me2SO for 5 days was fractionated on a 1.2% denaturing formaldehyde-agarose gel, transferred to a nylon filter, and hybridized with [32P]dATP-labeled full-length HL60 pcCMT cDNA in Express Hybridization solution (CLONTECH, Palo Alto, CA) at 68 °C. A human multiple-tissue Northern blot (CLONTECH) was hybridized with the same probe according to the manufacturer's instructions. The same filters were stripped and rehybridized with a β-actin probe.
Antiserum
A peptide corresponding to deduced amino acids 185–201 of HL60 pcCMT (FNHVVQNEKSDTHTLV) was synthesized, linked to keyhole limpet hemocyanin, and used to immunize rabbits. The resulting antiserum was used for immunoblotting of neutrophil light membranes prepared by nitrogen cavitation and discontinuous sucrose density sedimentation (12), for immunoprecipitation of lysates of HL60 cells metabolically labeled with l-[35S]methionine, and for indirect immunofluorescence of COS-1 cells.
Expression of Recombinant pcCMT
The 3.6-kb full-length HL60 pcCMT cDNA and an 852-bp cDNA fragment comprising the ORF were subcloned into the eukaryotic expression vectors pcDM8 and pcDNA3.1 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA). Myc-tagged pcCMT was made by adding a sequence encoding the 10-amino acid epitope of c-Myc recognized by monoclonal antibody 9E10 to the C terminus of pcCMT using patch PCR and subcloning into pcDNA3.1. pcCMT tagged at the C terminus with GFP was generated by subcloning the pcCMT ORF into the expression vector pGFP-N3 (CLONTECH). For pcCMT enzymatic assays, COS-1 cells were grown in 10-cm dishes and transfected with pcCMT with DEAE-dextran as described (13). For fluorescence microscopy, exponentially growing COS-1, CHO, and NIH3T3 cells were plated the day prior to transfection at 50–60% confluence and transfected with 2 μg of DNA using LipofectAMINE (Life Technologies, Inc.) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Cells were observed at 24 and 48 h after transfection.
Prenylcysteine Carboxyl Methyltransferase Assays
COS-1 cells transfected with HL60 pcCMT or vector alone were harvested at 48 h with 5 mm EDTA and subjected, in parallel with human neutrophils, to nitrogen cavitation and discontinuous sucrose density centrifugation as described (12). Light membranes were assayed for pcCMT activity qualitatively byS -adenosyl-l-[methyl- 3H]methionine labeling (SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and fluorography) of Rho GTPases partially purified from neutrophil cytosol and quantitatively by carboxyl methylation ofN -acetyl-S -trans,trans -farnesyl-l-cysteine (AFC) (heptane partition, alkaline hydrolysis, and measurement of vapor phase [3H]methanol) as described (14).
S. cerevisiae Strains, Growth, and ste14 Complementation
Complete (YEPD), synthetic (SD), and synthetic dropout media were prepared as described previously (15), except that dropout medium lacked cysteine. All experiments were performed at 30 °C. Yeast transformations were carried out by either the lithium acetate method (16) or the Elble method (17). The ste14 deletion strains used in this study are SM1188 (MATaΔste14–3::TRP1 trp1 leu2 ura3 his4 can1 ) and SM1639 (MATaΔste14–4::URA3 trp1 leu2 his4 can1 ) (5). Plasmid expression of Ste14p was accomplished by pSM1237 (CEN URA3 STE14 ). Human pcCMT was expressed in yeast by subcloning the HL60 pcCMT ORF into theBam HI/Sal I sites of the yeast expression plasmid pG1 (2μ TRP1 ) that utilizes a GPD promotor and a PGK transcription terminator and polyadenylation signal (18). The resulting construct was designated pG1-hCMT (2μ TRP1 hCMT ). Patch mating tests were carried out essentially as described previously (15). Briefly, patches of MATa cells grown on selective media were replica plated onto a lawn of theMATα mating tester, SM1068 (lys1 ), that had been spread on an SD plate. Plates were incubated at 30 °C for 3 days. Growth of the prototrophic diploids indicated mating.
Fluorescence Microscopy
Live cells that had been transfected with pcCMT-GFP and fixed/permeabilized (2% paraformaldeyde/0.2% Triton X-100 at 4 °C or methanol at −20 °C) cells stained with 9E10 anti-Myc antibody (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA), C6 anti-ribophorin I antiserum (provided by Dr. Gert Kriebich, NYU), or the anti-pcCMT antiserum described above, followed by Texas Red-conjugated secondary antisera, were imaged with a Zeiss Axioscope equipped with a Princeton Instruments cooled CCD camera and a KAF 1400 chip or a Molecular Dynamics confocal microscope equipped with an argon laser.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Repeated efforts to characterize mammalian pcCMT bySTE14 homology cloning and by enzyme purification and microsequencing were unsuccessful. However, we identified a partial murine cDNA (GenBank accession no. AA022288) in the EST data base of the National Center for Biotechnology Information that has sequence homology to Ste14p. Using primers based on this sequence, reverse transcription-PCR was employed to amplify from human myeloid HL60 cells a 218-bp homologous sequence. Using this fragment an HL60 cDNA library was screened and a single clone identified that contained a 3.6-kb insert. Sequencing revealed a 3595-bp cDNA (GenBank accession no. AF064084) with an ORF that predicted a 284-amino acid protein that is 26% identical to Ste14p (Fig.1). Hydropathy analysis revealed six hydrophobic sequences that may represent membrane-spanning domains (Fig. 1). This is consistent with the five or six putative membrane-spanning domains of Ste14p (5), with recent data demonstrating that Ste14p is an integral membrane protein2 and with our observation that active pcCMT cannot be extracted from membranes with detergents but can be partially reconstituted in phospholipid vesicles (19). The first 65 amino acids of human pcCMT, containing the first two hydrophobic sequences, are 36% identical to amino acids 750–821 of the human band 3 anion transporter, which represent the 11th and 12th of 14 well characterized membrane-spanning domains, further supporting the hypothesis that human pcCMT is a multiple membrane-spanning protein. Comparison of human pcCMT with all related sequences in the GenBank (Fig. 1) revealed the highest degree of divergence in the N-terminal third of the molecule, suggesting that the catalytic domain is C-terminal. Sequences homologous to theS -adenosylmethionine binding regions described in aspartyl and glutamyl protein carboxyl methyltransferases (20) were not apparent, arguing against an evolutionary link.

To determine whether the HL60 Ste14p homolog has prenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase activity, the cDNA was subcloned into a mammalian expression vector and transiently overexpressed in COS-1 cells. Membranes prepared from these cells were used as a source of recombinant enzyme. Farnesylated Ras GTPases require detergent for extraction from membranes. Therefore geranylgeranylated neutrophil cytosolic Rho GTPases that remain soluble by virtue of association with an accessory protein, guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitor (GDI), were utilized as endogenous substrates in an in vitro assay (Fig. 2). Untransfected COS-1 cell membranes had little pcCMT activity toward Rho proteins compared with that of membranes derived from human neutrophils (Fig. 2 a ). Transfection with the HL60 cDNA conferred pcCMT activity toward Rho GTPases on COS-1 membranes, and this activity was blocked by the competitive pcCMT inhibitor, AFC, with an ED50 (10 μm) identical to that for endogenous neutrophil pcCMT. Carboxyl methylation of Rac2 and RhoA by HL60 pcCMT-transfected COS-1 cell membranes was enhanced by GTPγS (Fig. 2 b ), similar to the activity observed in neutrophil membranes (7). Carboxyl methyltransferase activity was quantitated in membranes of COS-1 cells transfected with HL60 pcCMT using prenylcysteine analogs as defined substrates (14). Untransfected COS-1 cell membranes had 23 ± 10% (n = 5) of the pcCMT specific activity of neutrophil membranes toward AFC. Transfection of COS-1 cells with HL60 pcCMT resulted in an 18–53-fold increase in specific AFC carboxyl methyltransferase activity (3.0 ± 0.8 to 74.5 ± 6.8 pmol/mg·min, n = 5, p < 0.0005). Carboxyl methylation ofN -acetyl-S-all-trans -geranylgeranyl-l-cysteine (AGGC) was increased in parallel with methylation of AFC (18-versus 20-fold increase, n = 2), consistent with previous studies demonstrating that a single activity carboxyl methylated both farnesylated and geranylgeranylated substrates (21). The Michaelis constants of the recombinant enzyme,K m = 7 μm for AFC and 0.6 μm for AGGC, were similar to those for the endogenous neutrophil enzyme (19). Thus, the cDNA described above encodes authentic human myeloid pcCMT.

To determine whether human pcCMT could substitute in vivo for the S. cerevisiae pcCMT, Ste14p, we performed a complementation analysis using mating as a biological readout. The HL60 pcCMT cDNA expressed from a plasmid in a Δste14 yeast strain partially restored the mating phenotype (Fig.3), indicating that a-factor could be carboxyl methylated by human pcCMT. Thus, HL60 pcCMT is a functional human homolog of S. cerevisiae Ste14p.

Expression of the human pcCMT gene was examined by Northern analysis. HL60 cells expressed two pcCMT mRNAs, a 3.6-kb transcript consistent with the isolated cDNA and a 5-kb transcript suggesting a related gene or an alternatively spliced message (Fig.4 a ). The level of expression of both transcripts was diminished by granulocytic differentiation of HL60 cells induced by Me2SO, consistent with our observation that HL60 membranes have 5-fold greater specific pcCMT activity than membranes of mature, peripheral blood neutrophils.3 Both transcripts were ubiquitously expressed in human tissues (Fig.4 b ).

To characterize endogenous pcCMT, a polyclonal antiserum was raised against an internal HL60 pcCMT peptide (amino acids 185–201, Fig. 1). Immunoblots of neutrophil and pcCMT-transfected COS-1 cell membranes using this antiserum revealed a 33-kDa protein (Fig. 4 c ) corresponding to the predicted size of the protein encoded by the HL60 pcCMT cDNA, confirming that this cDNA, which lacked a termination codon 5′ of the ORF is, in fact, full-length. The same antiserum immunoprecipitated a 33-kDa protein from HL60 cells (Fig.4 c ). Although the deduced amino acid sequence of pcCMT reveals a potential N -glycosylation site (Fig. 1), these data argue against glycosylation.
Ras is constitutively carboxyl methylated (22) and expressed at the plasma membrane (23), a localization required for its biological activity (24). Like all CAAX proteins, Ras lacks a signal peptide, is synthesized in the cytosol, and modified immediately posttranslationally by a cytosolic prenyltransferase (25). Because prenylcysteine carboxyl methylation is catalyzed by an intrinsic membrane protein and represents the last of the three posttranslational modifications of the CAAX cysteine that enhance the affinity of Ras for membranes, the simplest model of plasma membrane targeting predicts pcCMT expression in the target membrane. However, activities associated with the further processing of prenylated proteins, including pcCMT (26), S -isoprenyl-CAAX high affinity binding (27), S -isoprenyl-CAAX protease (28, 29), and palmitoyltransferase (30) activities, have all been reported in microsomal fractions. Furthermore, one of the twoS -isoprenyl-CAAX proteases recently identified in yeast has a putative ER retention sequence (31, 32), and a double deletion of these genes led to mislocalization of yeast Ras2p to internal membranes and cytosol (31). Nevertheless, none of these studies excluded expression of prenylcysteine-modifying activities from plasma membranes. Indeed, we have reported pcCMT activity in neutrophil subcellular fractions enriched for surface membrane (19).
To determine the subcellular localization of pcCMT we constructed a recombinant pcCMT tagged at the C terminus with GFP. In CHO (Fig.5, a–c ), COS-1 (Fig. 5,d–e ), and NIH3T3 (not shown) cells, CMT-GFP was visualized in the ER, Golgi, and nuclear membranes but not in the plasma membrane. This assay afforded a sensitivity and resolution that allowed visualization of individual ER canaliculi extending to the periphery of the cell (Fig. 5, c and d ) and was therefore definitive in exlcuding expression in the plasma membrane. ER expression was confirmed by colocalization with ribophorin I (Fig.5 f ), a component of the glycosyl transferase complex restricted to ER. Because the 27-kDa GFP added to the C terminus of pcCMT might alter its native subcellular localization, the CMT-GFP localization was confirmed with a pcCMT tagged at the C terminus with a 10-amino acid Myc epitope (Fig. 5 g ). Finally, an anti-peptide antiserum reactive with pcCMT was used to confirm these data by localizing endogenous pcCMT to ER and nuclear membranes in COS-1 cells (Fig. 5, h–i ). The absence of Golgi staining for endogenous pcCMT suggests that the Golgi localization of ectopically expressed pcCMT may result from gene overexpression.

These data demonstrate that mammalian pcCMT is an intrinsic membrane protein localized to a compartment topologically removed from the plasma membrane. Similar observations have recently been made in yeast.4 It is curious that proteins such as Ras, synthesized on free ribosomes, prenylated in the cytosol, and destined for the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane, are diverted to the ER for processing. Moreover, the ER restriction of pcCMT suggests that an uncharacterized transport pathway must mediate the translocation of fully processed GTPases from internal membranes to the cell surface. Such a pathway could utilize the cytoplasmic surface of secretory vesicles, cytosolic accessory molecules analogous to GDI, or a novel transport system. Investigation of this aspect of Ras biology may open new approaches to the development of pharmacologic inhibitors of oncogenic Ras.

The 3.6-kb full-length HL60 pcCMT cDNA and an 852-bp cDNA fragment comprising the ORF were subcloned into the eukaryotic expression vectors pcDM8 and pcDNA3.1 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA).

Myc-tagged pcCMT was made by adding a sequence encoding the 10-amino acid epitope of c-Myc recognized by monoclonal antibody 9E10 to the C terminus of pcCMT using patch PCR and subcloning into pcDNA3.1. pcCMT tagged at the C terminus with GFP was generated by subcloning the pcCMT ORF into the expression vector pGFP-N3 (CLONTECH). For pcCMT enzymatic assays, COS-1 cells were grown in 10-cm dishes and transfected with pcCMT with DEAE-dextran as described (13). For fluorescence microscopy, exponentially growing COS-1, CHO, and NIH3T3 cells were plated the day prior to transfection at 50–60% confluence and transfected with 2 μg of DNA using LipofectAMINE (Life Technologies, Inc.) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Cells were observed at 24 and 48 h after transfection.
Prenylcysteine Carboxyl Methyltransferase Assays
COS-1 cells transfected with HL60 pcCMT or vector alone were harvested at 48 h with 5 mm EDTA and subjected, in parallel with human neutrophils, to nitrogen cavitation and discontinuous sucrose density centrifugation as described (12).

Light membranes were assayed for pcCMT activity qualitatively byS -adenosyl-l-[methyl- 3H]methionine labeling (SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and fluorography) of Rho GTPases partially purified from neutrophil cytosol and quantitatively by carboxyl methylation ofN -acetyl-S -trans,trans -farnesyl-l-cysteine (AFC) (heptane partition, alkaline hydrolysis, and measurement of vapor phase [3H]methanol) as described (14).
S. cerevisiae Strains, Growth, and ste14 Complementation
Complete (YEPD), synthetic (SD), and synthetic dropout media were prepared as described previously (15), except that dropout medium lacked cysteine. All experiments were performed at 30 °C. Yeast transformations were carried out by either the lithium acetate method (16) or the Elble method (17). The ste14 deletion strains used in this study are SM1188 (MATaΔste14–3::TRP1 trp1 leu2 ura3 his4 can1 ) and SM1639 (MATaΔste14–4::URA3 trp1 leu2 his4 can1 ) (5). Plasmid expression of Ste14p was accomplished by pSM1237 (CEN URA3 STE14 ). Human pcCMT was expressed in yeast by subcloning the HL60 pcCMT ORF into theBam HI/Sal I sites of the yeast expression plasmid pG1 (2μ TRP1 ) that utilizes a GPD promotor and a PGK transcription terminator and polyadenylation signal (18). The resulting construct was designated pG1-hCMT (2μ TRP1 hCMT ). Patch mating tests were carried out essentially as described previously (15).

Briefly, patches of MATa cells grown on selective media were replica plated onto a lawn of theMATα mating tester, SM1068 (lys1 ), that had been spread on an SD plate. Plates were incubated at 30 °C for 3 days. Growth of the prototrophic diploids indicated mating.
Fluorescence Microscopy
Live cells that had been transfected with pcCMT-GFP and fixed/permeabilized (2% paraformaldeyde/0.2% Triton X-100 at 4 °C or methanol at −20 °C) cells stained with 9E10 anti-Myc antibody (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA), C6 anti-ribophorin I antiserum (provided by Dr. Gert Kriebich, NYU), or the anti-pcCMT antiserum described above, followed by Texas Red-conjugated secondary antisera, were imaged with a Zeiss Axioscope equipped with a Princeton Instruments cooled CCD camera and a KAF 1400 chip or a Molecular Dynamics confocal microscope equipped with an argon laser.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Repeated efforts to characterize mammalian pcCMT bySTE14 homology cloning and by enzyme purification and microsequencing were unsuccessful. However, we identified a partial murine cDNA (GenBank accession no. AA022288) in the EST data base of the National Center for Biotechnology Information that has sequence homology to Ste14p.

Using primers based on this sequence, reverse transcription-PCR was employed to amplify from human myeloid HL60 cells a 218-bp homologous sequence. Using this fragment an HL60 cDNA library was screened and a single clone identified that contained a 3.6-kb insert. Sequencing revealed a 3595-bp cDNA (GenBank accession no. AF064084) with an ORF that predicted a 284-amino acid protein that is 26% identical to Ste14p (Fig.1). Hydropathy analysis revealed six hydrophobic sequences that may represent membrane-spanning domains (Fig. 1). This is consistent with the five or six putative membrane-spanning domains of Ste14p (5), with recent data demonstrating that Ste14p is an integral membrane protein2 and with our observation that active pcCMT cannot be extracted from membranes with detergents but can be partially reconstituted in phospholipid vesicles (19). The first 65 amino acids of human pcCMT, containing the first two hydrophobic sequences, are 36% identical to amino acids 750–821 of the human band 3 anion transporter, which represent the 11th and 12th of 14 well characterized membrane-spanning domains, further supporting the hypothesis that human pcCMT is a multiple membrane-spanning protein. Comparison of human pcCMT with all related sequences in the GenBank (Fig.

1) revealed the highest degree of divergence in the N-terminal third of the molecule, suggesting that the catalytic domain is C-terminal. Sequences homologous to theS -adenosylmethionine binding regions described in aspartyl and glutamyl protein carboxyl methyltransferases (20) were not apparent, arguing against an evolutionary link.

To determine whether the HL60 Ste14p homolog has prenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase activity, the cDNA was subcloned into a mammalian expression vector and transiently overexpressed in COS-1 cells. Membranes prepared from these cells were used as a source of recombinant enzyme. Farnesylated Ras GTPases require detergent for extraction from membranes. Therefore geranylgeranylated neutrophil cytosolic Rho GTPases that remain soluble by virtue of association with an accessory protein, guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitor (GDI), were utilized as endogenous substrates in an in vitro assay (Fig. 2). Untransfected COS-1 cell membranes had little pcCMT activity toward Rho proteins compared with that of membranes derived from human neutrophils (Fig. 2 a ). Transfection with the HL60 cDNA conferred pcCMT activity toward Rho GTPases on COS-1 membranes, and this activity was blocked by the competitive pcCMT inhibitor, AFC, with an ED50 (10 μm) identical to that for endogenous neutrophil pcCMT.

Carboxyl methylation of Rac2 and RhoA by HL60 pcCMT-transfected COS-1 cell membranes was enhanced by GTPγS (Fig. 2 b ), similar to the activity observed in neutrophil membranes (7). Carboxyl methyltransferase activity was quantitated in membranes of COS-1 cells transfected with HL60 pcCMT using prenylcysteine analogs as defined substrates (14). Untransfected COS-1 cell membranes had 23 ± 10% (n = 5) of the pcCMT specific activity of neutrophil membranes toward AFC. Transfection of COS-1 cells with HL60 pcCMT resulted in an 18–53-fold increase in specific AFC carboxyl methyltransferase activity (3.0 ± 0.8 to 74.5 ± 6.8 pmol/mg·min, n = 5, p < 0.0005). Carboxyl methylation ofN -acetyl-S-all-trans -geranylgeranyl-l-cysteine (AGGC) was increased in parallel with methylation of AFC (18-versus 20-fold increase, n = 2), consistent with previous studies demonstrating that a single activity carboxyl methylated both farnesylated and geranylgeranylated substrates (21). The Michaelis constants of the recombinant enzyme,K m = 7 μm for AFC and 0.6 μm for AGGC, were similar to those for the endogenous neutrophil enzyme (19). Thus, the cDNA described above encodes authentic human myeloid pcCMT.

To determine whether human pcCMT could substitute in vivo for the S.

cerevisiae pcCMT, Ste14p, we performed a complementation analysis using mating as a biological readout. The HL60 pcCMT cDNA expressed from a plasmid in a Δste14 yeast strain partially restored the mating phenotype (Fig.3), indicating that a-factor could be carboxyl methylated by human pcCMT. Thus, HL60 pcCMT is a functional human homolog of S. cerevisiae Ste14p.

Expression of the human pcCMT gene was examined by Northern analysis. HL60 cells expressed two pcCMT mRNAs, a 3.6-kb transcript consistent with the isolated cDNA and a 5-kb transcript suggesting a related gene or an alternatively spliced message (Fig.4 a ). The level of expression of both transcripts was diminished by granulocytic differentiation of HL60 cells induced by Me2SO, consistent with our observation that HL60 membranes have 5-fold greater specific pcCMT activity than membranes of mature, peripheral blood neutrophils.3 Both transcripts were ubiquitously expressed in human tissues (Fig.4 b ).

To characterize endogenous pcCMT, a polyclonal antiserum was raised against an internal HL60 pcCMT peptide (amino acids 185–201, Fig. 1). Immunoblots of neutrophil and pcCMT-transfected COS-1 cell membranes using this antiserum revealed a 33-kDa protein (Fig.

4 c ) corresponding to the predicted size of the protein encoded by the HL60 pcCMT cDNA, confirming that this cDNA, which lacked a termination codon 5′ of the ORF is, in fact, full-length. The same antiserum immunoprecipitated a 33-kDa protein from HL60 cells (Fig.4 c ). Although the deduced amino acid sequence of pcCMT reveals a potential N -glycosylation site (Fig. 1), these data argue against glycosylation.
Ras is constitutively carboxyl methylated (22) and expressed at the plasma membrane (23), a localization required for its biological activity (24). Like all CAAX proteins, Ras lacks a signal peptide, is synthesized in the cytosol, and modified immediately posttranslationally by a cytosolic prenyltransferase (25). Because prenylcysteine carboxyl methylation is catalyzed by an intrinsic membrane protein and represents the last of the three posttranslational modifications of the CAAX cysteine that enhance the affinity of Ras for membranes, the simplest model of plasma membrane targeting predicts pcCMT expression in the target membrane. However, activities associated with the further processing of prenylated proteins, including pcCMT (26), S -isoprenyl-CAAX high affinity binding (27), S -isoprenyl-CAAX protease (28, 29), and palmitoyltransferase (30) activities, have all been reported in microsomal fractions.

Furthermore, one of the twoS -isoprenyl-CAAX proteases recently identified in yeast has a putative ER retention sequence (31, 32), and a double deletion of these genes led to mislocalization of yeast Ras2p to internal membranes and cytosol (31). Nevertheless, none of these studies excluded expression of prenylcysteine-modifying activities from plasma membranes. Indeed, we have reported pcCMT activity in neutrophil subcellular fractions enriched for surface membrane (19).
To determine the subcellular localization of pcCMT we constructed a recombinant pcCMT tagged at the C terminus with GFP. In CHO (Fig.5, a–c ), COS-1 (Fig. 5,d–e ), and NIH3T3 (not shown) cells, CMT-GFP was visualized in the ER, Golgi, and nuclear membranes but not in the plasma membrane. This assay afforded a sensitivity and resolution that allowed visualization of individual ER canaliculi extending to the periphery of the cell (Fig. 5, c and d ) and was therefore definitive in exlcuding expression in the plasma membrane. ER expression was confirmed by colocalization with ribophorin I (Fig.5 f ), a component of the glycosyl transferase complex restricted to ER.

Because the 27-kDa GFP added to the C terminus of pcCMT might alter its native subcellular localization, the CMT-GFP localization was confirmed with a pcCMT tagged at the C terminus with a 10-amino acid Myc epitope (Fig. 5 g ). Finally, an anti-peptide antiserum reactive with pcCMT was used to confirm these data by localizing endogenous pcCMT to ER and nuclear membranes in COS-1 cells (Fig. 5, h–i ). The absence of Golgi staining for endogenous pcCMT suggests that the Golgi localization of ectopically expressed pcCMT may result from gene overexpression.

These data demonstrate that mammalian pcCMT is an intrinsic membrane protein localized to a compartment topologically removed from the plasma membrane. Similar observations have recently been made in yeast.4 It is curious that proteins such as Ras, synthesized on free ribosomes, prenylated in the cytosol, and destined for the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane, are diverted to the ER for processing. Moreover, the ER restriction of pcCMT suggests that an uncharacterized transport pathway must mediate the translocation of fully processed GTPases from internal membranes to the cell surface.

Such a pathway could utilize the cytoplasmic surface of secretory vesicles, cytosolic accessory molecules analogous to GDI, or a novel transport system. Investigation of this aspect of Ras biology may open new approaches to the development of pharmacologic inhibitors of oncogenic Ras.

The molecular basis of glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency

Glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder and the second most commoninborn error of folate metabolism, is presumed to be due to defects in the bifunctional enzyme glutamateformiminotransferase-cyclodeaminase (FTCD). Features of a severe phenotype, first identified in patients ofJapanese descent, include elevated levels of formiminoglutamate (FIGLU) in the urine in response to histidineadministration, megaloblastic anemia, and mental retardation. Features of a mild phenotype include highurinary excretion of FIGLU in the absence of histidine administration, mild developmental delay, and nohematological abnormalities. We found mutations in the human FTCD gene in three patients with putativeglutamate formiminotransferase deficiency. Two siblings were heterozygous for missense mutations, c.457C4T(R135C) and c.940G4C (R299P). Mutagenesis of porcine FTCD and expression in E. coli showed that theR135C mutation reduced formiminotransferase activity to 61% of wild-type, whereas the R299P mutationreduced this activity to 57% of wild-type. The third patient was hemizygous for c.1033insG, with quantitativePCR indicating that the other allele contained a deletion. These mutations are the first identified in glutamateformiminotransferase deficiency and demonstrate that mutations in FTCD represent the molecular basis for themild phenotype of this disease. Hum Mutat 22:67–73, 2003. r 2003 Wiley-Liss, Inc.

INTRODUCTIONG

lutamate formiminotransferase-cyclodeaminase(FTCD, MIM# 229100) is a bifunctional enzyme thatcatalyzes the folate-dependent degradation of N-formi-minoglutamic acid to form 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofo-late, glutamate, and ammonia, the final two reactions ofthe pathway responsible for the degradation ofL-histidine. The metabolic pathway that degradesL-histidine is shown in Figure 1. The formiminotransfer-ase domain catalyzes the transfer of a formimino group totetrahydrofolate from N-formiminoglutamate, freeingglutamate in the process. The second reaction, catalyzedby the cyclodeaminase domain, frees ammonia fromformiminotetrahydrofolate, generating 5,10-methenylte-trahydrofolate [Rosenblatt and Fenton, 2001].

Human FTCD maps to 21q22.3 and its majortranscript encodes a protein containing 541 amino acids.The genomic sequence of human FTCD consists of 15 exons and generates at least five different transcripts.The two most frequently found transcripts encode for thesame protein but differ in their 30 UTRs [Solans et al.,2000]. The physiological significance for the differenttranscripts is currently unknown. FTCD is detected atthe highest levels in the liver, with kidney and testis showing lower levels of transcription [Solans et al.,2000]. Enzymatic activity of human FTCD can bedetected on extracts of liver but not in those offibroblasts or blood cells [Erbe, 1986].The protein sequence of porcine FTCD is 81%identical (87% conserved) as compared to the humanprotein [Solans et al., 2000]. The porcine enzyme ismade up of eight identical subunits, with each subunitcontaining a formiminotransferase domain and a cyclo-deaminase domain [Beaudet and MacKenzie, 1976].These two domains are connected by a short chain ofamino acids, known as the ‘‘linker’’ region. Whenassembling to form the active enzymatic form, eachdomain dimerizes with a like-domain from anothersubunit [Findlay and MacKenzie, 1987]. Dimers of onetype are connected to dimers of the other type by thelinker region. The final enzymatic structure is anoctameric ring containing four formiminotransferaseactive sites and four cyclodeaminase active sites.Dimerization is absolutely essential for each enzymaticfunction; octamerization is not required for the indivi dual activities but is required to form the completebifunctional enzyme. It has been demonstrated thatisolated formiminotransferase dimers and isolated cyclo-deaminase dimers retain full catalytic function [Murleyand MacKenzie, 1995]. In octameric form, the productfrom the formiminotransferase active site is channeled tothe cyclodeaminase active site [MacKenzie and Baugh,1980]. Channeling is dependent on the length of theglutamate residue chain of the folate molecule. It hasbeen shown that glutamate chains containing fiveresidues channel most efficiently [Paquin et al., 1985].Glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency is anautosomal recessive disorder of folate metabolism. Twophenotypes, a severe and a mild form, have beendescribed with their genetic basis not yet elucidated. Asevere form has been identified in five patients ofJapanese descent. Common features among the patientsincluded mental and physical retardation, elevated serumfolate, and the presence of FIGLU in the urine followingthe administration of L-histidine. For the initial twocases, enzyme activities were performed on liver biopsiesfrom the patients. The first identified patient’s FTCDactivity was 33% of normal levels while the secondreported case had 30–50% of normal levels [Arakawaet al., 1963, 1965, 1968]. A mild form has beenidentified in patients from a variety of ethnic origins.Disease features among these patients include theexcretion of far higher levels of FIGLU in the absenceof histidine loading, normal serum folate, and slightdevelopmental delay. No enzyme assays have beenperformed on liver biopsies from patients presentingwith the mild phenotype [Erbe, 1986; Niederwieser et al.,1976; Perry et al., 1975]. Diagnosis of FTCD deficiency issuggested by the presence of high levels of FIGLU in theurine. However, confirmation of a deficiency wouldrequire assays of the activity of the enzyme from liverbiopsies. A specific diagnosis is important because highFIGLU excretion may also occur due to other causes offolate or methylcobalamin deficiency [Erbe, 1986].

MATERIALS AND METHODS

Cell LinesFibroblasts from three patients with putative glutamateformiminotransferase deficiency were obtained from the Reposi-tory for Mutant Human Cell Strains, Montreal Children’sHospital. The first two patients, whose cultured cell lines aredesignated WG 1758 and 1759, are siblings [Perry et al., 1975].The third patient’s cultured cell line is designated WG 1795 [Becket al., 1981]. DNA was then extracted from fibroblasts usingstandard phenol-chloroform protocols. These studies were ap-proved by the Research Ethics Board of the Royal VictoriaHospital.

PCR and Sequencing

Genomic organization of the coding region was obtained fromGenBank (GenBank accession number AP001759), which con-tains the complete intron and exon sequences of the humanFTCD gene (complement of nucleotides 154005 to 173295). PCRand sequencing primers utilized for these experiments weredesigned using the Primer 3.0 software available on the WhiteheadInstitute/MIT Centre for Genomic Research server.

The FTCD gene consists of 15 exons over 19.3 kB of genomicDNA. Primers were designed within regions flanking the exons;when possible, primers were designed to include two exons. Primersequences and PCR conditions are shown in Table 1. Each PCRreaction was carried out in a total volume of 50 ml following theprotocol indicated by either PE Biosystems or Qiagen, dependingon the source of the Taq polymerase. Each PCR which followedthe PE Biosystems protocol contained 2.5 U of Amplitaq Goldt(Perkin-Elmer Cetus, Shetton, CT), 1  GeneAmpt PCR buffer(Perkin-Elmer Cetus) supplemented with the indicated concen-tration of MgCl 2 , 200 mM of dNTPs, and 20 ng of DNA template.PCR performed using Qiagen protocols contained 2.5 units ofHotstarTaqt (Qiagen, Mississagua, Canada), 1  HotstarTaqtbuffer (Qiagen), supplemented with the indicated amount ofMgCl 2 , 200 mM of dNTPs, and 20 ng of DNA template.Prior to sequencing, each PCR product was purified using theMultiscreent PCR purification plate (Millipore, Bedford, MA).Sequencing was done using Big Dye Terminatort Sequencing kitversion 2 (Perkin-Elmer Cetus) and analysis was performed usingthe ABI 3700 capillary sequencing system (Perkin-Elmer Cetus).Sequencing results were processed and analyzed using ABI PrismtSequence A software, version 1.12 (Perkin-Elmer Cetus) andAutoassemblert version 2.11 (Perkin-Elmer Cetus).

Restriction Digest Analysis
Sequence changes detected by sequence analysis were con-firmed by restriction endonuclease analysis of PCR products.Digestion products were separated by electrophoresis into 2%agarose gels or into 10% polyacrylamide (29:1 acrylamide:bis-acrylamide) gels, depending on the sizes of the products to beseparated. All restriction enzymes were purchased from NewEngland Biolabs (Mississauga, Canada). For c.940G4C andc.1033insG, DNA was amplified using the same primers used forsequencing and the PCR product was digested with theappropriate restriction endonuclease, using the buffer and reactionconditions specified by the manufacturer. For c.940G4C muta-tion, located in exon 7, amplified fragments were digested withAlwI. For the c.1033insG mutation, located in exon 9, amplifiedfragments were digested with Eco0109I.Because the c.457C4T mutation did not create or destroy arestriction site, an artificial HinFI site was created to assess thepresence of the mutation. Alternative primers were designed(sense 50-ggcagccaggatggagagt-30, antisense 50-cttagggagggcctcg-tact-30). DNA was amplified using the Qiagen protocol with anannealing temperature of 551C, and 1.5 mM MgCl 2 . Digestionusing HinFI was then carried out according to manufacturer’sspecifications.

Quantitative PCR
Exon 9 in WG 1795 was examined by quantitative PCR toassess whether c.1033insG was homozygous or hemizygous in thisindividual. The approach used is the same as described previously[Aarskog and Vedeler, 2000]. The primers used were the same aspreviously described for exon 9. The exon 9 probe was labeled withthe fluorescent dye FAM in addition to the quencher TAMRA(Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA). Hydrolysis of the probe occurs at thesame rate as the generation of the amplicon; therefore, thefluorescence levels within a sample are proportional to the rate ofamplification. The nucleotide sequence for the probe is 50-gcaagtccctgcgcgccttc-30. Amplification was performed using theABI 7700 (Perkin Elmer, Shetton, CT) using the previouslydescribed amplification conditions for exon 9, with fluorescencelevels read and recorded at the end of step 4 of each cycle.To correct for differing amounts of starting template betweenthe control and WG 1795, a standard amplification curve wasgenerated for each sample by using a quantitative PCR of exon 3of the Kit Ligand gene (KITLG) located on chromosome12q21.32. Amplification was performed using forward (50-tttgtgtgcttttctccaaag-30) and reverse (5-tgagctactaaaatgaaactca-gaaa-30) primers. The nucleotide sequence for the FAM andTAMRA labeled probe is 50-tcttccaaaagactacatgataaccctca-30. Thequantitative PCR reaction used the PE systems protocol in thepresence of 4.5 mM MgCl 2 at an annealing temperature of 621C.Fluorescence levels were read and recorded at the end of step 4 ofeach cycle.

Site-Directed Mutagenesis
The effects of the identified mutations on the formiminotrans-ferase activity were assessed through mutagenesis of the porcineFTCD expressed in E. coli [Murley et al., 1993; Murley andMacKenzie, 1995]. Vectors that express either the entire porcineenzyme (FTCD) or the separate transferase (FT) domain with sixhistidine tags [Murley and MacKenzie, 1995] were used to createmutants using in vitro overlap extension PCR mutagenesis[Cormack, 1997]. The PCR product and the expression constructtemplate were digested with appropriate restriction enzymes (NEB,Mississauga, Canada; Invitrogen; MBI Fermentas, Burlington,Canada) and ligated. Clones were screened for the mutation bythe introduction or removal of restriction enzyme sites, confirmedand shown to be free of any other mutations by automatedsequencing (Sheldon Biotechnology Center, McGill University).

Protein Expression and Purification
Wild-type and mutant constructs were transformed into E. coliBL21(DE3) cells and expressed as described previously [Murleyet al., 1993]. The R135C and R299P mutant proteins were further purified as described previously [Murley and MacKenzie, 1995].The c.1033insG mutant could not be further purified due to theloss of the six histidine tag because of the introduced mutation.The protein content of the enzyme samples was determined induplicate using the Bradford assay with BSA as a standard[Bradford, 1976].

Formiminotransferase Assay
Formiminotransferase activity was measured as describedpreviously [Findlay et al., 1989; Drury et al., 1975]. Activitiesare expressed as the average of two triplicate determinations.Sodium formiminoglutamate and (6R,S)-tetrahydrofolate wereprepared as described previously [Drury et al., 1975].

Western Blot
Samples of crude extracts (10 mg of total protein) were analyzedby immunoblot assay using polyclonal rabbit anti-porcine FTCDserum [Murley et al., 1993] pre-absorbed with 1mg protein/mL ofsonicated E. coli BL21(DE3) for 1 hr at room temperature,followed by an HRP conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG antibody (Fabspecific, BioCan Scientific Inc., Mississauga, Canada). Bands werevisualized by enhanced chemiluminescence (Western Lightning,Perkin Elmer Life Sciences).

RESULTS
Sequencing Analysis
Three sequence changes were identified in DNAextracted from fibroblasts from the patients. In DNAfrom cell lines WG 1758 and WG 1759 (siblings), twoheterozygous mutations were found. The first isc.457C4T (exon 4) which converts arginine to cysteineat amino acid position 135. The second is c.940G4C(exon 9), which converts arginine to proline at aminoacid position 299. In DNA from WG 1795, c.1033insGwas identified as the only sequence present. Allsequencing results are shown in Figure 2. The frameshift created by c.1033insG results in a premature stopcodon two amino acid positions downstream. Thepresence of all three mutations was confirmed in DNAfrom patients by restriction enzyme analysis. Thec.457C4T mutation resulted in loss of an artificialHinFI restriction site introduced into exon 4. Thec.940G4C mutation resulted in loss of an AlwIrestriction site in exon 7. Both were present in theheterozygous state in DNA from WG 1758 and WG1759. The c.1033insG mutation, which resulted in gainof Eco0109I restriction site, was the only form present inDNA from WG 1795. All three mutations were absent in100 alleles from anonymous controls.A common polymorphism c.1313C4T (exon 12,A438E) was identified in four of 19 controls tested (datanot shown). Expression analysis indicated that thepolymorphism does not affect enzyme function (datanot shown).

Quantitative PCR
Quantitative PCR analysis demonstrated that in WG1795, three additional PCR cycles were required forfluorescence from the FTCD reaction to reach itsthreshold level compared to the control KITLG reaction(Table 2). This difference was not observed for DNA from any of the other controls utilized. These resultssuggest that the amount of DNA at the FTCD exon 9locus is reduced in WG 1795 relative to the controlKITLG locus.

Expression Analysis
Site-specific mutagenesis was performed for all threeidentified mutations using expression vectors thatexpressed either the formiminotransferase domain ofporcine FTCD (R135C and R299P) or full-lengthporcine FTCD (c.1033insG). The specific activity ofthe wild-type formiminotransferase domain is 10.2 mmolof 5-formiminotetrahydrofolate formed/min/mg protein.R135C reduced formiminotransferase activity to 61% ofthe wild-type activity (6.24 mmol of 5-formiminotetrahy-drofolate formed/min/mg protein), while R299P reducedactivity to 57% of the wild-type activity (5.80 mmol of 5-formiminotetrahydrofolate formed/min/mg protein). The specific activity value represents an average of twotriplicates.Formiminotransferase activity of full length FTCDcontaining the c.1033insG mutation remained intact(0.87 U/mg protein), an elevated value compared towild-type activity (0.087 U/mg protein). Western blotanalysis demonstrated that the protein generated by thec.1033insG construct was truncated due to the loss ofthe cyclodeaminase domain and that the protein wasmore highly expressed in E. coli than the wild-typeprotein (Fig. 3). This accounts for the elevatedformiminotransferase activity.

DISCUSSION
Glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency is thesecond most frequent of the inborn errors of folatemetabolism. Based on the elevated excretion of urinaryFIGLU, several apparently affected individuals have beenidentified; however, in most cases, it has not beenpossible to confirm the diagnosis by enzyme assays fromliver biopsies. Identification of the human FTCD gene onchromosome 21 has now made it possible to assesswhether mutations in this gene underlie the disorder. Wehave sequenced the entire coding sequence in threepatients with putative glutamate formiminotransferasedeficiency and have identified disease-causing mutationsin the FTCD gene.Patients represented by cell lines WG 1758 and WG1759 were siblings diagnosed with glutamate formimino-transferase deficiency after extremely high levels ofFIGLU were detected in the urine. The boy (WG1758), diagnosed at age 2 years, showed signs of physicalretardation, general hypotonia, and mild delay in speechdevelopment. The girl (WG 1759), diagnosed at age 8years, was hypotonic and showed some electroencepha-lographic abnormalities. Liver biopsies were not per-formed on either patient. Both patients were consideredto have a mild phenotype [Perry et al., 1975; Erbe,1986].Direct sequencing of FTCD in these two celllines revealed two mutations present in the hetero-zygous state. The R135C mutation affects a conservedresidue in an extended loop in the formiminotransferasedomain that interacts with the polyglutamate chain ofthe bound folate molecule. This loop extends from the surface of the formiminotransferase domain and into thecyclodeaminase domain [Kohls et al., 2000; Solans et al.,2000]. The loss of specific activity to 61% of the wild-type may be due to conformational changes in the activesite of the protein. This mutation may also affect thechanneling of the product to the cyclodeaminasedomain, but this possibility has not been assessed in thiswork.The second mutation observed in WG 1758 and WG1759 is c.940G4C (R299P). Residues 288–316 in theformiminotransferase domain form an a-helix that makesextensive hydrogen bonding contacts within the for-miminotransferase dimerization interface [Kohls et al.,2000]. The introduction of a proline may disrupt the a-helix, possibly resulting in an alteration of the structureof the C-terminal region and a change in the dimerinterface. The mutant protein has only 57% specificactivity when compared to wild-type.The activity values for the constructs containingthe mutations of the two patients are relativelyhigh. However, Arakawa and colleagues obtainedactivities of 30–50% of wild-type for the initial glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency patients with the severephenotype [Arakawa et al., 1963; Arakawa et al., 1965;Arakawa et al., 1968]. Therefore, it is possible thatcomplete loss of activity is not a requirement for diseasepresentation. In addition, activity of mixed R135C andR299P dimers has not been assessed; activity of suchdimers may differ from that of unmixed dimers.The patient represented by WG 1795 is considered topresent with the mild phenotype for glutamate formimi-notransferase deficiency. At the time of diagnosis at age 2years, the boy appeared to be mildly developmentallydelayed, was hypotonic, and had high levels of FIGLU inhis urine [Beck et al., 1981]. Direct sequencing thispatient’s FTCD gene revealed the c.1033insG mutation;no wild-type allele was detected at this locus. Theinsertion changes the reading frame and creates a stopcodon two positions downstream in the middle of thelinker region between the formiminotransferase domainand the cyclodeaminase domain. Previous work hasshown that the formiminotransferase domain candimerize and function in the absence of the cyclodeami-nase [Murley and MacKenzie, 1995]. Activity of thec.1033insG protein in vitro shows that this is the case forthis patient. As a result of this mutation, we infer thatWG 1795 is capable of catalyzing the formation offormiminotetrahydrofolate but is unable to complete thesecond reaction. Results of quantitative PCR stronglysuggest that only a single FTCD allele, containing thec.1033insG mutation, is present in WG 1795; there hasbeen loss of the second allele.It has been suggested that patients with the mild formof the disease have a block in the formiminotransferasereaction, while patients with the severe form of thedisease had blocks in the cyclodeaminase reaction[Rowe, 1983]. Blocks in the formiminotransferasereaction would result in all FIGLU generated beingexcreted in the urine, while blocks in the cyclodeaminasereaction would allow conversion of some FIGLU to5-formiminotetrahydrofolate, thus reducing the FIGLUlevels excreted into the urine. According to thishypothesis [Rowe, 1983], WG 1795, with normalformiminotransferase activity by no active cyclodeami-nase domain, should have severe disease; however, this isnot the case. These results suggest that blocks in theformiminotransferase and cyclodeaminase both result inthe same clinical phenotype and that the cause of thesevere and mild forms of the disease is due to otherfactors.
