Oligonucleotides were synthesized on an Applied Biosystems 380B DNA Synthesizer (Applied Biosystems Inc., Foster City, CA, USA). Restriction enzymes and their buffers were obtained from MBI Fermentas (NY, USA) (Alw 26I), New England Biolabs (Beverly, MA, USA) (Fok I, Bsp MI, Stu I, Mlu I, Ase I), Pharmacia Biotech (Uppsala, Sweden) (Bam HI) and Boehringer Mannheim (Mannheim, Germany) (Hin dIII). Sequencing was performed using the ThermoSequenase cycle sequencing kit (Amersham Life Science, Sydney, Australia). [α-33P]dATP was obtained from Amersham (Bucks., UK).

EST database screening
The EST database is accessible through the National Centre for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) web page (http://www.ncbi.nlm.gov/). Database screening was carried out by application of the BLAST alignment tool (Altschul et al., 1997), accessed through the home page of the NCBI. The human EST database was searched using the GSTZ1 cDNA sequence (accession number U86529). An advanced BLAST search using the `flat master-slave with identities' alignment view option presents the EST sequences as a multiple alignment as displayed in Fig. 1.

EST clones were obtained from the IMAGE consortium through Genome Systems, Inc. (St Louis, MI, USA).

Analysis of polymorphisms in a control population
DNA was extracted from blood samples by standard methods. The control population consisted of unselected Australian European blood donors (Harris et al., 1998). The average age of the 141 individuals analysed in this study was 40 years (range 16–69 years) with 68 women and 73 men.

The polymorphic region of the GSTZ1 gene was amplified from genomic DNA samples using the primers ZseqA8 and Zexon3B, designed from the flanking intronic regions of exon 3 such that both variable nucleotides could be investigated within the one PCR product. The primer sequences are presented in Table 1. PCR was performed with 25–50 ng genomic DNA with 300 pmol/ml of each primer in a 20 μl reaction volume containing 1X Advanced Biotechnologies (Epsom, UK) buffer IV (20 mm (NH4)2SO4, 75 mm Tris-HCl pH 9.0, 0.01% Tween), 1.5 mm MgCl2 (Advanced Biotechnologies) 200 μm dNTPs and 0.5 U of Taq polymerase.

The cycling conditions were 95 °C 2 min, followed by 35 cycles of 95 °C 20 s, 60 °C 15 s, 72 °C 30 s with a final cycle of 72 °C for 3 min.

An A to G transition at nucleotide position 94 was detected by digestion of the PCR product with Alw 26I and analysis of the digestion products by 10% polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE). An A to G transition at nucleotide position 124 was detected by digestion of the PCR product with Fok I and analysis of the digestion products by 8% PAGE. Alw 26I was used at 0.1 U/μl in 1X MBI buffer Y with 0.1 mg/ml BSA, while Fok I was used at 0.05 U/μl in 1X NEB buffer 4. In each case, 2–4 μl of the PCR product was digested in a 15 μl volume at 37 °C overnight. PAGE was performed using Accugel (29:1, National Diagnostics, Atlanta, GA, USA) with 1X TBE (0.09 m Tris-borate, 2 mm EDTA) gel and running buffer.

In individuals heterozygous at both polymorphic sites, allele-specific PCR for nucleotide 124 was performed followed by digestion with Alw 26I to determine the haplotypes present.

PCR was performed as described above, using the primer ZseqA8 in combination with one of the allele-specific primers, Zeta124G or Zeta124A (Table 1), at 200 pmol/ml. The allele-specific primers were designed with the polymorphic nucleotide in the terminal 3′ position and with a mismatch at the adjacent nucleotide (Newton et al., 1989;Kwok et al., 1990). The cycling conditions were 95 °C 2 min, followed by 35 cycles of 95 °C 20 s, 55 °C 20 s, 72 °C 30 s with a final cycle of 72 °C for 2 min. The 202 bp product was digested with Alw 26I overnight, and the fragments were separated by 10% PAGE.

Chi-squared analysis was performed to test for linkage disequilibrium between the two polymorphic sites, and for agreement with Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

Bacterial expression and purification of variant GSTZ1 proteins
The GSTZ1 proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli as 6X His-tagged proteins and were purified by Ni-agarose column chromatography. The coding region of GSTZ1 was PCR-amplified as a 686 bp product from EST clones containing the appropriate sequence variations at nucleotides 94 and 124: N31040 A94A124 (Board et al., 1997); T35781 A94G124; R67650 G94G124.

The forward primer (PQEZ1) was designed to replace the initiating methionine with a Bam HI restriction site, and the reverse primer (Z1exB2) introduced a Hin dIII restriction site 18 bp beyond the stop codon (Table 1). The amplified product was digested with Bam HI and Hin dIII, and ligated into the pQE30 vector (Qiagen, Clifton Hill, Australia), which encodes the 6X His-tag at the N-terminus of the protein, and transformed into E. coli JM103. After selection of expressing clones and nucleotide sequencing to ensure the absence of PCR-induced errors, the constructs were transformed into E. coli M15[pREP4] for large scale expression.

During sequencing of the pQEZ1 constructs, a sequence variation was found in the G94G124 clone, pQC21. Sequencing of the EST clone R67650 showed that this variation, a C to T transition at nucleotide 245 of the coding region, was present in the PCR template. To create a pQEZ1C without this variation, a 419 bp Bsp MI/ Stu I fragment from nucleotides 171–590 of the cDNA was excised from pQC21 and replaced with the same fragment from pQEZ1B.

The presence of the C at nucleotide 245, which introduces a Mlu I restriction site, was detected by digestion of the plasmid DNA with Mlu I and Ase I. The new pQEZ1C construct was sequenced in the modified region to confirm that no other variations had been introduced. The constructs were now identical in sequence to the coding region of pGSTZ1 (Board et al., 1997) except for the variations at nucleotides 94 and 124 as follows: pQEZ1A – A94A124; pQEZ1B – A94G124; pQEZ1C – G94G124.

Cultures of M15[pREP4] containing pQEZ1 plasmids were grown in LB broth supplemented with 100 μg/ml ampicillin and 25 μg/ml kanamycin at 37 °C. To induce protein expression, cultures were grown overnight in the presence of 0.1 mm isopropyl thio-β-d-galactoside. Purification procedures followed the QIA expressionist protocol for purification of 6X His-tagged proteins under native conditions (Qiagen).

To prepare cleared bacterial lysates, bacteria were pelleted by centrifugation, resuspended in buffer A (50 mm sodium phosphate, 300 mm NaCl pH 7.5), lysed either by incubation with 1 mg/ml lysozyme on ice for 1 h followed by sonication, or by passage through a Ribi cell fractionator model RF-1 (Sorvall, Newton, VA, USA), and the lysates cleared by centrifugation at 10 000 g for 15 min at 4 °C. Cleared lysates were incubated with Ni-agarose resin (Porath & Olin, 1983) for 1–2 h at 4 °C on a rotary mixer. The resin was collected by centrifugation and washed extensively with buffer A, and then packed under gravity into a small column. The column was equilibrated with several volumes of buffer A containing 10% glycerol and proteins were eluted with 50 mm and 500 mm imidazole in buffer A containing 10% glycerol. Fractions containing recombinant GSTZ1 were identified by SDS-PAGE, pooled and dialysed overnight against buffer consisting of 5 mm Hepes pH 7.0, 1 mm dithiothreitol and 10% glycerol.

The proteins were stored at −20 °C, and the protein concentration was determined by the Lowry method after thawing of aliquots.

Enzyme assays
The formation of glyoxylate from dichloroacetate and chlorofluoroacetate was measured spectrophotometrically as previously described (Tong et al., 1998a). Reaction mixtures for these assays contained 1 μg purified GSTZ1 and were incubated at 37 °C for 20 min. The measurement by HPLC of S-carboxymethylglutathione and S-(α-methylcarboxymethyl)glutathione formation from fluoroacetate and 2-halopropionates, respectively, has also been described elsewhere (Tong et al., 1998b). The amount of purified GSTZ1 and incubation time at 37 °C for the reaction mixtures were as follows: 11–13 μg and 80 min with fluoroacetate; 2 μg and 45 min with R-2-chloropropionate; and 4–13 μg and 45 min with S-2-chloropropionate. Glutathione conjugating activity towards a range of electrophilic substrates was measured spectrophotometrically under the following previously described conditions: 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, 1,2-dichloro-4-nitrobenzene, ethacrynic acid, p-nitrophenyl acetate, 1,2-epoxy-3-(4-nitrophenoxy)propane (Habig et al., 1974;Mannervik & Widersten, 1995); 7-chloro-4-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazole (Ricci et al., 1994);trans-alk-2-enals and trans,trans-deca-2,4-dienal (Brophy et al., 1989).

Results
When GSTZ1 was first characterized, the available sequence from 13 ESTs encoding GSTZ1 was examined by alignment for evidence of polymorphism.

This revealed consistent variability at two sites, with an A or G variably found at both nucleotide positions 94 and 124 (Board et al., 1997). A more recent BLAST search of the human EST database retrieved 90 sequences matching some part of the GSTZ1 cDNA, of which 84 were clearly clones of the GSTZ1 cDNA. Of these, 26 entries matched some part of the sequence of exon 3 of GSTZ1, with 23 sequences containing both nucleotides 94 and 124. These sequences are aligned in Fig. 1.

Numerous sequence variations are observed in such an alignment of EST sequence data. In looking for polymorphisms in these sequences, the occurrence of errors due to single pass automated sequencing must be considered, and attention focused on variations that occur in multiple ESTs. The nucleotides found at position 94 were 11 As and 15 Gs, which is a ratio unlikely to be due to random sequencing errors. At position 124, only four As were found, matching pGSTZ1, while 17 sequences contained G, matching the gene sequence. While variation at this site is far less common than at nucleotide 94, no other positions display variation at this frequency (Fig.

1), thus supporting the possibility that the sequence variation is due to allelic variation rather than random sequencing errors.

Both polymorphic sites are found within exon 3 (nucleotides 68–135) of the GSTZ1 gene (Blackburn et al., 1998) and result in changes in restriction enzyme sites. Thus amplification of a single 308 bp segment of the gene, covering exon 3 and its flanking intronic regions, followed by digestion with the appropriate restriction enzyme allows determination of the nucleotides present at the polymorphic sites. The A to G polymorphism at position 94 results in the presence (G) or absence (A) of an Alw 26I site in the 308 bp PCR product, in addition to an invariant Alw 26I site which yields a 125 bp fragment. This invariant site serves as an internal control for digestion efficiency. Three possible genotypes are defined by three distinct banding patterns as displayed in Fig. 2 a: A94/A94 (186 and 125 bp fragments), A94/G94 (186, 159, 125 and 26 bp fragments), and G94/G94 (159, 125 and 26 bp fragments).

Similarly, the A to G polymorphism at position 124 results in the presence (G) or absence (A) of a Fok I site, resulting in the banding patterns seen in Fig. 2 b: A124/A124 (308 bp fragment only), A124/G124 (308, 193 and 115 bp fragments), and G124/G124 (193 and 115 bp fragments). This method was used to determine the frequency of the variants in a control population consisting of 141 unselected controls of Caucasian origin (Table 2). G was more common than A at both positions 94 and 124, and the distribution of G or A at each position was in agreement with that expected in a Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

The presence of two polymorphic sites results in four possible haplotypes: A94A124, A94G124, G94G124 and G94A124. Of the 21 EST sequences which included unambiguous bases at both nucleotide 94 and 124, four were A94A124, six were A94G124 and 11 were G94G124 (Fig. 1). There was no evidence in the EST database for the occurrence of a variant G94A124. In the control population, examination of the genotypes at both nucleotide positions allowed the determination of the alleles present in the majority of individuals.

Fifteen people were heterozygous at both nucleotides 94 and 124, and therefore their genotypes could not be determined by this approach. Allele-specific PCR for nucleotide 124 was conducted on these samples, generating a 202 bp product which was digested with Alw 26I to determine the base present at nucleotide 94. The 202 bp product contained both the invariant and polymorphic Alw 26I sites, such that an A at nucleotide 94 produced fragments of 122 and 80 bp, while a G at nucleotide 94 produced fragments of 122, 54 and 26 bp (Fig. 3). It was found that all alleles containing an A at nucleotide 124 also contained an A at nucleotide 94. Thus all double heterozygotes were of genotype A94A124/G94G124 and the fourth possible variant, G94A124, was not present in our control population.

Based on this data, three variants of GSTZ1 were designated GSTZ1*A, GSTZ1*B and GSTZ1*C in accordance with the proposed nomenclature for allelic GST gene variants (Mannervik et al., 1992). GSTZ1*A refers to pGSTZ1, which has an A at both variant positions (A94A124) (Board et al., 1997).

GSTZ1*B differs from GSTZ1*A by having an A to G transition at nucleotide 124 (A94G124) while GSTZ1*C differs from GSTZ1*B by having an A to G transition at nucleotide 94 (G94G124). The frequencies of the alleles Z1*A, Z1*B and Z1*C in the control population were determined (Table 2). Chi-squared analysis of these alleles indicated there is significant linkage disequilibrium between the two loci (P  < 0.005), caused by the absence of the fourth variant. The frequency of the three alleles is in agreement with that expected in a Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

The nucleotide variations identified at positions 94 and 124 are both non-synonymous, and thus result in variation of the amino acids encoded by codons 32 and 42, respectively, in the three alleles as follows:Z1*A Lys32, Arg42;Z1*B Lys32, Gly42;Z1*C Glu32, Gly42. The three variant proteins corresponding to the three identified alleles were expressed in E. coli and purified to investigate their activity towards a range of GST substrates. The activities of the enzymes towards dichloroacetate and several other α-haloacids were investigated (Table 3).

There was no difference in activity between GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c, however, the activity of GSTZ1a-1a was markedly different from GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c towards four of the five α-haloacids tested. GSTZ1a-1a possessed higher activity towards dichloroacetate (3.6-fold) and R-2-chloropropionate (3.8-fold), and lower activity towards fluoroacetate (0.26-fold) and S-2-chloropropionate (0.3-fold). All three proteins possessed similar activity towards chlorofluoroacetate. For comparison, the activity of purified rat liver GST Zeta towards these substrates, as reported by Tong et al., 1998b, is also included in Table 3. The activity of GSTZ1a-1a towards R-2-chloropropionate and dichloroacetate was higher than rat GSTZ (3.5- and 1.6-fold, respectively), while GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c possessed very similar activity towards R-2-chloropropionate. In all other cases, the rat enzyme was more active than the human enzymes with 2–8-fold the activity of GSTZ1c-1c. Interestingly, human GSTZ1 enzymes showed higher activity towards the R enantiomer of 2-chloropropionic acid while activity of rat GSTZ1 was greater with the S-enantiomer (Tong et al., 1998b).

Activity of human GSTZ1 was previously observed towards the substrates ethacrynic acid, 7-chloro-4-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazole and p-nitrophenyl acetate (Board et al., 1997).

Comparing the variant proteins, GSTZ1a-1a possessed higher activity towards ethacrynic acid and 7-chloro-4-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazole compared with GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c, while there was no difference between the three enzymes towards p-nitrophenyl acetate (Table 3). The activities towards these substrates were much lower than for dichloroacetate. No activity was detected for the variant proteins towards 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, 1,2-dichloro-4-nitrobenzene, trans-non-2-enal, trans-oct-2-enal, trans,trans-deca-2,4-dienal, and 1,2-epoxy-3-(4-nitrophenoxy)propane.

Discussion
As our appreciation grows of the subtle contributions many genes can make to complex genetic disorders and disease susceptibility, a systematic approach to discovering polymorphisms and understanding their consequences is required. This study has demonstrated how analysis of the human EST database can be used to facilitate the identification and investigation of genetic polymorphisms in enzymes and proteins of physiological interest.

This approach provides a convenient first step in the detection of variant alleles compared to previous approaches, which have depended on isolating clones of interest from cDNA libraries of many individuals (Ali-Osman et al., 1997) or on the observation of phenotypic differences between individuals (Board, 1981;Seidegard et al., 1988;Blum et al., 1991;Pemble et al., 1994).

The availability of sequence information in the human EST database for any given cDNA will depend on the tissue expression patterns of the gene, the stability of the mRNA and the size of the cDNA. For each clone, the sequence data are incomplete because they are sequenced from the ends only. However, as the ESTs vary in length at the 5′ end, this sequence information may extend considerably into the centre of the cDNA of interest. GSTZ1 is very widely expressed, resulting in a large number of ESTs being identified from different libraries by the BLAST search. The 5′ and 3′ ends of the 1162 bp cDNA were represented by 25 and 34 ESTs, respectively.

The least well represented portion of the cDNA, a 200 bp region around nucleotides 400–600 of the coding sequence, was present in eight EST sequences, thus keeping open the possibility of identifying common variable nucleotides in this region. In the case of GSTZ1, this information was sufficient to detect the nucleotide 124 polymorphism, which occurred at a frequency of only 9% in controls. Since the EST database is accumulating partial cDNA sequences from an increasing number of individuals, it is clearly a valuable tool for the investigation of genes where there is some expectation of polymorphism.

Many members of the GST gene family have been found to be polymorphic in human populations, thus when the human GSTZ1 cDNA was characterized, the possibility of variants of this gene occurring was considered. Examination of the EST sequences for GSTZ1 revealed two sites which are variable in numerous clones. Development of PCR/RFLP methods and population analysis of the variant nucleotides have shown that the variations identified in the EST database are genuine polymorphisms, and that the three alleles identified are present at significant frequencies in the Australian European population.

The three alleles characterized have been designated GSTZ1*A, GSTZ1*B and GSTZ1*C.

The investigation of the activities of the recombinant proteins encoded by these alleles indicates that GSTZ1a-1a has different catalytic properties from GSTZ1b-1b and GSTZ1c-1c (Table 3). Thus, while the Glu32 to Lys substitution has little effect on protein activity, the Gly42 to Arg alters enzyme function considerably. Molecular modelling of the N-terminal domain of GSTZ1 was performed when the protein was originally characterized (Board et al., 1997). Based on the Lucilia cuprina GST structure, it was predicted that residue 32 would not interact directly with the active site. The enzyme activities presented here support that prediction, as the substitution of a 4-carbon, positive residue for a 2-carbon, negative residue made little difference to enzyme activity towards the diverse range of substrates tested.

The effect of the Gly42 to Arg substitution was not predictable from the molecular modelling as residue 42 fell in the β2 to α2 loop region which varies significantly in the solved GST structures (Board et al., 1997).

The results in Table 3 suggest that residue 42 influences the active site, with the Gly42 to Arg substitution resulting in higher activity towards dichloroacetate, R-2-chloropropionate and lower activity towards fluoroacetate and S-2-chloropropionate. The arginine residue introduces both a positive charge and a much larger side chain, factors which may contribute to both the electrostatic interactions and the architecture of the active site. It is interesting to compare the enantioselectivity of the human and rat enzymes towards 2-chloropropionate, with the relative activities of GSTZ1a-1a, GSTZ1b-1b and rat (Tong et al., 1998b) being R  > S, R  ∼ S, R  < S, respectively, suggesting that the active site of the rat enzyme has features different from both GSTZ1a-1a and GSTZ1b-1b.

GSTZ1 has been demonstrated to have activity towards both xenobiotic and endogenous substrates. GSTZ1 was identified as the major enzyme in rat liver responsible for the metabolism of dichloroacetate (Tong et al., 1998a), a compound which has therapeutic applications but is also hepatocarcinogenic in rodents (Stacpoole, 1989;Bull et al., 1990;DeAngelo et al., 1996). The discovery of genetic variants in GSTZ1 which have variable ability to metabolize this compound may be important in understanding the clinical efficacy and toxicity of this compound.

GSTZ1 has also been identified as maleylacetoacetate isomerase, converting maleylacetoacetate to fumarylacetoacetate in the catabolism of aromatic amino acids (Fernandez-Canon & Penalva, 1998). In the absence of readily available maleylacetoacetate, we have been unable to investigate the activity of these variant enzymes towards the endogenous substrate. While many diseases, including alkaptonuria and phenylketonuria, have been identified where a complete block in this metabolic pathway occurs, it is not known what the consequences of a partial block or altered flux through this pathway may be. Accumulation of maleylacetoacetate, fumarylacetoacetate and their reduced counterpart succinylacetoacetate are thought responsible for the pathology of hereditary tyrosinemia type 1, a severe genetic disease resulting from complete lack of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, although the mechanism by which these metabolites are toxic is not well understood (Tanguay et al., 1996). The use of the EST database to find novel genetic variations opens the opportunity to investigate the consequences of subtle variations in enzyme activity which may not have been discovered by phenotypic approaches for the discovery of genetic variation.
